## d0002-s2-sparse-copy-symlink — Sparse remote fetch fallback follows dependency-controlled symlinks while copying

### Source

- Attacker-controlled remote Git repository selected as a sparse monorepo package source
- A malicious remote Git subtree can contain tracked symlinks with absolute or checkout-escaping targets.
- A sparse remote Git source contains an escaping symlink selected into the checkout.
- Malicious remote package repository commits a symlink inside a selected member to an absolute host file/directory or escaping relative target.
- A malicious remote dependency repository containing a symlink in a sparsely checked-out member.
- Symlink entries committed in an attacker-controlled remote monorepo member.

### Privileged boundary

- Remote repository tree to developer filesystem/package cache and package build inputs
- The package fetcher crosses from untrusted repository contents into the developer's same-user host filesystem and trusted source cache.

### Closest control

- Package validation rejects symlinks after materialization, but the cross-filesystem copy fallback follows them and converts their targets into ordinary copied files or directories first
- The checkout is sparse, but `copy_tree` uses `Path::is_dir`, `std::fs::copy`, and `std::fs::metadata`, all of which follow symlinks; it never uses `symlink_metadata` or a no-follow open.
- Package source validation rejects symlinks only after publication; the fallback copier has already dereferenced them into ordinary files.
- Sparse checkout limits tracked paths, but git preserves symlinks and copy_tree uses following metadata; no no-follow or canonical-root enforcement.
- Later validate_core_source_tree rejects symlinks, but the copy fallback dereferences them before that validation.
- Sparse checkout constrains tracked paths, but copy_tree classifies and copies the materialized filesystem objects with symlink-following APIs.

### Sink or broken control

- copy_tree uses is_dir and std::fs::copy on symlink paths
- When rename from the OS temp directory to the source cache fails (notably across filesystems), `copy_tree` recursively dereferences symlinked directories and copies symlinked file targets as regular cached files.
- When the temp and cache paths cannot be renamed across filesystems, copy_tree reads the symlink target and publishes its contents to the source cache.
- Recursive copy reads symlink targets outside the checkout and materializes their contents into package cache.
- copy_tree uses following metadata/is_dir and std::fs::copy on dependency-controlled entries.
- copy_tree can copy bytes or recursively traverse a symlink target outside the checkout into the trusted package source cache.

### Impact

- Copies readable host file or directory contents into the source cache and potentially into a package realization, disclosing or incorporating host data
- A malicious package source can copy developer-readable host files or directory trees into the package source cache, where later build/package logic can consume or disclose them.
- A remote package source can cause victim-local files to be copied into an otherwise validated package tree and consumed by later build/package operations.
- Host file disclosure into attacker-influenced build/cache inputs, unbounded copying of host directories, or recursion through symlink cycles during package fetch.
- Reading and materializing host files reachable from a dependency symlink into the source cache/package flow.
- Disclosure and cache materialization of arbitrary readable host files, recursive traversal outside the checkout, or resource exhaustion.

### Impact path

- Remote repo -> sparse checkout -> cross-filesystem rename fallback -> symlink-following recursive copy -> host file read.
- remote Git symlink -> sparse checkout temporary tree -> rename failure -> copy_tree symlink follow -> cache regular file/tree

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Centralized validation should confirm Git checkout preserves the relevant symlink in sparse mode and force EXDEV to demonstrate post-copy validation bypass.
- Validation should force EXDEV between temp and cache roots and test file- and directory-valued symlink targets.
- The cross-filesystem fallback depends on deployment layout; validate a concrete cache/temp arrangement and downstream read primitive.
- Later source-tree validation and actual filesystem layout determine exfiltration route; copy-time out-of-root read is direct.
- Requires environment with a cross-filesystem temp/cache boundary; validate cleanup and later exposure.
- Candidate-local review did not dynamically force EXDEV; centralized validation should reproduce on split filesystems and confirm Git checkout symlink behavior.

### Preconditions

- Sparse monorepo path is selected
- Temp and cache rename fails, commonly across filesystems
- Symlink target is readable
- Sparse member fetch is selected
- Rename from system temp to cache fails across filesystems
- Checked-out sparse tree contains a symlink to a readable host path
- Subsequent package use includes the copied material
- Sparse monorepo fetch succeeds and cache publication uses the copy fallback; the referenced host path exists and is readable.
- Sparse checkout is used.
- The rename from temporary checkout to cache fails, commonly because the paths are on different filesystems.
- The symlink target exists and is readable.
- Sparse member path selected
- Rename from temp to cache fails (commonly cross-filesystem)
- Host symlink target exists and is readable
- Victim fetches an attacker-controlled sparse monorepo and rename(tmp, cache) fails, commonly when temporary and cache directories are on different filesystems; symlink target is readable.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Requires cross-filesystem rename fallback
- Malicious remote source is untrusted
- Later symlink rejection is defeated because the copy changes file type
- Remote dependency authors control Git symlink entries.
- The later validator cannot distinguish the dereferenced regular file.
- Attacker controls remote tree entries
- Host read is limited to victim account permissions
- Fallback requires rename failure

## s0-devserver-unbounded-header-line — Devserver accepts unbounded HTTP request and header lines

### Source

- Bytes from a local TCP client connected to the devserver.
- A local network client connecting to the loopback-only jet dev HTTP listener and withholding line terminators or streaming oversized headers.
- A local network client controls the request line and headers.
- A local attacker opens many loopback TCP connections and slowly supplies or withholds header terminators.

### Closest control

- Content-Length is capped at 1 MiB only after all header lines are read; there is no request-line, header-line, aggregate-header, connection-count, or read-timeout bound in this path.
- The 1 MiB Content-Length check applies only after all headers have been read; no read deadline, line/header byte ceiling, header-count ceiling, or connection concurrency bound exists.
- Body length is capped, but header allocation and blocked per-connection threads are not.
- The parser caps only body length at 1 MiB; there is no request-line limit, cumulative header budget, header count, read deadline, or connection/thread bound.
- Request bodies are capped at 1 MiB.

### Sink or broken control

- Unbounded BufRead::read_line allocation for request metadata.
- Blocking, unbounded BufRead::read_line allocation in a dedicated thread for every accepted connection.
- BufRead::read_line grows String buffers until newline or EOF, and serve_forever creates one thread per connection.
- There is no header byte/count cap, socket read deadline, or connection/thread limit before spawning one thread per connection.

### Impact

- A client can consume memory and worker threads, reducing or terminating devserver availability.
- A malicious local process can consume threads and memory until the developer process becomes unavailable or is terminated.
- Memory/thread exhaustion and denial of the long-lived dev-server process.
- A local attacker can consume unbounded memory/threads and stall or terminate the persistent development server.
- Thread and file-descriptor exhaustion causing the development server to hang or fail.

### Impact path

- Connections -> thread::spawn per stream -> blocking BufRead::read_line -> unbounded allocation/threads.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validation should confirm whether TcpStream limits/timeouts are configured outside the shown handler.
- Later validation should calibrate OS thread/socket limits and whether surrounding launch environments impose connection deadlines.
- Loopback exposure lowers severity; browser connection limits may bound a web-only attacker, while a local client is unrestricted.
- Direct remote exposure is prevented by the fixed loopback bind, so severity depends on local/browser reachability.
- The service is loopback-only, so impact is local/developer-session availability rather than remote production availability.

### Preconditions

- A process can connect to the loopback listener and keep sending or withhold delimiters.

- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:39-54` (primary) — Unbounded line reads precede the body-only cap.

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:816-825` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Every accepted connection receives a new thread.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:39-49` (root_control) — read_line appends into unbounded Strings for request and header lines, with no total header/count limit or read timeout.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:50-54` (closest_control) — The 1 MiB check applies only after headers and only to the declared body.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:38-54` (root_control) — Only Content-Length/body is capped; read_line buffers the request line and every header to attacker-selected lengths.

## s0-jit-http-simple-unbounded-response — Simple JIT HTTP client buffers responses without a total cap

### Source

- Response bytes and Content-Length supplied by the remote cleartext HTTP server.
- Bytes and Content-Length supplied by any cleartext HTTP server contacted through the exported JIT HTTP GET or POST functions.

### Privileged boundary

- Remote HTTP peer to JIT process memory.

### Closest control

- Five-second per-read timeout does not cap bytes and is not the canonical total/read policy used by AOT.
- Per-read timeout only; canonical AOT transport and policy are bypassed.
- Socket read/write timeouts limit idle periods only. The canonical implementation bounds response heads and exposes a streaming ResponseBodyReader at crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/HTTP.rs:3566-3604 and 4004-4108.
- A five-second read timeout applies only to an individual stalled read; a peer that sends data steadily can keep resetting progress. No maximum header or response-body size is enforced.

### Sink or broken control

- The complete response is accumulated in a Vec with no maximum body size; absent Content-Length reads continue until EOF, and a peer can keep progress inside the per-read timeout.
- Unbounded Vec growth occurs before parsing the response into JetHTTPResponse.

### Impact

- Remote peer can exhaust memory in long-running JIT/dev execution; behavior also violates security-relevant execution-tier parity.
- Remote memory exhaustion of JIT/dev application and tier-specific security behavior.
- A malicious or compromised HTTP endpoint can exhaust the JIT process memory or keep it consuming memory and time indefinitely.
- Remote denial of service through process memory exhaustion, potentially terminating a long-lived JIT application or service.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Convenience API exposure is clear in lower_ctx; final severity depends on deployment longevity and caller URL control.
- Caller may voluntarily constrain endpoint, but API supplies no hard JIT response bound.
- Operational process limits may contain impact outside the code; validate practical termination behavior under a steadily streaming response.
- Impact is availability-only and may be reduced by an external process/container memory limit. Validate which language-level APIs expose these legacy hosts and whether deployment supervision restarts the process.

### Preconditions

- Safe Jet code is permitted to request an attacker-controlled cleartext HTTP endpoint.
- Jet program runs via JIT/dev
- Program requests attacker-controlled cleartext HTTP endpoint
- POST destination or peer response is attacker-controlled
- Code runs through the JIT basic HTTP host helpers.
- The destination uses cleartext http://.
- The attacker controls or can influence the responding server.
- JIT-compiled application invokes the legacy HTTP GET or POST host function
- Remote cleartext HTTP endpoint is attacker-controlled or compromised
- JIT program issues http.get or http.post to an attacker-controlled or compromised server
- A Jet JIT program is permitted to make HTTP requests
- The destination server is attacker-controlled or compromised

### Severity-relevant facts

- Code runs through the JIT basic HTTP host helpers.
- The destination uses cleartext http://.
- The attacker controls or can influence the responding server.
- A malicious or compromised HTTP endpoint can exhaust the JIT process memory or keep it consuming memory and time indefinitely.
- Uncertainty: Operational process limits may contain impact outside the code; validate practical termination behavior under a steadily streaming response.

- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:900-979` (primary) — Simple HTTP response accumulation is unbounded.

## s0-jit-http-request-unbounded-response — Configurable JIT HTTP request host buffers responses without a cap

### Source

- Response bytes and Content-Length supplied by the remote cleartext HTTP server.
- Bytes and Content-Length supplied by any cleartext HTTP server contacted through the configurable JIT HTTP request API.

### Privileged boundary

- Remote HTTP peer to JIT process memory.

### Closest control

- Request body text has an 8 MiB read bound and socket reads have a five-second idle timeout; neither bounds response memory.
- Socket timeouts do not bound total bytes. The canonical implementation bounds response heads and streams bodies at crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/HTTP.rs:3566-3604 and 4004-4108.
- The request may configure a read timeout, but the implementation hard-codes a five-second per-read timeout and has no cumulative byte, header, or body budget. The 8 MiB limit at lines 1433-1436 applies only to the outbound request body.
- Connect/read/write timeouts bound stalled I/O, but not a peer that continuously sends bytes.

### Sink or broken control

- The request-builder response path accumulates the entire message in memory without a cumulative limit; active streaming defeats the idle timeout.
- Unbounded response bytes are appended to buf before conversion into JetHTTPResponse.
- The JIT host accumulates the full response in process memory without bounding declared length, received body size, or total allocation.

### Impact

- Remote memory exhaustion or debug-build arithmetic panic in JIT/dev applications.
- A malicious or compromised HTTP endpoint can exhaust memory or indefinitely consume JIT process resources.
- Remote denial of service through process memory exhaustion in JIT applications using the newer request builder/sender API.
- Remote memory exhaustion and process crash, especially in developer or long-running JIT services that contact attacker-controlled endpoints.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Overflow outcome differs by build profile; unbounded buffering does not.
- Operational process limits may contain impact outside the code; validate practical termination behavior under large declared and chunkless streaming responses.
- Availability severity depends on application longevity, endpoint trust, and external memory limits. Validate language-level exposure and expected response-size semantics.
- Allocator/process limits eventually terminate growth; practical severity depends on embedding context and any caller-level response-size policy.

### Preconditions

- Safe Jet code invokes the configurable cleartext request API against an attacker-controlled endpoint.
- Jet program uses generic HTTPRequest.send in JIT/dev
- Remote response is attacker-controlled
- Code runs through the JIT request-builder host function.
- The destination uses cleartext http://.
- The attacker controls or can influence the responding server.
- JIT-compiled application sends a configurable cleartext HTTP request
- Remote endpoint is attacker-controlled or compromised
- JIT program sends a structured request to an attacker-controlled or compromised cleartext HTTP endpoint
- A Jet JIT program uses HTTPRequest.send against an attacker-controlled or compromised server
- JIT-compiled code sends a cleartext HTTP request to an attacker-controlled or compromised server.
- The server continuously sends a sufficiently large response.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Code runs through the JIT request-builder host function.
- The destination uses cleartext http://.
- The attacker controls or can influence the responding server.
- A malicious or compromised HTTP endpoint can exhaust memory or indefinitely consume JIT process resources.
- Uncertainty: Operational process limits may contain impact outside the code; validate practical termination behavior under large declared and chunkless streaming responses.

## s0-bash-prompt-label-injection — Project prompt label is embedded unescaped in generated Bash startup code

### Source

- Attacker-controlled env.jet prompt label containing a single quote followed by shell syntax
- Project env.jet prompt.label string (and the legacy prompt label path)
- A malicious repository controls env.jet prompt text, including command substitutions for Bash/Zsh or quote/newline payloads that break Fish initialization syntax.
- An attacker-controlled project env.jet file supplies the prompt label used when entering the environment.
- Attacker-controlled prompt directive in a malicious project's env.jet.

### Closest control

- Environment trust gating occurs, but the call shown omits label from its explicit authority inputs; no sink-side quoting or label character validation exists.
- Jet parsing requires a string value but performs no Bash quoting or character restriction.
- The evaluator enforces only that the label is a quoted string; the project trust prompt is the nearest broader boundary, and no shell-context escaping occurs.
- External packages, secrets, and lifecycle facts are trust-gated, but prompt text is neither escaped for each shell nor included in trust sensitivity/hash calculations.
- The generated startup script is intentionally shell code, but the label is inserted inside single quotes without shell escaping or validation.
- Project trust gating covers declared refs, secrets, and environment behavior, but the prompt label is not escaped for shell source and can be present without other trust-sensitive declarations.

### Sink or broken control

- Bash parses the generated rcfile and executes injected statements while entering the environment.
- Generated bash rc file executed by bash --rcfile -i
- Generated shell startup programs execute the unescaped label when jet env enters Bash, Zsh, or Fish.
- bash_rc formats Env.label directly into PS1 assignments that are sourced by Bash.
- bash_rc inserts label verbatim into executable rc text; a single quote terminates PS1 and permits arbitrary shell syntax when Bash sources the file.

### Impact

- Host command execution under the developer account during jet env shell entry/activation, potentially after an earlier trust grant if prompt is not covered by the grant identity.
- Opening an attacker-controlled Jetpack environment can execute commands with the developer's privileges.
- Command execution with the privileges and environment of the developer entering the project shell.
- Opening an interactive Jet environment in an untrusted repository can execute arbitrary commands as the developer.
- Entering a malicious project environment can execute arbitrary shell commands with the developer's privileges.
- Arbitrary command execution as the developer when entering the project environment with Bash.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- The broader trust engine may hash the entire env.jet file outside the explicit parameters seen here; dynamic validation should establish whether prompt-only edits re-prompt. Sink injection itself is direct.
- Static interpolation is direct. Central validation should confirm the exact env.jet literal syntax and whether project trust is considered to authorize arbitrary host command execution.
- The exact payload differs by shell; runtime PoCs should validate quoting and prompt expansion on supported versions.
- The generated rc is sourced as shell syntax, so a label containing a quote and command syntax is expected to break out; validation should exercise the exact generated quoting.
- Validation should use a harmless marker payload and confirm the minimal prompt-only project does not trigger a prior trust prompt.

### Preconditions

- User invokes jet env/auto-activation for an attacker-influenced project; exploitability without a fresh prompt depends on trust-hash coverage.
- The victim runs the Jet environment-entry workflow for an attacker-controlled checkout and uses Bash.
- Victim enters the environment using Bash and the project/environment definition is attacker-controlled or compromised.
- Victim trusts/enters the attacker-influenced project environment
- Bash is selected
- Label contains Bash-breaking quote/newline syntax
- Victim runs jet env/enter in an attacker-controlled repository
- Selected shell evaluates the generated startup program
- Victim invokes jet env in an attacker-controlled project, Bash is detected/selected, and the malicious prompt uses quote-breaking shell syntax.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:364-432` (primary) — Unescaped project label enters single-quoted Bash PS1 source.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:364-432` (mirrored worktree) — Same Bash rc generator in the worktree copy.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/EnvFile.rs:53-61,188-194` (attacker_source) — env.jet prompt is parsed as an unrestricted string and returned verbatim.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/CLI/realize.rs:568-577,597-652` (flow) — Legacy and typed plans copy the prompt string into RunPlan.label.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:669-683` (closest_control) — Trust gate receives refs/table/secrets/environment but not plan.label, so label changes are not visibly bound to this control.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:257-263,364-435` (sink/bash) — Label is interpolated unescaped inside single-quoted PS1 assignments in a sourced bash rc file.

## s0-zsh-prompt-label-injection — Project prompt label is embedded unescaped in generated Zsh startup code

### Source

- Attacker-controlled prompt label containing quote-breaking Zsh syntax
- Project env.jet prompt.label string (and the legacy prompt label path)
- An attacker-controlled project env.jet file supplies the prompt label used when entering the environment.
- Attacker-controlled prompt directive in a malicious project's env.jet.

### Closest control

- The module evaluator enforces string type only; no Zsh literal escaping occurs.
- Quoted-string type checking and the project trust prompt; no zsh literal escaping is applied.
- The generated startup script enables prompt substitution but inserts the label in single quotes without shell escaping or validation.
- No Zsh quoting/escaping is applied to label; project trust evaluation does not appear to treat prompt-only content as executable behavior.

### Sink or broken control

- Interactive Zsh parses the generated .zshrc and executes the injected command.
- Generated .zshrc executed after setting ZDOTDIR and starting zsh -i
- zsh_rc formats Env.label directly into PROMPT source evaluated by Zsh.
- zsh_rc formats label into shell source, allowing quote termination and command syntax when .zshrc is sourced.

### Impact

- Entering a malicious environment with Zsh can execute arbitrary commands as the developer.
- Command execution with the privileges and environment of the developer entering the project shell.
- Entering a malicious project environment can execute arbitrary shell commands with the developer's privileges.
- Arbitrary command execution as the developer when entering the project environment with Zsh.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Static interpolation is direct. Central validation should confirm a minimal parser-accepted payload and the intended authority conferred by project trust.
- The generated rc is evaluated as shell syntax; validation should confirm the shortest breakout payload under Zsh's prompt rules.
- Validate both NO_COLOR and colored $'...' branches because Zsh quoting semantics differ, and confirm prompt-only trust behavior.

### Preconditions

- The victim runs the Jet environment-entry workflow for an attacker-controlled checkout and uses Zsh.
- Victim enters the environment with Zsh and consumes an attacker-controlled environment/module.
- Victim trusts/enters the attacker-influenced project environment
- Zsh is selected
- Label contains Zsh-breaking quote/newline syntax
- Victim runs jet env in an attacker-controlled project and Zsh is detected/selected.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:439-472` (primary) — Unescaped project label enters Zsh PROMPT with prompt_subst enabled.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:439-472` (mirrored worktree) — Same Zsh rc generator in the worktree copy.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Eval.rs:490-516` (source) — A module Prompt label accepts any evaluated string.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:264-269,454-473` (sink) — The raw label is inserted into single-quoted PROMPT assignments in a .zshrc that Zsh loads.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Eval.rs:501-515` (unrestricted label source) — Checks only for a quoted string and stores the value verbatim.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Source.rs:320-332` (plan propagation) — Copies the prompt value into the environment plan.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:264-269` (Zsh initialization entrypoint) — Writes zsh_rc output to .zshrc and starts zsh with that ZDOTDIR.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:439-473` (unescaped Zsh sink) — Enables prompt_subst and interpolates label directly inside quoted PROMPT assignments.
- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvFile.rs:57-62,169-194` (source) — Project prompt text becomes the environment label without shell escaping.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs:314-323` (wrapper) — Run-plan label is copied into Env.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:264-269,439-476` (concrete_implementation) — Zsh selection writes generated .zshrc and starts interactive zsh via ZDOTDIR.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:469-472` (sink) — Raw label is interpolated into quoted PROMPT assignments in executable .zshrc.

## s0-fish-prompt-label-injection — Project prompt label is embedded unescaped in Fish startup commands

### Source

- Attacker-controlled prompt label containing a quote and Fish command separator
- Project env.jet prompt.label string (and the legacy prompt label path)
- An attacker-controlled project env.jet file supplies the prompt label used when entering the environment.
- Attacker-controlled prompt directive in a malicious project's env.jet.

### Closest control

- Only the Jet string syntax is checked; the value is not escaped as a Fish literal.
- Quoted-string type checking and the project trust prompt; no Fish literal escaping is applied.
- The generated Fish command string does not quote or escape the label for Fish syntax.
- No Fish string escaping is applied before the label is placed in startup code; label-only input is not visibly included in trust-sensitive project checks.

### Sink or broken control

- fish -C parses the generated initialization program before opening the interactive shell.
- fish -C argument generated by fish_init and executed before the interactive session
- fish_init formats Env.label directly into commands subsequently passed to Fish with `-C`.
- fish_init returns command text containing the raw label, and Shell::enter supplies that text to fish -C.

### Impact

- Entering a malicious environment with Fish can execute arbitrary commands as the developer.
- Command execution with the privileges and environment of the developer entering the project shell.
- Entering a malicious project environment can execute arbitrary shell commands with the developer's privileges.
- Arbitrary command execution as the developer when entering the project environment with Fish.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Static interpolation is direct. Central validation should confirm a minimal parser-accepted payload and the intended authority conferred by project trust.
- The command string is directly parsed by Fish; validation should confirm the exact delimiter payload for the generated form.
- Validation should test Fish quote-breaking syntax and confirm the prompt-only project reaches shell entry without trust approval.

### Preconditions

- The victim runs the Jet environment-entry workflow for an attacker-controlled checkout and uses Fish.
- Victim enters the environment using Fish and the environment definition is attacker-controlled.
- Victim trusts/enters the attacker-influenced project environment
- Fish is selected
- Label contains Fish-breaking quote/statement syntax
- Victim runs jet env in an attacker-controlled project and Fish is detected/selected.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:272,479-505` (primary) — Unescaped project label enters commands parsed by `fish -C`.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:272,479-505` (mirrored worktree) — Same Fish initializer in the worktree copy.
- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvFile.rs:58-61,160-194` (source) — An arbitrary prompt string is loaded from env.jet.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:271-273,479-510` (sink) — The raw label appears in single-quoted Fish command arguments passed directly through fish -C.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Eval.rs:501-515` (unrestricted label source) — Checks only for a quoted string and stores the value verbatim.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Source.rs:320-332` (plan propagation) — Copies the prompt value into the environment plan.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:271-273` (Fish initialization entrypoint) — Passes fish_init output as the -C command string.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:479-507` (unescaped Fish sink) — Interpolates label directly into single-quoted echo/printf arguments in the executed Fish program.
- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvFile.rs:57-62,169-194` (source) — Project prompt text becomes the environment label without shell escaping.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs:314-323` (wrapper) — Run-plan label is copied into Env.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:271-273,479-510` (concrete_implementation) — Fish selection passes generated initialization code through fish -C.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Shell.rs:503-505` (sink) — Raw label is inserted in single-quoted Fish commands.

## s0-web-test-prefix-traversal — Web-test file server uses prefix-only path containment

### Source

- A request containing parent traversal into a sibling whose path shares the root string prefix
- Attacker-selected HTTP request path such as an encoded parent traversal resolving to a sibling whose name shares the configured root prefix.

### Closest control

- normalize removes dot segments, but the prefix comparison lacks a path-separator boundary and does not resolve symlinks.
- String prefix comparison is incomplete: /a/root2 passes as contained under /a/root.

### Sink or broken control

- createReadStream discloses the escaped file through the loopback HTTP origin.
- createReadStream serves any existing accepted path.

### Impact

- Hostile web content served during tests can same-origin fetch and exfiltrate local sibling files readable by the developer.
- Arbitrary local file disclosure within paths reachable via the sibling-prefix bypass to a client able to request the loopback test server.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Test-only invocation and browser same-origin policy may make practical exfiltration low severity; direct local clients remain possible.

### Preconditions

- The test server is running, a sensitive readable sibling directory shares the served root's string prefix, and the attacker can reach the loopback service.
- A sensitive sibling path shares the document-root prefix, or the served tree contains an outward symlink, and attacker-controlled page content runs in the test browser.
- Browser-test server is running
- Attacker can reach its loopback port and knows/guesses a useful sibling path

### Affected locations

- `scripts/web-test/serve.mjs:27-32,44-55` (primary) — String prefix containment permits root-name-prefixed sibling paths.
- `scripts/web-test/serve.mjs:27-30` (source) — The decoded request path is joined and normalized against a caller-selected document root.
- `scripts/web-test/serve.mjs:30-32` (broken_control) — Containment uses string startsWith(root), so /tmp/site-secret passes for root /tmp/site; symlinks are also not canonicalized.
- `scripts/web-test/serve.mjs:35-55` (sink) — The accepted path is statted and streamed to the HTTP client.
- `scripts/web-test/serve.mjs:27-30` (source) — Request URL is percent-decoded then joined and normalized, allowing encoded parent traversal to resolve into a sibling path.
- `scripts/web-test/serve.mjs:30-32` (root_control) — Containment checks joined.startsWith(normalize(root)) without a path-separator boundary or relative-path validation.
- `scripts/web-test/serve.mjs:43-54` (sink) — The accepted path is statted and streamed to the client.
- `scripts/web-test/serve.mjs:35-56` (entrypoint/wrapper) — HTTP server accepts req.url and listens on 127.0.0.1.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained as a distinct actionable issue because no other supplied candidate had the same remediation-subsuming source/control/sink/impact tuple. ## s1-root-net-file-unbounded — Compile-time file fetch can exhaust memory on an endless special file (root)

### Source

- Attacker-controlled Jet source invokes core.net.fetch with file:///dev/zero and any sha256 string.

### Closest control

- The fetch is sha256-pinned, but digest comparison occurs only after the entire source has been buffered; no impure gate or byte cap applies.

### Sink or broken control

- std::fs::read attempts to read the non-terminating special file into a Vec until allocation failure or process termination.

### Impact

- A malicious dependency or source file can reliably exhaust compiler memory during ordinary compilation without explicit impure authority.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Low on Linux; final validation should run under a strict memory/time limit.

### Preconditions

- Unix-like host exposes /dev/zero or another endless readable special file
- Attacker-controlled source is compiled

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-net/src/lib.rs:144-150` (root_control) — file:// paths are read wholesale with no byte limit
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:769-806` (entrypoint/wrapper) — safe compile-time core.net.fetch reaches jet_net::fetch before validating the supplied digest

## s1-root-net-http-unbounded — Compile-time HTTP fetch buffers an unbounded response before digest verification (root)

### Source

- Remote HTTP(S) server selected by project/comptime source controls response length and chunking.
- Remote server selected by a project core.net.fetch URL, including a compromised endpoint for an otherwise pinned input
- Response bytes from a source-selected HTTP or HTTPS endpoint.
- A remote server selected or contacted through fetch.
- Attacker-selected URL/server response
- A URL supplied to core.net.fetch points to a server that returns an extremely large or endless response body.
- An attacker-controlled project selects an HTTP(S) endpoint whose response body size and transfer behavior are attacker-controlled.
- An untrusted project or dependency supplies a URL whose server returns an arbitrarily large or continuously progressing response.
- Attacker-controlled Jet source points core.net.fetch at an attacker server that streams a large or continuous response.
- An attacker-controlled HTTP(S) server named by Jet source can return or continuously stream a very large body.
- An attacker-controlled URL responds to core.net.fetch with a very large or continuously streamed body.
- An untrusted Jet project selects an HTTP(S) URL for core.net.fetch, and the remote server controls the response stream.
- Malicious project points core.net.fetch at an attacker server that streams a large response.

### Privileged boundary

- Remote network response into the compiler process during compile-time evaluation.

### Closest control

- Network speed and allocator limits affect exploit size; reproduce with fast chunked responder.
- Thirty-second connect/read timeout and SHA-256 verification after complete buffering; neither bounds bytes allocated before verification
- Connect and read timeouts are set, but there is no Content-Length cap, streaming byte budget, or take(limit) guard.
- 30-second connect/read timeouts bound individual stalled reads but do not bound total bytes or total transfer duration.
- Timeouts only bound idle/read calls and SHA validation occurs after the complete allocation.
- Connect and per-read timeouts exist, but no content-length, aggregate-byte, or total-duration limit is enforced.
- Connect and read timeouts exist, but no response-size or decompressed-size budget is enforced in this helper.
- Connect and read timeouts are configured for HTTP(S).
- Connection/read timeouts are configured, but no response-byte ceiling, Content-Length bound, or limited reader is used.
- The 30-second connect/read timeout bounds inactivity, not total transfer size or total duration. SHA-256 verification occurs only after full buffering.
- Connect/read timeouts bound idle time but do not bound total response bytes; a continuously active peer can fill memory before the post-fetch hash check.
- Thirty-second connect/read timeouts and a required SHA-256 pin; the hash is checked only after the entire body is buffered and the timeout does not impose a byte quota.
- Connect/read timeouts are configured, but no maximum response size is enforced.
- Connect and read timeouts bound inactivity, and SHA-256 pins reject incorrect content only after the full body has been accumulated; neither bounds total bytes.
- Thirty-second connect/read timeout and post-download hash; neither limits bytes or aggregate allocation.
- URL scheme checks, a read timeout, and mandatory SHA-256 pin protect transport class, duration, and integrity, but none caps response size before buffering.

### Sink or broken control

- ureq reader is consumed with read_to_end and only read/connect timeouts, with no byte limit or Content-Length cap.
- read_to_end grows an in-memory Vec without a maximum response size
- Unbounded read_to_end of a network response before digest verification.
- read_to_end grows bytes for the entire response.
- `Read::read_to_end` grows a `Vec<u8>` until EOF; neither Content-Length nor streamed bytes are capped.
- The response reader calls read_to_end with no Content-Length policy or streaming byte ceiling.
- `into_reader().read_to_end(&mut bytes)` grows a Vec until EOF before hashing or UTF-8 validation.
- Unbounded response buffering during compilation.
- Read::read_to_end grows bytes without a response-size limit.
- Read::read_to_end grows the response Vec without a maximum.
- Response::into_reader().read_to_end(&mut bytes) grows memory until EOF/error.
- ureq response.into_reader().read_to_end grows a Vec until EOF before eval_net_fetch hashes the bytes.
- Read::read_to_end buffers the entire HTTP response in compiler memory before SHA-256 validation.
- The HTTP body is read_to_end into process memory without a maximum; integrity verification occurs after allocation completes.

### Impact

- Compiler/IDE process memory exhaustion and build denial before SHA-256 verification.
- Compiler/build/CI process memory exhaustion or severe resource consumption before content integrity can be checked
- A large response can exhaust compiler or long-lived build-service memory and availability.
- Memory exhaustion can abort compiler, editor, or long-lived build worker while checking attacker-supplied source.
- Compiler/editor worker memory exhaustion or prolonged denial of service during routine project processing.
- Memory exhaustion and compiler/runtime denial of service.
- A dependency build or CI check can exhaust compiler memory or spend unbounded time receiving data, causing reliable denial of service.
- Compiler/comptime process memory exhaustion from a hostile or unexpectedly large remote response.
- A malicious or compromised fetch endpoint can exhaust memory and terminate the compiler/build process.
- A dependency build can exhaust compiler memory or hold the build worker indefinitely enough to deny service before the content pin can reject it.
- Compiler memory exhaustion or severe resource consumption while compiling an untrusted package/source.
- Compiler or build-worker memory exhaustion and build denial of service before integrity verification.
- Memory exhaustion or severe resource consumption in compiler, IDE, or CI processes.
- A malicious or compromised fetch endpoint can exhaust compiler or CI memory and terminate builds even when its response cannot satisfy the declared digest.
- Reliable memory exhaustion or severe resource consumption in developer and CI compiler processes handling an untrusted project.
- Memory exhaustion and compiler/build-service denial of service while evaluating core.net.fetch.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- SSRF and file:// read semantics are left to sibling-owned comptime source candidate; this candidate covers only unbounded response buffering.
- ureq timeout semantics and host memory limit affect exact exhaustion threshold.
- Validation should measure the HTTP library timeout semantics and identify hosted or long-lived compiler consumers.
- Exact operational severity depends on whether outer compiler invocations impose memory/time limits.
- A one-shot CLI crash is lower impact, but editor/long-lived compiler integrations raise relevance.

- A fixed read timeout may terminate sufficiently slow streams, but a fast peer can allocate large memory before it fires.
- Validation should measure ureq timeout semantics and confirm there is no outer process memory limit.
- External process/container memory limits may contain impact in some deployments.
- Low-to-medium; timeout semantics and achievable allocation rate should be measured during validation.
- Runtime behavior of ureq's per-read timeout should be confirmed, but a finite large response is sufficient to exercise the missing byte limit.
- Runtime/proxy limits may cap some deployments; a bounded local test should measure termination behavior.

- Process memory limit and ureq transport behavior affect exact crash threshold.

## s1-root-studio-remote-read — Non-loopback jetos Studio exposes system projection and config.jet without authentication (root)

### Source

- HTTP GET /studio/source from a remote client when --serve is non-loopback, or a hostile browser origin/local client when loopback
- Unauthenticated GET /studio/source from a peer reaching an explicitly non-loopback --serve address.
- An unauthenticated network peer reaching an operator-selected non-loopback --serve address.
- Any network client that can reach an explicitly non-loopback --serve address requests /studio/source or projection endpoints.
- Unauthenticated request path from a reachable client.
- A browser or local/network process requests /studio/source; DNS rebinding can bypass the browser's cross-origin read barrier on a loopback bind.
- Unauthenticated HTTP GET to /studio/source after an operator supplies a reachable --serve address
- A peer reaches an explicitly exposed Studio listener.
- Any client able to reach the Studio listener; a browser-origin attacker may also attempt loopback access.
- An unauthenticated GET /studio/source request.

### Privileged boundary

- Network caller to developer-owned JetOS Studio process and project files

### Closest control

- Default interactive startup binds 127.0.0.1, but explicit --serve accepts any address and neither path authenticates requests or validates Host/Origin.
- The CLI defaults to 127.0.0.1:0, but serve_studio accepts any supplied address and adds no authentication or origin/session proof after bind.
- The error guidance recommends loopback, but TcpListener::bind accepts arbitrary addresses and the route has no authentication fallback.
- The CLI suggests loopback in an error string, but accepts arbitrary bind addresses and establishes no token, session, or client identity for reads.
- Route only checks that StudioContext exists; it does not check session, token, loopback peer, or origin.
- Interactive mode defaults to 127.0.0.1:0 and explicit --serve is documented with a loopback example.
- The default interactive path binds loopback, but the explicit --serve value is accepted unchanged; the handler has no authentication or caller validation
- The default address is loopback with an ephemeral port; non-default serving and browser origin confusion weaken that boundary.
- No token, peer check, Host, or Origin validation protects the source endpoint.
- The CLI recommends/defaults to loopback but serve_studio does not enforce it or authenticate callers.
- The route requires StudioContext, but does not authenticate the peer or require a loopback bind.
- No authentication, session, or origin control is applied; listener reachability is the only practical boundary.

### Sink or broken control

- std::fs::read(context.config)
- fs_read_for_http(&context.config) returns the complete JetOS project configuration.
- fs_read_for_http of the JetOS configuration followed by an HTTP response.
- fs_read_for_http reads config.jet and projection artifacts into unauthenticated HTTP responses.
- fs_read_for_http returns raw selected config file bytes.
- The route reads context.config and returns its bytes without Host, Origin, or capability validation.
- fs_read_for_http(&context.config)
- The HTTP handler ignores Host, Origin, and authorization, then returns context.config bytes.
- fs_read_for_http returns config.jet over HTTP.
- The request path directly reads and returns the project config source.
- fs_read_for_http reads config.jet and the response returns its contents.
- fs_read_for_http reads context.config and returns the full config.jet body.

### Impact

- Disclosure of the active JetOS config, including host/environment structure and any inline sensitive values, to an unauthorized HTTP client.
- Disclosure of project and system configuration, which may reveal host layout, providers, services, and other sensitive deployment facts.
- Disclosure of project and system configuration, including deployment topology and service/package settings.
- Disclosure of JetOS configuration, services, packages, options, host metadata, and project source to LAN/tailnet peers.
- Disclosure of project or JetOS configuration source, including topology and referenced secret/config names.
- Disclosure of JetOS configuration source, including host and deployment intent contained in config.jet.
- Disclosure of config.jet and associated Studio metadata to any caller that can reach the selected address
- Disclosure of the user's JetOS configuration and its revision/context to a remote web attacker.
- Disclosure of system/project configuration and potentially sensitive operational details.
- Disclosure of JetOS project configuration/source to an unauthorized client.
- Disclosure of project configuration, including potentially sensitive topology, provider, deployment, or environment metadata present in config.jet.
- A remote peer can obtain system configuration, host/package choices, paths, and potentially sensitive deployment details.

### Impact path

- network GET /studio/source -> unauthenticated handler -> fs_read_for_http -> response bytes

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- No dynamic request was sent; candidate-local evidence is a complete static route-to-read trace.

## s1-root-studio-remote-write — Unauthenticated non-loopback Studio clients can mint sessions and overwrite config.jet (root)

### Source

- Any local client, or remote client when --serve binds non-loopback, requests op:session then stages and applies an edit using returned session/token.
- Unauthenticated HTTP client obtains a session, stages set-option changes, then sends op=apply
- Unauthenticated JSON bodies sent to POST /studio/transaction by a network peer.
- Any network client reaching Studio, which first requests op=session and then stages/applies its own changeset.
- A network peer able to reach a non-loopback JetOS Studio listener and request its own session identifier.
- A remote network client requests an unauthenticated Studio session, stages set-option edits, and submits the returned changeset token to apply.
- HTTP request body from any process that can reach the Studio listener.
- Remote HTTP transaction body
- Attacker-controlled Studio transaction JSON after minting a server session and reading the staged changeset response through same-origin reachability.
- Unauthenticated HTTP clients can first mint a session and then submit stage/apply transaction operations
- A reachable client can request op=session, stage set-option values, and apply the resulting changeset. A browser can potentially do this after DNS rebinding because Host is ignored.
- Any client that can reach the Studio listener supplies JSON operations; a browser-origin client can first request op=session.
- A network client able to read and write HTTP responses to the Studio listener.
- An unauthenticated client reaching POST /studio/transaction.

### Privileged boundary

- Network caller to developer project source integrity

### Closest control

- Default automatic bind is loopback; explicit --serve can widen exposure.
- Changeset ownership and source revisions prevent concurrency mistakes but do not distinguish an authorized UI from an arbitrary HTTP client because session creation is public.
- A server-issued session and changeset token protect sequencing/concurrency, but the session mint operation is itself unauthenticated and therefore supplies no authorization boundary.
- Server-issued session and changeset-owner tokens are self-service and unauthenticated, so they do not distinguish the operator from an attacker.
- Session, changeset token, file identity, and revision checks prevent cross-session races and lost updates, but the session itself is issued without authenticating the requester.
- Session and revision tokens provide concurrency ownership, not authentication; any caller can mint the initial session.
- Session ownership checks exist, but the same unauthenticated endpoint grants sessions to arbitrary callers; no user identity, secret, or origin is bound.
- Changesets require a server-issued session and revision match, but both are available to the same unauthenticated client.
- The workflow requires a server-issued session, changeset token, and source revision.
- A server-issued session is required after the session operation, but the same unauthenticated caller can mint that session
- Sessions, changeset ownership tokens, revision matching, and file locks prevent races, but the server issues the initial session to every requester and has no network authority check.
- Session IDs, change-set tokens, and base revisions prevent stale/cross-session application but not unauthorized session creation.
- Changeset token, revision, and ownership bind workflow consistency to the anonymously minted session, not to a trusted user.
- Revision, file-lock, and changeset-token checks protect concurrent integrity but the token is issued to unauthenticated callers and is not an authorization credential.
- Transaction session identifiers coordinate edits but are issued anonymously and are not an authentication boundary.
- A server-issued session and changeset ownership check exist, but the server issues the credential to unauthenticated callers, so the check proves continuity rather than authorization.
- Mutation requires a server-issued session ID and changeset ownership tokens, but unauthenticated op=session issues the initial credential to any caller.

### Sink or broken control

- Session proves only that caller contacted the unauthenticated endpoint; it is not bound to user/browser origin.
- atomic_write_studio_source_if_revision writes the staged source to config.jet
- set-option stages raw key/value text and apply atomically replaces config.jet.
- atomic_write_studio_source_if_revision persists attacker-selected supported config changes.
- The server-issued session establishes changeset ownership but not caller identity; the same unauthenticated peer can stage raw key/value source fragments and apply them to config.jet.
- atomic_write_studio_source_if_revision persists the attacker's configuration transaction over config.jet.
- studio_changeset_apply atomically replaces config.jet after attacker-controlled set-option staging.
- The server has no authentication or request-origin enforcement; the session token is issued to any requester and therefore provides concurrency ownership, not identity.
- Session issuance itself is unauthenticated, and the service has no trusted-origin or user-authorization boundary; apply atomically replaces config.jet.
- atomic_write_studio_source_if_revision renames attacker-selected staged source over config.jet
- An unauthenticated server-issued session authorizes atomic replacement of the project config.jet.
- Session and change-set tokens establish request consistency but are freely issued without caller authentication; apply reaches an atomic config write.
- The server-issued session is the only auth-like control, but any caller can mint one anonymously.
- atomic_write_studio_source_if_revision writes the project config after attacker-controlled set-option staging.
- The unauthenticated caller can request a session, stage set-option operations, and apply them to the source file.
- studio_changeset_apply writes attacker-selected option changes to config.jet.
- The caller can stage a set-option changeset and apply it through atomic_write_studio_source_if_revision, replacing config.jet.

### Impact

- Unauthorized config.jet modification under Studio user account.
- Unauthorized persistent modification of JetOS configuration, enabling follow-on builds or activation of attacker-selected settings.
- Remote durable modification of project/system configuration; newline-bearing values may inject arbitrary configuration/source statements later consumed by JetOS build and switch operations.
- Unauthorized modification of JetOS configuration, affecting later plan, build, proof, and switch workflows.
- An unauthorized network peer can persist attacker-chosen source fragments into the project's config.jet, corrupt configuration, alter system options, and potentially influence later privileged build/proof workflows.
- Unauthorized modification of system source, potentially influencing later privileged builds or switches.
- Unauthorized mutation of the selected JetOS/project configuration, followed by projection rebuild.
- A remote unauthenticated client can stage and persist attacker-selected project configuration changes, which can influence later builds or system operations.
- Modification of the active JetOS project configuration with the developer's filesystem authority.
- Persistent unauthorized modification of JetOS project configuration under the developer account
- Project configuration can be modified, affecting later builds, proofs, and generation activation.
- Unauthorized persistent modification of JetOS system configuration source.
- Unauthorized persistent config.jet option changes after stage/apply workflow completion.
- Unauthorized persistent project/system configuration mutation under developer privileges.
- Unauthorized modification of project/operating-system configuration, potentially preparing later privileged actions.
- Unauthorized persistent modification of project configuration and subsequent influence over builds, providers, workloads, or deployment behavior.
- A network peer can modify OS configuration source, leading to attacker-chosen configuration being built or activated later.

### Impact path

- POST op=session -> receive session id -> POST staged edit -> POST apply -> atomic source write

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate complete session→set-option→apply sequence on disposable config.
- Exact option semantics vary; the unauthorized write primitive is statically established.
- The exact grammar-level power of injected key/value text requires validation, but authorized remote file modification exists even with well-formed option values.
- Edits are structured and staged; validation should exercise a meaningful supported option and confirm apply through a fresh attacker-created session.
- The documented deployment is loopback-oriented; validate whether non-loopback --serve is supported/expected and which injected option/source forms survive subsequent parsing.
- Low; validation should use a disposable config.jet and read back the applied change.
- Browser same-origin policy may prevent a cross-origin page from reading the minted session response, but direct local/network clients are unaffected.
- Confirm intended remote-serving support and whether an external authenticated reverse proxy is a documented mandatory precondition.
- Blind CSRF cannot read the session or changeset token, but DNS rebinding and non-browser clients can.
- The complete transaction grammar and a working request sequence were not dynamically exercised.
- Default-loopback exploitation needs browser validation; explicit non-loopback binding does not.
- The supported option set limits arbitrary bytes, but changes can still alter security-sensitive system behavior.
- Validation should perform full session, stage, token extraction, and apply sequence against a disposable config.
- Low: the full session-to-write chain is visible; browser private-network policy may affect cross-site delivery but is not the only attacker path.
- No live transaction sequence was executed.
- Validation should exercise the exact set-option grammar and confirm which security-sensitive options can be changed.
- Validate the full session, set-option, and apply exchange and security relevance of supported keys.

- Studio bound to a reachable non-loopback address
- Project context is present
- Studio is explicitly bound to a reachable non-loopback address.
- A project context/config file is loaded.
- Studio is reachable, especially via a non-loopback --serve address.
- A project context is loaded.
- JetOS Studio is running with project context.
- --serve is bound to a reachable non-loopback address.
- The attacker can read normal HTTP responses to retain the issued session and changeset token.
- Studio is running; attacker is a local process or can directly reach an explicitly non-loopback --serve address.
- Operator starts Studio with a reachable non-loopback --serve address
- JetOS Studio service is running
- The attacker can read responses, e.g. via DNS rebinding, a non-loopback --serve bind, or a malicious local process
- Operator explicitly binds JetOS Studio to a reachable address

- Attacker supplies a valid transaction sequence and current revision
- jetos Studio is running with project context.
- Remote reachability is direct when --serve binds a non-loopback address; browser loopback reachability needs local-network access.
- JetOS Studio is running and reachable from a local process, browser-origin path, or explicitly exposed address.

- The attacker can read the session response, such as a direct LAN/tailnet peer on a non-loopback --serve address

### Severity-relevant facts

- --serve is bound to a reachable non-loopback address.
- The attacker can read normal HTTP responses to retain the issued session and changeset token.
- An unauthorized network peer can persist attacker-chosen source fragments into the project's config.jet, corrupt configuration, alter system options, and potentially influence later privileged build/proof workflows.

## s1-root-studio-remote-run — Unauthenticated non-loopback Studio clients can invoke JetOS build, proof, and switch actions (root)

### Source

- Cross-origin browser or direct client sends JSON action:"check".
- Cross-origin browser or direct client sends JSON action:"plan".
- Cross-origin browser or direct client sends JSON action:"build" while no changeset is staged.
- Cross-origin browser or direct client sends JSON action:"proof".
- Cross-origin browser or direct client sends JSON action:"switch" after a matching proof exists.
- Unauthenticated POST /studio/run requests selecting proof followed by switch
- Unauthenticated JSON action sent to POST /studio/run by a peer reaching the Studio listener.
- An unauthenticated network peer selecting check, plan, build, proof, switch, or generations.
- Any network client reaching an explicitly non-loopback --serve address; browser-origin requests to the default loopback service are a secondary possible source.
- An HTTP POST body from a network peer when --serve is bound beyond loopback, or potentially a cross-origin browser request to a loopback Studio.
- A remote peer submits JSON such as {"action":"build"}, {"action":"proof"}, or {"action":"switch"} to /studio/run.
- Attacker-controlled action in a reachable HTTP POST body.
- Remote HTTP run body
- Attacker-controlled JSON naming an allowlisted Studio action.
- Unauthenticated POST /studio/run choosing a supported action
- A reachable HTTP client chooses action=build.
- A reachable HTTP client chooses action=proof.
- A reachable client requests proof and then switch, or races an existing proved state.
- A direct network client, or a malicious browser page able to POST to the Studio listener.
- An HTTP client sends action=build to POST /studio/run, including a browser targeting loopback or a peer reaching an external --serve bind.
- An HTTP client sends action=proof to POST /studio/run without presenting authority.

## s1-root-studio-loopback-csrf — A malicious website can trigger loopback Studio JetOS subprocess actions via CSRF (root)

### Source

- A malicious web page can issue a simple cross-origin text/plain POST containing JSON to the victim's loopback Studio service; a network peer can do the same when --serve is bound beyond loopback.
- A malicious browser origin or reachable network client can submit proof and later switch actions to /studio/run.
- An attacker website sends a simple no-cors text/plain POST containing JSON to the victim's loopback Studio /studio/run endpoint.
- A malicious web origin can send a CORS-simple text/plain POST containing exact JSON to the Studio listener.

### Privileged boundary

- A web page outside the Studio origin crosses into a local developer service that can execute JetOS lifecycle actions.

### Closest control

- The action name is allowlisted and staged changesets block build/proof, but request authority and browser origin are never established.
- Switch requires a successful proof bound to the unchanged source and generation, but that proof can itself be requested through the same unauthenticated endpoint.
- Transaction endpoints use sessions, but /studio/run does not; SOP blocks response reading but not simple cross-origin POST delivery.
- The transaction endpoint mints and checks sessions, but /studio/run omits that control; the JSON parser does not require application/json and no Origin/Host/CSRF check is made.

### Sink or broken control

- Unauthenticated /studio/run requests reach Command::new(jet) for build/proof operations.
- The server invokes jet os switch --yes without authenticating the requester.
- The unauthenticated action reaches build/proof/switch subprocess execution.
- run_studio_command_target spawns jet os build/proof/switch and supplies --yes for switch.

### Impact

- A web origin or reachable network client can trigger expensive builds and proof generation with the victim's filesystem, package credentials, CPU, disk, and Jet privileges.
- An attacker can activate a new OS generation on the victim system after driving the exposed proof workflow.
- Drive-by resource exhaustion from builds/proofs and possible unauthorized system switching when prerequisites are satisfied.
- A visited website can trigger expensive builds or a system switch using the victim's project and account, potentially exercising privileged JetOS deployment behavior.

### Impact path

- hostile page -> simple text/plain POST -> unauthenticated /studio/run -> action dispatch -> jet os switch --yes/build

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- No runtime browser proof was executed during discovery; validation should confirm current browser private-network request behavior.
- Timing and any downstream elevation prompts need runtime validation.
- Low for triggering check/build-style actions; switch consequences depend on current proof state and privileges.
- Default interactive port is ephemeral and browser Private Network Access behavior varies; explicit --serve examples use a stable loopback port.

### Preconditions

- Victim runs Studio on loopback
- Victim visits attacker-controlled web content
- JetOS project and sibling binary are available
- Victim runs JetOS Studio service
- For remote network exploitation, --serve is bound to a reachable address
- Victim runs Studio with a configuration that can be proved and switched
- Jet process has authority to activate a generation
- Studio is running on a known or discoverable port; browser local-network request policy allows the request; meaningful switch impact may require the victim's normal privilege setup.

### Severity-relevant facts

- No response read is required for the run action
- Switch confirmation is supplied by server code
- Port discovery affects exploitability

## s2-fenced-range-expansion-dos — Numbered fence ranges can exhaust compiler memory

### Source

- Attacker-controlled Jet source containing a numbered fence such as `$[t0..t18446744073709551615]$`.

### Closest control

- Range syntax verifies a shared prefix and ascending endpoints, and endpoint parsing must fit usize.

### Sink or broken control

- The inclusive range is collected without a maximum, then the enclosing statement is copied once per entry.

### Impact

- A malicious source file or dependency can force excessive CPU/allocation or abort the compiler through OOM.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- No dynamic reproduction was performed in discovery; exact failure mode depends on allocator and build profile.

### Preconditions

- Victim parses or checks attacker-controlled Jet source.
- The supplied numeric endpoint fits the platform usize.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-parser/src/FencedNames.rs:411-442` (unbounded range materialization) — Parses usize endpoints then collects every value in the inclusive range with no cardinality limit.
- `crates/jet-parser/src/FencedNames.rs:247-264` (statement-copy amplification) — Uses the expanded fence count to reserve and duplicate the whole statement.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-parser/src/FencedNames.rs:247-264,411-442` (alternate worktree copy) — Byte-identical buildable copy has the same behavior.

## s2-runtime-json-depth-dos — Runtime JSON parser has unbounded recursive nesting

### Source

- Application-controlled or externally received JSON text passed to public core encoding JSON decode/parse APIs.
- Untrusted JSON text supplied to core encoding/auth/data APIs reaches parse_json or parse_json_strict.
- Application-supplied JSON text
- JSON text supplied to AOT/JIT/tier-0 runtime JSON parsing APIs.
- Attacker-controlled deeply nested JSON supplied to the shared runtime JSON codec

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted runtime data to application call stack

### Closest control

- Strict mode rejects duplicate keys only. Foundation protocol JSON separately enforces MAX_JSON_DEPTH=64, but this runtime parser does not use that implementation.
- Syntax and duplicate-key checks exist, while the separate streaming JSON reader enforces max_depth; neither limit is applied to this DOM parser.
- Strict mode rejects duplicate keys but does not constrain bytes or nesting depth.
- The foundation canonical JSON parser enforces `MAX_JSON_DEPTH = 64`, but this canonical std-only runtime parser does not carry or check depth.
- JSONParser records characters, position, and duplicate-key mode but has no nesting-depth budget

### Sink or broken control

- Recursive array/object parsing consumes one native stack frame per nesting level with no maximum depth.
- Recursive container parsing has no maximum nesting depth and can exhaust the native stack.
- Arrays and objects recursively call JSONParser::value without a structural depth ceiling.
- Each nested array/object adds Rust stack frames through `value -> array/object -> value` with no recursion guard.
- value recursively calls array/object, which call value for members

### Impact

- Deeply nested JSON can overflow the process stack and abort a compiled/JIT application or service.
- Deeply nested JSON can crash a native Jet application or worker, causing denial of service.
- Deeply nested JSON can overflow an application thread stack and remotely deny service in callers that expose JSON parsing.
- Deeply nested JSON can overflow the process stack or cause disproportionate parser work, terminating a service.
- Stack exhaustion and process abort in AOT/JIT/tier-0 consumers using the shared codec

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exact crash depth varies with target, thread stack size, and build mode; confirm with a generated nested-array input.
- The precise nesting level needed to overflow depends on target stack size and optimization.
- Confirm emitted AOT/JIT call sites and stack threshold with a representative service.
- Validation should establish the smallest safe nesting cap across supported targets and confirm which generated tiers embed this exact prelude.
- Reachability is application-dependent and trigger depth was not measured.

### Preconditions

- Application parses attacker-controlled JSON with Jet standard-library JSON APIs.
- Input nesting is deep enough to exhaust the runtime stack.
- An application parses attacker-controlled JSON with the DOM parser on an AOT/JIT path.
- A generated application parses attacker-controlled JSON
- A long-lived Jet application parses attacker-controlled deeply nested JSON using the generated runtime.
- A Jet application parses attacker-controlled JSON
- Input nesting is sufficient to exhaust its stack

### Severity-relevant facts

- An application parses attacker-controlled JSON with the DOM parser on an AOT/JIT path.
- Deeply nested JSON can crash a native Jet application or worker, causing denial of service.
- Uncertainty: The precise nesting level needed to overflow depends on target stack size and optimization.
- Shared codec is used across runtime tiers
- Application/network exposure depends on consumer
- Separate from the comptime parser

## s2-comptime-json-depth-dos — Comptime JSON parsing can overflow the compiler stack

### Source

- Jet source, build-time data, or package-supplied text evaluated by comptime/core JSON decoding.
- Untrusted JSON or JSONL records supplied to resident/comptime encoding operations reach JSONInterp::parse_json.
- JSON text evaluated by comptime, REPL, or interpreter execution.
- Attacker-controlled deeply nested JSON parsed at comptime or in the REPL interpreter

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted source/data string to compiler/interpreter call stack

### Closest control

- Trailing-text and syntax checks exist, but no maximum depth or shared Foundation safe parser is used.
- The resident streaming reader has explicit max_depth controls, but this DOM/JSONL helper does not reuse them.
- The foundation canonical JSON implementation uses a 64-level maximum, but this interpreter-specific implementation does not.
- Parser tracks only characters and position; no depth counter or iterative stack bounds recursive arrays and objects

### Sink or broken control

- Recursive array/object parsing consumes compiler/interpreter stack without a nesting cap.
- Recursive parsing has no depth budget and can exhaust the compiler/interpreter thread stack.
- Nested arrays and objects recursively grow the host Rust stack without enforcing depth.
- parse_value recursively calls array/object, which recursively call parse_value

### Impact

- A malicious project or dependency can crash the compiler, REPL, or comptime evaluator during build/check.
- A deeply nested payload can abort compilation, REPL evaluation, interpreter execution, or a deoptimized service path.
- A deeply nested input can abort or stall compiler, REPL, or interpreter processes, including persistent tooling.
- Compiler/interpreter stack exhaustion and process abort on sufficiently nested input

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exact build input reachability depends on evaluated program paths; confirm with a minimal comptime JSON decode fixture.
- The exact externally reachable execution tier and overflow threshold need runtime validation.
- Validation should confirm reachable APIs and calibrate the depth that fails under supported thread stack sizes.
- Trigger depth and process behavior require dynamic validation.

### Preconditions

- Project invokes the comptime JSON decoder on attacker-controlled or package-controlled text.
- Attacker-controlled JSON reaches a resident, comptime, REPL, or interpreter parser path.
- Untrusted JSON reaches a Jet program evaluated in the comptime/REPL/interpreter tier.
- Untrusted code reaches the comptime JSON parse method with a deeply nested valid value
- Platform stack is exhausted before another resource limit rejects the input

### Severity-relevant facts

- Attacker-controlled JSON reaches a resident, comptime, REPL, or interpreter parser path.
- A deeply nested payload can abort compilation, REPL evaluation, interpreter execution, or a deoptimized service path.
- Uncertainty: The exact externally reachable execution tier and overflow threshold need runtime validation.
- Deterministic local compiler availability impact
- No network requirement
- Separate implementation from runtime codec

## s2-comptime-toml-depth-dos — Comptime TOML parsing has unbounded recursive nesting

### Source

- Jet source, build-time data, or package-supplied TOML/YAML evaluated by comptime/core encoding APIs.
- Project/dependency TOML is decoded during compiler or interpreter evaluation.

### Closest control

- Both parsers validate syntax but neither carries a depth counter or delegates to a bounded parser.
- The parser validates syntax but has no maximum nesting depth.

### Sink or broken control

- The resident TOML parser recurses through nested collection values without a maximum depth.
- Arrays and inline tables recursively call value.

### Impact

- A malicious project or dependency can stack-overflow and crash compiler, REPL, or comptime evaluation through TOML input.
- Deep TOML can overflow the compiler/interpreter stack.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate TOML and YAML payloads independently; exact stack threshold and build-path reachability vary.
- Measure exact accepted depth and crash threshold.

### Preconditions

- A project passes attacker-controlled or package-controlled TOML to the comptime decoder.
- attacker-controlled TOML reaches comptime decoding

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/EncodingLite.rs:168-185` (TOML entry point) — Initializes a TOML parser without nesting state.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/EncodingLite.rs:604-617,777-846` (recursive arrays/tables) — Arrays and inline tables call `value()` recursively with no depth limit.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/EncodingLite.rs:168-185,604-617,777-846` (alternate worktree copy) — Byte-identical worktree copy has the same behavior.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/EncodingLite.rs:168-185,460-464,604-617,777-845` (TOML parser) — TOML arrays and inline tables recurse through value without depth accounting. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/TypedDecode.rs:685-686` (Typed decode surface) — Comptime typed TOML/YAML decoding reaches these parsers. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/core_calls.rs:1280-1300` (Core-call surface) — Interpreter core TOML/YAML parse calls reach the same seam. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/EncodingLite.rs:168-185` (entry and parser)
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/EncodingLite.rs:604-617,777-846` (recursive values)

## s2-comptime-yaml-depth-dos — Comptime YAML parsing has unbounded recursive nesting

### Source

- Jet source, build-time data, or package-supplied TOML/YAML evaluated by comptime/core encoding APIs.
- Project/dependency YAML is decoded during compiler or interpreter evaluation.
- YAML text evaluated in comptime, REPL, or interpreter execution.

### Closest control

- Both parsers validate syntax but neither carries a depth counter or delegates to a bounded parser.
- YAMLParser tracks lines, position, and anchors but no depth budget.
- The same file's XML and CBOR decoders enforce configurable depth maxima, but the YAML parser does not.

### Sink or broken control

- The resident YAML parser recurses through nested collection values without a maximum depth.
- Block and flow parsing recurse for every nested value.
- Attacker-selected YAML nesting recursively grows the host Rust stack in both block and flow paths.

### Impact

- A malicious project or dependency can stack-overflow and crash compiler, REPL, or comptime evaluation through YAML input.
- A crafted source/dependency can stack-overflow the compiler or interpreter.
- Deeply nested YAML can terminate or stall compiler and persistent interpreter tooling.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate TOML and YAML payloads independently; exact stack threshold and build-path reachability vary.
- Measure exact recursion threshold.
- Validation should confirm runtime reachability in each tier and identify a parity-preserving cap.

### Preconditions

- A project decodes attacker-controlled or package-controlled YAML at comptime.
- attacker-controlled YAML reaches core encoding during evaluation
- Untrusted YAML reaches core.encoding.yaml while running in the interpreter/comptime tier.

- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/EncodingLite.rs:1003-1023` (YAML entry point) — Begins parsing without a depth budget.
