## s2-devserver-source-disclosure — Loopback devserver exposes project source without Host or session authentication

### Source

- Hostile browser origin using DNS rebinding/private-network reachability, or another local client, requests Canvas read endpoints
- HTTP request from a hostile local client or browser origin reaching the loopback dev server through DNS rebinding
- Any process able to reach the victim's loopback devserver.
- A hostile web origin whose DNS is rebound from an attacker server to 127.0.0.1 while retaining the same browser origin and port.
- Attacker-controlled same-origin DNS name rebinding to 127.0.0.1, or another local process.
- A hostile web origin uses DNS rebinding so its hostname resolves to a running Canvas listener on 127.0.0.1 while preserving browser same-origin access.
- A malicious web origin able to DNS-rebind a hostname to 127.0.0.1 while Jet devserver is running.
- Attacker-controlled HTTP Host/Origin and path from a malicious browser origin that DNS-rebinds its hostname to 127.0.0.1 while `jet dev` is running.
- An HTTP caller chooses the Canvas source endpoint and source_id.
- A browser or local process requests a Canvas source URL; DNS rebinding or origin confusion can make the loopback service same-origin to an attacker page.
- A loopback peer or browser origin after DNS rebinding can issue GET /canvas/source with an optional source_id.
- A hostile website controls a DNS name that first resolves to its server and then to 127.0.0.1 while a developer runs jet dev.
- Loopback HTTP GET with an attacker-selected projected source_id
- Any script executing in the built application's dev-server origin can enumerate open project metadata and fetch projected Jet sources.
- A malicious browser origin can rebind its hostname to the loopback dev server and request Canvas source routes as same-origin resources.
- A malicious web origin can change its DNS answer to 127.0.0.1 and issue same-origin requests carrying the attacker hostname in Host.

### Privileged boundary

- Local HTTP caller to developer project confidentiality

### Closest control

- Loopback binding limits direct remote connections but is not client authentication; Host and Origin are discarded.
- Loopback-only bind; no Host, Origin, nonce, or bearer check is available because headers are discarded
- Binding is loopback-only, but the repository threat model does not treat arbitrary local processes as trusted and no per-session capability protects project data.
- The listener is loopback-only and browser same-origin policy normally blocks an unrelated origin; neither control rejects a same-origin DNS-rebound Host.
- Loopback bind and source_id-to-project resolution limit reach and file set.
- Loopback binding limits direct network clients, but browsers and local processes still cross the boundary; no per-session token is present.
- Loopback binding, method checks, and optimistic revisions limit exposure but do not authenticate a browser origin; Host, Origin, and per-session token checks are absent.
- The listener binds loopback and routes enforce GET/POST, but HTTP headers are not retained and no Host/Origin/token validation occurs.
- Loopback-only bind; insufficient against DNS rebinding because Request::read drops Host/Origin and routes accept any resulting request.
- Loopback binding and SOP are the only barriers; Host/Origin/capability are not checked.
- The listener binds to 127.0.0.1 and source_id is restricted to projected .jet files.
- Source-id resolution confines ordinary reads to projected source roots but no caller, Origin, Host, token, or session is validated
- Source IDs are path-contained, but the server places application assets and privileged Canvas APIs on one origin and performs no client authentication.
- Loopback binding limits direct remote connections, but the HTTP layer does not validate Host or Origin.
- Loopback-only TcpListener binding; it does not prevent browser DNS rebinding and Request drops Host/Origin.
- TCP binding to 127.0.0.1; this limits direct network reachability but does not authenticate browser origins.

### Sink or broken control

- fs::read(source_path) and project_json_for_entry response bodies
- GET project, graph, source-control, proof, and source routes disclose workspace metadata and source bytes
- Unauthenticated fs::read and HTTP return of entry or project source.
- The server neither validates the Host header nor authenticates requests before returning local project source bytes.
- Project source bytes are returned without caller authorization.
- Project metadata and source responses are returned without authenticating Host, Origin, or a session token.
- GET graph/project/source routes return full source and project metadata to any connection.
- GET /canvas/source reads and returns the watched project entry file; related graph/project endpoints expose revisions and project metadata.
- The selected project source path is read and returned verbatim.
- The route returns fs::read(source_path) without checking Host, Origin, or an unguessable session capability.
- fs::read(&source_path) returned as text/plain
- Raw project source bytes are served to an unauthenticated same-origin client.
- The source route calls fs::read and returns project source to the requester.
- GET /canvas/source reads and returns project source with fs::read without authentication or host validation.
- Request parsing drops Host and Origin, and the GET routes return local project source and Git-derived state with no token or origin check.

### Impact

- Unauthorized disclosure of open-project source, topology, revisions, and environment/service metadata.
- Confidential project source, dependency, Git, proof, and runtime metadata disclosure to a less-trusted origin
- A lower-privileged local user or isolated process with host-loopback access can read source files available to the developer process.
- A hostile site may read local Jet project source and the revision material needed to drive write or execution routes.
- Private source code can be disclosed.
- Disclosure of project source, Git diffs/status, project layout, diagnostics, and current revision values that also unlock mutation routes.
- An attacker website can read project source, filesystem/project metadata, and revision values.
- A remote website can potentially read local Jet project source and metadata through DNS rebinding.
- Disclosure of private Jet project source and metadata to a remote website through the victim browser.
- DNS rebinding or a local peer can disclose developer project source and revisions used by mutating routes.
- Disclosure of open-project Jet source and project metadata to a malicious web origin or untrusted local process.
- Private project source and embedded secrets can be read; the returned bytes also reveal revisions/content needed to drive the command and edit routes.
- A remote website can read private project source and source-control state through a browser after DNS rebinding.
- Disclosure of Jet project source and revisions to a hostile local process or a browser-origin attack that can reach the listener
- A malicious frontend dependency or injected application script can read and exfiltrate proprietary source and source-embedded secrets available in projected Jet files.
- Disclosure of proprietary source code and embedded project secrets accessible to the developer.
- Disclosure of active project source to a remote website while jet dev is running; disclosed source and revisions enable follow-on edit/command requests.
- Disclosure of developer source, project structure, revisions, and uncommitted Git changes to a remote attacker.

### Impact path

- attacker origin/rebinding -> GET /canvas/source -> route selection -> fs::read -> HTTP response

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Modern browser private-network controls can reduce some cross-origin paths; no token/Host/Origin defense exists in the server.
- Modern browser private-network controls may reduce browser reachability; same-host clients remain reachable.
- Browser-origin response reading may be constrained by CORS; direct local clients are unaffected.
- Browser DNS cache, local-network-access permission, and rebinding defenses may reduce exploitability in some clients.
- Ordinary cross-origin fetch cannot read response under SOP; exploitation needs rebinding or local client.
- Browser DNS pinning and Private Network Access policy vary, but raw Host acceptance is definite.
- Central validation should test supported browsers, DNS pinning, connection reuse, and private-network controls.
- Browser/DNS rebinding behavior and port discovery need dynamic confirmation.
- Modern browser Private Network Access and DNS-rebinding defenses may block or prompt in some configurations; validation should test supported browsers and response/CORS behavior.
- Modern browser private-network policy can change browser preconditions.
- Browser private-network protections vary, but they do not replace server-side Host/Origin or capability validation and do not constrain malicious local processes.
- Browser exfiltration depends on a same-origin technique such as DNS rebinding; direct local peers can read immediately.
- Browser DNS pinning behavior and port discovery affect reliability; no server-side Host check exists.
- Browser reachability and bind behavior need centralized dynamic validation; a hostile local process is sufficient for the direct path.
- Projected file selection limits the disclosure to indexed Jet source rather than arbitrary host files.
- Validate browser rebinding behavior and enumerate which source identifiers are disclosed without prior graph knowledge.
- Browser DNS cache and rebinding timing vary, but missing Host validation is explicit and ports are a fixed ten-port range.
- Modern browser Private Network Access behavior may add prompts or blocking in some deployments, but it is not an application control and varies by browser/context.

### Preconditions

- Developer runs Jet devserver.
- Victim visits an attacker-controlled site capable of DNS rebinding to the selected loopback port.
- Browser permits the same-origin rebound request.

## s2-devserver-debug-trigger — Unauthenticated devserver endpoint can start project debug execution

### Source

- Same-origin project code, DNS-rebinding browser origin, or direct loopback client submits a debug request with the current revision
- A local loopback client supplying current revision, breakpoints, watches, and debugger commands.
- A hostile page submits a known source revision plus scripted debugger commands, watches, and breakpoints.
- Unauthenticated debug request carrying revision, breakpoints, watches, and commands.
- A malicious browser origin reaching the loopback devserver, including via DNS rebinding.
- Cross-origin browser or local process POST selecting debugger steps/continue commands.
- A caller supplies a Canvas debug POST body.
- Browser or local network caller capable of reaching loopback devserver, including DNS-rebinding origin.
- A local/rebound/same-origin web attacker controls the debug POST body.
- An attacker-controlled page can POST a text/plain JSON debug session request to the local Canvas service.
- A malicious browser page reaching the loopback Canvas server.
- An attacker-controlled origin can submit a simple text/plain POST with a known source revision and debugger inputs.

### Closest control

- Revision and schema validation constrain request shape/freshness but do not authenticate the requester or prove a user gesture.
- The current revision is available from unauthenticated graph/project APIs; no nonce, session token, or origin/peer authorization protects debugger execution.
- Revision and schema checks ensure freshness and shape; InterpreterBoundary rejects features unsupported by the dev interpreter but does not authenticate the requester.
- Current revision and fixed debugger command language restrict the request; they do not prove caller authority.
- Schema and source revision checks validate shape/freshness only.
- Schema and source revision checks validate shape/freshness, not caller authority.
- Debug requests require schema and current source revision, but the revision is disclosed by an unauthenticated graph response.
- Revision and schema checks do not identify an authorized Canvas session.
- Only schema and source revision are checked; caller authority is not.
- Loopback bind only; no Host, Origin, nonce, or bearer validation.
- The route validates schema and source revision but has no origin, token, or user-gesture authorization.
- Debugger command parsing and a loopback listener constrain syntax and network interface, but no origin or capability authorizes the session.
- Schema/revision checks and interpreter feature boundaries constrain input/effects but do not authorize requester.
- The service is loopback-only and checks source revision/schema, but the parser drops Origin and there is no session capability.
- Loopback-only binding and structured debugger commands are the only constraints.
- Revision/schema checks prevent stale requests but do not establish client authority.
- The handler checks schema version and an unkeyed source hash, but does not authenticate the browser origin or require a CSRF token.

### Sink or broken control

- jet_debug::run_session_result executes/debugs the watched source with caller-selected breakpoints, watches, and commands
- Starting and controlling a debugger session that executes project code under victim privileges.
- No authentication or origin validation separates an untrusted loopback POST from execution of the project run function.
- Dedicated debug action starts project debugging without an owner interaction/authentication proof.
- The POST route calls `debug_session_json_for_file`, which forwards attacker commands/breakpoints into `jet_debug::run_session_result` and runs the project session.
- jet_debug::run_session_result executes the watched program under the devserver process.
- Request-selected commands and breakpoints reach run_session_result for the watched project.
- jet_debug::run_session_result executes/interprets watched project.
- debug_session_json_for_file invokes jet_debug::run_session_result for the watched program.
- No caller validation precedes jet_debug::run_session_result and LLDB process creation.
- No request identity/origin check separates hostile input from a debugger session.
- The unauthenticated debug route reaches jet_debug::run_session_result with attacker-selected debugger commands and watches.
- The endpoint authenticates neither browser origin nor user intent before starting a debug session.
- jet_debug::run_session_result loads and interprets the open program.
- The endpoint invokes jet_debug::run_session_result for the victim project and accepts request-selected debugger commands.

### Impact

- Unauthorized debugger/program execution, local/output observation, and compute or effect consumption under developer authority.
- Unauthorized project execution/debugging and resource consumption, potentially triggering side effects in victim code.
- Project logic executes in the developer process context through the dev interpreter, enabling its permitted interpreter effects and resource consumption.
- Attacker can trigger execution of trusted project code and its side effects under developer account.
- Unauthorized project execution/debug control and possible exposure or side effects from debugger command processing.
- Forced program/debug execution, resource consumption, and disclosure of locals, watches, stack, and transcript under DNS rebinding.
- A remote website can potentially trigger project execution and its side effects under the developer's account.
- Unauthorized triggering of program side effects and devserver resource consumption.
- A rebound or local hostile web caller can trigger project execution and side effects.
- Unauthorized caller can execute project behavior and debugger commands with developer process authority.
- An attacker can trigger program evaluation/debug work and associated permitted effects or denial of service under the developer process.
- Unauthorized execution and debugger control of the project under developer authority, with access to process output and debug state.
- Triggers interpreter evaluation and project-specific permitted effects or resource use under the developer process.
- A hostile website can trigger execution/debugging of the developer's current project and drive supported debugger operations.
- Unauthorized program execution and debugger interaction in the developer's local context.
- Unauthorized project execution plus disclosure of locals, backtraces, and program output.
- A hostile page can cause the currently served program to be compiled/run under the debugger and exercise its runtime effects without a user gesture in the Jet UI.

### Impact path

- malicious page -> POST /canvas/debug -> debug request parser -> run_session_result -> compile/run target

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Interpreter/debug effect surface requires centralized validation; impact may be bounded for some program shapes.
- Debugger availability and exact project side effects are environment-dependent.
- Interpreter capability restrictions may make impact lower than the native jet run route, and browser loopback policy varies.
- Debugger behavior and program side effects need runtime confirmation.
- Need validate debugger command authority and whether transcript remains unreadable under SOP.
- Backend availability and platform tooling affect the exact execution path.
- Validation must confirm the debugger backend and observable side effects for a minimal project.
- Effectful program behavior in this interpreter path and browser request delivery need validation.
- Confirm a minimal observable side effect through the selected debug backend.
- Central validation should confirm browser delivery and debugger side effects.
- The interpreter refuses some native/unsafe features, so validate the strongest reachable effect set separately.
- The debugger command whitelist may narrow interaction, but starting the target remains a security-sensitive action.
- Validate browser loopback/Private Network Access behavior and the strongest action-specific runtime effect; static unauthenticated call paths are direct.
- Validate which debugger commands create externally visible effects; project execution itself is the protected action.
- A live debug session was not triggered.
- Programs requiring unsupported native debugging may be rejected.
- Medium: exact debugger effects depend on jet-debug command semantics and browser private-network controls, but starting the served program is the intended sink.

## cd005-comptime-embed-file-symlink — Compile-time embed_file follows project symlinks outside the source root

### Source

- An attacker-controlled project contains an in-tree symlink and calls embed_file on that lexical relative path.
- An untrusted Jet project supplies an embed_file string literal naming a project symlink to a predictable host file.

### Closest control

- Lexical absolute/ParentDir filtering; no canonical containment or symlink policy.
- check_literal_embed_path requires a literal relative path without `..`, but does not reject symlinks or compare the canonical target to canonical base_dir.

### Sink or broken control

- std::fs::read follows the repository symlink to an arbitrary host-readable file.
- std::fs::read follows the symlink and embeds target content in the compiled program/build result.

### Impact

- Host file contents can be embedded into compiler output or diagnostics during compilation.
- A malicious project compiled by a developer or CI can read and embed UTF-8 host secrets outside the workspace, violating the build-input boundary.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Final validation should confirm the exact public method spelling and output observability on each supported host.
- Git/platform symlink preservation and downstream artifact access determine practical exfiltration.

### Preconditions

- Victim compiles an attacker-controlled checkout that preserves symlinks.
- Repository preserves a symlink to a predictable readable host path; target contains UTF-8; build evaluates embed_file.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:304-334` (root_control) — Rejects absolute and lexical parent paths but does not canonicalize or reject symlinks.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:423-465` (filesystem sink) — Joins the relative path to the project base and reads it with std::fs::read.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:1497-1506` (public operation) — Dispatches the independently reachable embed_file method.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:304-334` (Lexical embed path check) — Only absolute paths and lexical ParentDir components are rejected.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:418-465, 1497-1499` (embed_file read sink) — eval_build_time_io uses std::fs::read(base_dir.join(rel)), follows symlinks, and returns UTF-8 bytes as a String.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained as a distinct actionable issue because no other supplied candidate had the same remediation-subsuming source/control/sink/impact tuple. ## cd005-comptime-embed-bytes-symlink — Compile-time embed_bytes follows project symlinks outside the source root

### Source

- An attacker-controlled project supplies an in-tree symlink and calls embed_bytes.
- An untrusted Jet project supplies an embed_bytes string literal naming a project symlink to a predictable host file.

### Closest control

- Lexical path checks do not establish canonical containment.
- check_literal_embed_path requires a literal relative path without `..`, but does not reject symlinks or establish canonical containment.

### Sink or broken control

- The host filesystem read follows the symlink.
- std::fs::read follows the symlink and embed_bytes returns the bytes as CtValue::Bytes.

### Impact

- Arbitrary host-readable bytes can cross the project boundary into compiled artifacts.
- A malicious project compiled by a developer or CI can read and embed arbitrary binary host secrets outside the workspace.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Dynamic validation should confirm output extraction for non-UTF-8 secrets.
- Git/platform symlink preservation and artifact access affect practical exfiltration.

### Preconditions

- Victim compiles an attacker-controlled symlink-bearing checkout.
- Repository preserves a symlink to a predictable readable host path; build evaluates embed_bytes.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:304-334` (root_control) — Performs only lexical path filtering.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:423-465` (filesystem sink) — Reads base_dir.join(relative_path), following symlinks.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:1497-1506` (public operation) — Dispatches embed_bytes separately from embed_file.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:304-334` (Lexical embed path check) — Only absolute paths and lexical ParentDir components are rejected.

## cd005-build-embed-symlink — BuildContext embed follows project symlinks outside the source root

### Source

- Malicious build logic selects a repository symlink as a BuildContext embed input.
- Untrusted build logic passes b.embed a relative path naming a project symlink to a predictable host file.

### Closest control

- Absolute/parent-component rejection only.
- The b.embed path check rejects absolute and `..` syntax, but does not reject symlinks or validate the canonical target.

### Sink or broken control

- std::fs::read follows the joined symlink target.
- std::fs::read(base_dir.join(path)) follows the symlink and returns target text as a comptime value.

### Impact

- Build-time code can disclose host files through embedded output without the impure authority gate.
- Malicious build logic can read and embed UTF-8 host secrets outside the selected source directory into build outputs.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Final validation should distinguish all build-mode policy layers outside this method.
- Need confirm all b.embed call paths are enabled for ordinary untrusted projects and whether sandboxing occurs before this host-side read.

### Preconditions

- Victim evaluates attacker-controlled build logic.
- Project preserves a symlink to a predictable readable UTF-8 host path and its build plan evaluates b.embed.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:510-558` (build operation) — Checks the lexical relative path, then reads the joined path without canonical containment.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/eval_method.rs:2071-2073` (method exposure) — Routes the BuildContext embed method to eval_build_embed.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch.rs:510-558` (Build embed validation and read) — b.embed rejects absolute and lexical ParentDir paths, then reads base_dir.join(path) without canonical/no-follow containment.

## cd005-comptime-fetch-local-disclosure — Hermetic compile-time fetch can disclose arbitrary local text files

### Source

- Untrusted project or dependency source evaluated at build time controls a file:// URL and the expected hash argument.
- A URL literal from untrusted Jet source evaluated by core.net.fetch.
- Untrusted source supplies a file:// URL and digest.
- Untrusted file URL at dispatch.rs:774-801

### Closest control

- SHA-256 pinning and UTF-8 decoding occur only after the unauthorized read; neither authorizes the path.
- A required SHA-256 value is compared only after the file has already been read; there is no path allowlist, project-root confinement, or explicit filesystem authority check at this sink.
- Post-read SHA-256 verification is not path authorization and mismatch output provides a digest oracle.
- The caller requires a SHA-256 and UTF-8, but neither limits which host path may be opened.
- SHA-256 checks integrity after the read; mismatch diagnostics reveal the actual digest but do not authorize the path.
- The sha256 pin is checked only after the host file has already been read; it provides content integrity, not filesystem authority. The mismatch diagnostic also reveals the actual digest, enabling a two-stage hash oracle.
- SHA-256 is checked only after the host file has been read; it is content integrity, not filesystem authorization.
- Caller-supplied SHA-256 verifies content but does not authorize host path.

### Sink or broken control

- The compiler reads any process-accessible filesystem path with no workspace containment or permission gate, then includes the actual content hash in a mismatch diagnostic.
- Unrestricted std::fs::read of the file:// path during compilation.
- jet_net strips file:// and reads the caller-selected path before verification.
- The absolute or relative path after `file://` reaches `std::fs::read` without canonicalization or project/workspace-root authorization.
- Unrestricted std::fs::read of a caller-selected local path occurs before digest verification.
- std::fs::read(path) on the absolute or relative path after file://.
- std::fs::read of an absolute attacker-selected host path during compilation.
- std::fs::read on arbitrary file URL during compilation.

### Impact

- An attacker can use one compile to learn a target file's hash and a subsequent compile to return and potentially exfiltrate UTF-8 secrets or source files accessible to the build account.
- A build of untrusted source may read host files into compile-time values, crossing the safe-source-to-host-filesystem boundary.
- A two-pass compile can return arbitrary developer-readable UTF-8 file contents.
- Host files readable by the compiler can be embedded into generated program data when their digest is known; mismatches also expose a SHA-256 oracle for arbitrary paths.
- A two-pass adaptive request, or a known digest, can return arbitrary host-readable UTF-8 file contents during compilation.
- Host file disclosure into compiler output/generated artifacts; predictable files are directly readable, and low-entropy or observable files can be targeted through the digest oracle.
- Source with knowledge of a target file hash can import host-readable file contents into compile-time evaluation and generated output; mismatches also disclose the target file hash/existence through diagnostics.
- Malicious source can read host files, disclose digest, and embed known-hash UTF-8 content for later disclosure.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exfiltration depends on attacker visibility into diagnostics or ability to submit a follow-up build and on the target being valid UTF-8; the initial unauthorized read is unconditional.
- Validation should confirm the governing effect/authority policy and whether ordinary safe Jet projects can reach this evaluator without a separate trusted opt-in.
- Confirm the diagnostic exposes the actual digest in the active CLI path.
- Validate whether sema/package policy restricts file URLs to trusted first-party source or supplies an external filesystem capability boundary.
- Central validation should confirm diagnostic digest visibility and the easiest content-exfiltration channel.
- Medium: reachability is direct; practical exfiltration of unknown high-entropy content depends on learning or guessing the digest.
- Need demonstrate a complete exfiltration channel and whether dependency code can surface the returned text without a separate grant.
- Some workflows trust package source, but dependency/compiler analysis crosses untrusted content boundaries.

### Preconditions

- The victim compiles source containing the fetch and the supplied digest matches the targeted file content; downstream use must make the value observable for disclosure.
- Victim compiles attacker-controlled source.
- Target file is readable and valid UTF-8 for direct return.

- target is readable UTF-8

- Victim compiles attacker-controlled source

- Content embedding needs known digest; mismatch leaks actual digest

## cd005-tower-token-dns-rebind — Tower token authentication is bypassed for DNS-rebound loopback requests

### Source

- A malicious web origin rebinds its hostname to 127.0.0.1 and sends same-origin requests to Tower.

### Closest control

- A configured bearer/cookie token and owner challenge exist, but loopback skips token authentication and a navigation mints the required owner session without Host or Origin validation.

### Sink or broken control

- The attacker can read APIs, mutate board state, and drive challenge/resolve owner-verification routes from the forged same-origin page.

### Impact

- Confidential board-data theft, arbitrary workflow mutation, and unauthorized acceptance decisions despite configured authentication.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate browser DNS caching, SameSite cookie behavior under the rebound hostname, and the two-request owner challenge flow.

### Preconditions

- Tower is running locally.
- Victim visits an attacker origin capable of DNS rebinding.
- Tower is running on the victim workstation.
- The victim visits an attacker-controlled origin capable of DNS rebinding to Tower's port.

### Affected locations

- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:123-170` (authentication bypass) — isLocal requests are accepted without the configured bearer token and ownerTrusted is unconditional.
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:64-98,215-394` (state/mutation routes) — Read and mutation APIs trust the bypassed request.
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:411` (listener) — Server binding and Host handling provide no DNS-rebinding defense.
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:108-110` (loopback exemption) — Trust is based on socket remoteAddress only.
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:152-169` (auth bypass) — Every loopback request bypasses a configured token; Host and Origin are not checked.
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:205-212` (owner-session minting) — A navigation receives an owner session because ownerTrusted is unconditional.
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:324-363` (owner action sink) — Same-origin requests with the minted session can challenge and resolve owner-verification ballots.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained as a distinct actionable issue because no other supplied candidate had the same remediation-subsuming source/control/sink/impact tuple. ## cd005-auth-predictable-session-id — Auth runtime issues predictable session identifiers

### Source

- A remote application client guesses the monotonic sess-N identifier.
- Attacker-chosen session_id or observation of any issued session.
- An attacker can submit guessed session identifiers to core.auth.session_validate; valid counters are also disclosed in every issued session cookie and share next_id with other auth flows.
- A remote client guesses sess-N.
- A remote attacker can submit guessed session IDs to core.auth.session_validate; every store starts at counter zero and all auth operations expose the sequence.
- Attacker-controlled session_id supplied to the exported core.auth.session_validate API; an attacker can infer adjacent IDs after observing or creating one session.
- A remote application user can obtain one session identifier or estimate the small counter and submit neighboring sess-N values.
- An attacker able to estimate issuance order and submit session IDs.
- An attacker able to estimate the shared issuance counter and submit guessed session IDs.
- An attacker who can observe or estimate the per-process issuance counter and present a candidate session ID.

### Privileged boundary

- The passwordless login flow crosses into an authenticated user session.
- The OAuth flow crosses into an authenticated provider identity.
- Generated app authentication treats the session ID as the bearer credential.

### Closest control

- Session lookup and expiry exist, but identifiers have no cryptographic entropy.
- Credential/password check at issuance and expiry at validation; no entropy or MAC protects session IDs.
- HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookie attributes protect browser transport but add no identifier entropy; expiry limits duration but not guessing.
- Expiry and lookup exist, but issuance uses a process-local monotonic counter with no entropy.
- Session existence and expires_at are checked, but identifier generation has no cryptographic entropy and no client/channel binding.
- Expiry is checked after direct identifier lookup, but identifiers have no cryptographic entropy, per-user binding at presentation, or secondary cookie proof.
- Cookie attributes and expiration exist, but no cryptographic session identifier or signed cookie is generated.
- Cookie transport flags and expiry exist, but the session value is neither random nor signed.
- HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookie attributes protect browser transport but do not add entropy or a signature to the bearer value.

### Sink or broken control

- Possession of the guessable identifier authenticates as the associated user.
- jet_auth_session_validate searches sessions by raw ID and returns the associated user.
- Session identifiers are format!("sess-{}", next_id) and validation performs only equality plus expiry checks.
- session_validate treats exact possession as authentication.
- Sequential sess-N value authorizes session lookup and is installed directly as the HttpOnly/Secure cookie bearer value.
- Predictable sess-N bearer IDs authorize any stored live session.
- session_validate returns the magic-authenticated user for a guessed sess-N value.
- session_validate returns the OAuth identity for a guessed sess-N bearer.
- session_validate accepts predictable sess-N identifiers and returns the associated authenticated user session.

### Impact

- Session hijacking and account impersonation in applications using the core auth runtime.
- Session hijacking and account impersonation in applications using the advertised session batteries.
- Guessing an active identifier could return another user's authenticated JetAuthSession and enable session hijacking/account takeover in applications using the shipped core.auth session API.
- Attackers can hijack live sessions and impersonate users.
- Prediction of another user's live session ID can yield that user's session and authentication state.
- Session guessing and account impersonation in applications using the documented core.auth session batteries.
- Attackers can enumerate or guess another user's active session and impersonate that user.
- Hijacking sessions created through passwordless login.
- Hijacking sessions created through OAuth completion.
- Session hijacking and impersonation of a user authenticated through password login.

### Impact path

- issuance counter guess -> sess-N -> validation -> magic-authenticated user
- counter observation -> sess-N guess -> validation -> OAuth-authenticated identity
- counter observation/guess -> sess-N bearer -> session_validate lookup -> authenticated user session

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Application wrappers may add independent cookies or entropy; centralized validation must trace a concrete generated app.
- An application could wrap these primitives in an independent unpredictable token layer, but the shipped safe-default battery does not.
- The reviewed shard does not establish how a concrete application routes these helpers or whether an outer deployment layer replaces the identifier before exposure.
- Outer wrappers may add independent entropy or rate limits.
- Application routing and rate limiting are outside this file; centralized validation should confirm a deployed call path.
- The in-memory thread-local store may limit current production usefulness, but that does not add unpredictability to the bearer credential.
- Thread-local storage may complicate cross-request reachability depending on server scheduling; centralized validation should test normal HTTP framework integration.
- Requires centralized confirmation that no wrapper transforms/signs the session ID.
- The worktree variant fixes session entropy; the candidate is specific to the current top-level implementation and needs integration tracing.
- Candidate-local static review cannot establish whether an outer generated-app layer signs the returned cookie; centralized validation should trace emitted HTTP integration.

### Preconditions

- Application exposes these runtime auth APIs and accepts session IDs from remote clients.
- Application exposes session_validate to incoming cookies or tokens.
- At least one target session exists in the same auth store/thread.
- An application exposes a request path that passes a client session identifier to core.auth.session_validate.
- The attacker can estimate or enumerate the small shared counter while a victim session is live.
- application exposes the auth runtime
- target session exists
- Attacker can reach an application endpoint that forwards a session ID to session_validate and can estimate or observe the small global counter.
- Application uses core.auth password_login/session_validate as an authentication boundary
- Attacker can submit guessed session IDs
- application exposes core.auth sessions to more than one trust principal
- attacker can submit a session ID to session_validate
- Application exposes validation attempts and a magic-link session was issued; unreviewed outer controls do not replace the ID.
- An OAuth session has been issued and the application exposes validation attempts; an outer session wrapper does not replace the value.
- Generated application exposes these auth batteries and an attacker can make validation attempts; rate limiting/integration behavior is not visible here.

### Severity-relevant facts

- An application exposes a request path that passes a client session identifier to core.auth.session_validate.
- The attacker can estimate or enumerate the small shared counter while a victim session is live.
- Guessing an active identifier could return another user's authenticated JetAuthSession and enable session hijacking/account takeover in applications using the shipped core.auth session API.
- Uncertainty: The reviewed shard does not establish how a concrete application routes these helpers or whether an outer deployment layer replaces the identifier before exposure.
- Independent issuance path
- Counter shared with tokens and OAuth state
- Expiration does not prevent guessing
- Current implementation only
- Shared counter leaks across auth operations
- No signature in helper
- Bearer value has counter entropy only
- Applies to a documented core.auth surface
- Outer signing control is unproven

## cd005-auth-predictable-magic-token — Auth runtime issues predictable magic-login tokens

### Source

- An attacker guesses the counter and target user identifier used in a magic token.
- Attacker guess of shared next_id and chosen target user_id.
- An attacker who knows a target user id can guess the shared next_id and submit candidate magic-<n>-<user> values.
- An attacker predicts magic-counter-user_id.
- An attacker who knows a target user identifier can derive magic-<counter>-<user> candidates from the process-wide counter.
- Attacker-influenced user_id and token arguments at documented core.auth.magic_link_issue/consume entrypoints.
- A remote attacker chooses/knows a target user ID and predicts the small issuance counter.
- An attacker who knows a target user identifier and can estimate the shared issuance counter.

### Privileged boundary

- The magic-link token is a passwordless authentication credential.

### Closest control

- Tokens expire and are single-use, but token material is deterministic and enumerable.
- Expiry and one-time removal; neither adds token unpredictability.
- Tokens expire and are removed after use, but neither control prevents pre-use guessing during the validity window.
- Expiry and single use do not compensate for deterministic enumerable token material.
- Consume checks exact token presence, one-time removal, and expiry, but issue neither authenticates the requested user nor creates an unpredictable secret.
- TTL and one-time removal limit replay duration but do not make an unobserved token unguessable.
- Expiry and one-time removal exist, but no cryptographic randomness, MAC, or delivery binding is present in this implementation.

### Sink or broken control

- A matching predictable token is accepted as proof of account control.
- magic_link_consume creates a full session solely from the predictable token.
- A deterministic string is used as the sole magic-link bearer credential for session issuance.
- A matching token is accepted as account-control proof and mints a session.
- A matching deterministic token is exchanged for an authenticated JetAuthSession.
- Predictable magic-link token is sufficient to mint a session for the named user.
- magic_link_consume accepts the guessable token and creates an authenticated session for its embedded user.

### Impact

- Passwordless account takeover.
- Passwordless account takeover where applications expose the documented magic-link flow.
- A guessed live token could be redeemed for the target user's session, causing authentication bypass and account takeover.
- Guessing an outstanding token permits passwordless account takeover and returns a session cookie.
- Forged or self-issued magic links can create sessions for another user when these session batteries back a web login flow.
- Account takeover through guessed passwordless-login links.
- Passwordless account takeover through prediction of a live magic-link credential.

### Impact path

- known user + counter guess -> magic-N-user token -> consume -> authenticated session

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exploitability depends on user-ID observability and request-rate controls outside this runtime.
- A caller might keep issuance private and add out-of-band controls, but core.auth itself provides no such binding.
- Concrete rate limiting and endpoint wiring are outside this shard; either could reduce practical guessing but does not restore token entropy.
- Application-level rate limits may affect exploitability.
- External route throttling is not visible; validate the concrete magic-link endpoint.
- Applications could add an external delivery/authorization layer, but the exported battery itself does not enforce one.
- Rate limiting may exist in application code outside this helper; no rate or entropy control appears in the reusable core mechanism.
- Outer delivery/rate controls are not present in the reviewed prelude and require centralized tracing.

### Preconditions

- Application exposes magic-link token consumption to untrusted clients.
- Application exposes magic-link consumption.
- Attacker can estimate a live token counter before expiry.
- The application exposes magic-link consumption to an attacker.
- The attacker knows or can infer the target user id and can enumerate plausible counter values before expiry.
- application exposes magic consume
- attacker knows user id and estimates counter
- Target user ID is known and attacker can submit token guesses during its TTL.
- Application exposes a magic-link request/consume flow backed by these helpers
- Attacker can invoke or predict issue ordering
- application exposes magic-link consume endpoint
- target has a pending unexpired link
- attacker can estimate issuance count
- A live token exists, attacker can attempt guesses before expiry, and no outer rate limit or signing layer blocks attempts.

### Severity-relevant facts

- The application exposes magic-link consumption to an attacker.
- The attacker knows or can infer the target user id and can enumerate plausible counter values before expiry.
- A guessed live token could be redeemed for the target user's session, causing authentication bypass and account takeover.
- Uncertainty: Concrete rate limiting and endpoint wiring are outside this shard; either could reduce practical guessing but does not restore token entropy.
- Token reveals user ID
- Shared sequential counter
- One-time and expiration controls narrow the window

## cd005-auth-oauth-predictable-state — OAuth state values are predictable and not bound to a browser session

### Source

- An attacker can guess the provider and shared counter and submit a chosen subject with the predicted state.
- An attacker predicts or obtains oauth-counter-provider state.
- An attacker can predict oauth-<counter>-<provider> state values because the provider is public and the process counter starts at zero.
- A remote attacker predicts a pending OAuth state and supplies an arbitrary subject to the callback-facing helper.
- An attacker predicts or obtains a pending OAuth state and submits it through the callback path.
- An attacker who knows the provider and can estimate the shared auth issuance counter.

### Privileged boundary

- OAuth state is intended to bind a browser callback to the initiating login flow.

### Closest control

- State is single-use and provider must be nonempty, but those checks do not make it unpredictable or bind it to the initiating browser and provider response.
- Pending membership and expiry exist, but state has no CSPRNG entropy or initiating-browser binding.
- State is single-use, but predictable and unbound to a browser, redirect URI, provider response, authorization code, nonce, or PKCE verifier.
- Pending-state membership and expiry; no cryptographic entropy or user-agent binding.
- State is one-time because the matching entry is removed, but it has no cryptographic unpredictability or browser-session binding.

### Sink or broken control

- OAuth completion treats a deterministic state lookup and caller-provided subject as sufficient to issue a session; no verified authorization response, nonce, redirect binding, or PKCE evidence is consumed here.
- oauth_finish consumes the predictable state as callback correlation.
- Weak state plus unverified caller-supplied subject creates an authenticated provider:subject session.
- The predictable state is accepted as CSRF/callback correlation.
- A predicted state passes the only callback correlation check.

### Impact

- Depending on route wiring, an attacker could force or forge OAuth completion, causing login CSRF, account confusion, or unauthorized session issuance.
- OAuth login CSRF or session confusion.
- A predicted outstanding state can break OAuth request/callback binding and may let an attacker bind or authenticate an attacker-selected subject.
- Login CSRF or account impersonation for arbitrary OAuth identities.
- OAuth login CSRF or session confusion in applications relying on this runtime.
- OAuth login CSRF/account-confusion precondition, compounded by the callback's trust in caller-supplied subject.

### Impact path

- provider + counter guess -> oauth-N-provider -> finish correlation passes

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- An unreviewed application adapter may authenticate the callback before invoking this primitive; validation should trace a concrete route and intended API contract.
- Outer adapters may independently bind and verify state.
- Provider callback verification and HTTP routing may add controls outside this helper; validate end-to-end.
- An application could verify provider responses before calling this helper, but the shipped core API accepts raw state/subject and documents route generation as the normal surface.
- A concrete wrapper may add an outer state/cookie binding.
- Exploit outcome depends on HTTP callback integration and provider validation outside this file.

### Preconditions

- Application exposes begin/finish OAuth calls over a remote callback flow.
- A web callback exposes core.auth.oauth_finish without an outer adapter independently verifying and binding the provider response.
- The attacker can estimate the counter and provider string.
- application directly exposes begin/finish callback flow
- Attacker can trigger or race an OAuth callback and estimate the shared counter.
- application maps an OAuth callback to oauth_finish
- attacker can estimate a live state counter
- A live OAuth flow exists and attacker can invoke the callback before the legitimate user; outer provider callback checks are unproven.

### Severity-relevant facts

- A web callback exposes core.auth.oauth_finish without an outer adapter independently verifying and binding the provider response.
- The attacker can estimate the counter and provider string.
- Depending on route wiring, an attacker could force or forge OAuth completion, causing login CSRF, account confusion, or unauthorized session issuance.
- Uncertainty: An unreviewed application adapter may authenticate the callback before invoking this primitive; validation should trace a concrete route and intended API contract.
- One-time state
- No browser-session binding
- Predictability combines with unverified subject candidate

## cd005-auth-oauth-unverified-subject — OAuth completion trusts a caller-supplied subject without provider proof

### Source

- An untrusted callback client supplies a chosen OAuth subject alongside a valid/predicted state.
- Callback state and caller-controlled subject parameters.
- An untrusted callback supplies provider and subject with a valid/predicted state.
- The exported core.auth oauth_finish operation accepts state and subject strings from the application callback path.
- Request-derived provider, state, and subject supplied to the documented core.auth OAuth entrypoints.
- Any caller that obtains or predicts a valid outstanding OAuth state and supplies an arbitrary subject string.

### Privileged boundary

- OAuth completion should establish identity only from a verified provider response.

### Closest control

- State/provider matching occurs, but no authorization code, signed identity token, or provider response is verified here.
- One-time state lookup by predictable string.
- State/provider matching occurs, but no authorization code, signed token, or provider response is verified.
- State must exist once, but it is deterministic and not tied to a browser; no proof binds subject to a validated identity-provider response.
- Both versions validate state existence and identifier syntax; neither accepts or verifies provider callback evidence.

### Sink or broken control

- The supplied subject is treated as authenticated identity and a session is minted.
- Automatic provider:subject registration and session creation without IdP evidence.
- The supplied subject becomes the authenticated identity and receives a session.
- oauth_finish constructs provider:subject, auto-registers it, and issues a session.
- The function creates provider:attacker_selected_subject and returns an authenticated session.

### Impact

- Account impersonation or arbitrary account creation.
- Login as an arbitrary provider subject when applications wire callbacks to the advertised primitive.
- Arbitrary account creation or impersonation.
- A caller who can initiate an OAuth flow can choose another user's provider subject and receive an authenticated session for that identity.
- Authentication as an arbitrary OAuth subject/account if an application treats oauth_finish as its advertised callback battery.
- Impersonation or creation of arbitrary OAuth-backed identities under the selected provider.

### Impact path

- valid OAuth state -> arbitrary subject -> user creation -> authenticated session

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Callers might independently verify the subject before invocation; centralized validation must inspect generated integration code.
- A sophisticated caller could validate subject externally before calling finish, but this is neither required nor represented by the API.
- Callers might independently verify subject evidence.
- Validation should confirm whether higher-level generated routes add an external verification step; the primitive and reference signature themselves do not carry proof of one.
- A caller may validate provider data before calling oauth_finish; later validation should determine whether app.auth-generated routes do so.
- Centralized validation must trace generated route glue to determine whether subject is pre-verified before this helper is invoked.

### Preconditions

- Application delegates provider verification directly to this runtime completion function.
- Application exposes OAuth begin/finish as its callback mechanism.
- Attacker obtains or predicts an unconsumed state.
- application delegates OAuth completion directly to this runtime
- An application exposes the advertised OAuth begin/finish primitives to normal callback requests without separately verifying and substituting a provider-authenticated subject.
- Application uses core.auth.oauth_begin/oauth_finish for login callbacks
- Attacker can reach callback or invoke exported helper
- Attacker can invoke the generated OAuth callback/API with a live state; no outer wrapper independently verifies and substitutes the subject.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Direct authentication sink
- Affects current and hardened worktree implementations
- Outer verification is the key proof gap

## runtime-toml-depth-dos — Runtime TOML parser has unbounded recursive nesting

### Source

- Application-controlled or externally received TOML passed to public core encoding TOML parse/decode APIs.

### Closest control

- Syntax validation rejects malformed values but imposes no depth or input-size ceiling.

### Sink or broken control

- Recursive array/inline-table parsing has no maximum nesting depth.

### Impact

- Deeply nested TOML can overflow the process stack and abort a compiled/JIT application or service.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm maximum syntactically accepted nesting and crash threshold on representative targets.

### Preconditions

- TOML arrays and inline tables are values and may nest recursively, reaching self.value() for every level.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/TOML.rs:33-50,226-232` (Public parser) — Parser state has characters, position, and line only. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/TOML.rs:367-379,554-625` (Recursive descent) — Nested arrays and inline tables recursively call value without depth accounting. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/DataFmt.rs:527-559` (Runtime call surface) — Core TOML parsing and typed decode helpers pass caller text to parse_to_tree. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently: the runtime TOML parser has its own recursive control and requires a TOML-specific nesting budget. Current reduction: carried forward with its original source-ledger identities and no cross-root collapse. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## runtime-yaml-depth-dos — Runtime YAML parser has unbounded recursive nesting

### Source

- Application-controlled or externally received YAML passed to public core encoding YAML parse/decode APIs.
- Attacker-controlled YAML containing thousands of nested block mapping or sequence levels
- Attacker-controlled single-line YAML with deeply nested flow arrays or objects
- Application-controlled YAML reaches the public runtime parser.
- YAML text supplied to the AOT core.encoding.yaml parser.

### Closest control

- Document/syntax checks and alias lookup exist, but no nesting budget is enforced.
- Indentation and syntax are validated, but input depth is not bounded and recursion is not converted to an explicit stack.
- Character scanning ensures progress for ordinary input but does not impose maximum nesting depth.
- Syntax is checked but Parser carries no depth or node budget.
- Other structured-data decoders in the runtime carry explicit maximum-depth settings, while this YAML parser state contains no depth or item budget.

### Sink or broken control

- Block and flow collection parsers recurse per nested value without maximum depth.
- Recursive parser frames consume the native thread stack until overflow/abort.
- Recursive descent consumes the native stack until process abort.
- Nested block/flow nodes recursively call parse_node or parse_flow_at.
- Block, anchor, and flow parsing recurse on attacker-selected nesting depth.

### Impact

- Deeply nested YAML can overflow the process stack and abort a compiled/JIT application or service.
- Parsing crafted YAML can crash the consuming process, causing denial of service.
- A compact crafted YAML value can crash an application during decode.
- Deep YAML can overflow a generated application stack and abort the service.
- Deeply nested YAML can exhaust the host stack or CPU and terminate a service.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm crash depth separately for block, flow, and anchor nesting on representative targets.
- Measure the smallest crashing nesting depth on representative targets.
- Validation should distinguish stack exhaustion from earlier syntax rejection and set a compatible shared depth limit.

### Preconditions

- Both indentation-driven nesting and compact flow collections reach unbounded recursive functions.
- An application decodes untrusted YAML through Jet's core encoding API.
- An application passes untrusted YAML to the Jet YAML parser.
- application parses attacker-controlled YAML
- An application parses attacker-controlled YAML through the generated AOT runtime.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/YAML.rs:17-44` (Public parser) — Parser state tracks lines, position, and anchors but no depth. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/YAML.rs:72-90,108-170,219-231` (Block recursion) — Nested block and anchored values recursively enter parse_node/parse_inline_value. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/YAML.rs:253-323` (Flow recursion) — Flow arrays/maps recursively call parse_flow_at without a depth limit. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/DataFmt.rs:560-592` (Runtime call surface) — Core YAML parsing and typed decode helpers accept caller-provided text. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/YAML.rs:17-38` (entrypoint) — parse_to_tree accepts an arbitrary input string with no nesting budget.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/YAML.rs:72-123,129-160` (sink) — Nested block sequences and maps recursively call parse_node once per indentation level without a depth limit.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/YAML.rs:219-258` (entrypoint) — Inline arrays and objects route into parse_flow_at without a nesting budget.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/YAML.rs:258-325` (sink) — Each nested [ or { causes a recursive parse_flow_at call.

## devserver-windows-absolute-static-path — Windows absolute paths can escape the devserver static build root

### Source

- An HTTP requester controls the raw URL path served by the local devserver.
- An HTTP request target such as /C:\Windows\win.ini supplied to a jet dev instance on Windows.
- The HTTP request target supplies a Windows drive-qualified path such as /C:/path.
- An HTTP client controls the request target path.
- Attacker-controlled raw HTTP request target on a Windows host

### Privileged boundary

- HTTP request path to developer host filesystem

### Closest control

- Loopback binding limits ordinary network exposure and .. is rejected, but local clients and DNS-rebinding browsers remain possible and absolute paths bypass the lexical traversal check.
- The traversal substring check blocks dot-dot forms but does not reject Windows prefixes, rooted backslash paths, alternate separators, or verify the resolved path remains under build.
- Leading forward slashes are trimmed and '..' substrings rejected; these do not handle Windows prefixes/root components or symlink containment.
- A substring .. check blocks conventional traversal but not absolute/prefixed paths whose Path::join semantics replace the base.
- The textual '..' predicate is incomplete for Windows path semantics.
- static_path rejects only literal dot-dot and trims the leading slash.
- Rejecting '..' blocks one traversal spelling but does not reject Windows Prefix/RootDir components or verify the resolved path remains under build.
- Rejects only literal two-dot substrings and strips only forward-slash prefixes; no Windows prefix/root rejection or canonical containment check

### Sink or broken control

- On Windows, a path such as /C:/Windows/win.ini becomes C:/Windows/win.ini after slash trimming; Path::join with a drive-absolute child can replace the build root.
- std::fs::read of a PathBuf::join result that can discard the build prefix for an absolute Windows child.
- Path::join replaces the relative build root with the absolute Windows path and fs::read returns it.
- fs::read consumes the PathBuf returned by root.join(attacker_path).
- fs::read(file_path)

### Impact

- A requester able to reach the devserver may read arbitrary files accessible to the developer account on Windows.
- Disclosure of arbitrary files readable by the jet dev process through the static HTTP response.
- Host file disclosure to malicious project web code, which can exfiltrate the response.
- Arbitrary readable-file disclosure from the developer host while the dev server is running.
- Arbitrary readable host files may be returned by the generated dev server on Windows.
- A network caller can read arbitrary developer-readable files on Windows.
- On Windows, a drive-qualified or rooted request path can select and disclose an arbitrary readable host file through the loopback devserver.
- Potential disclosure of a readable file outside build on Windows

### Impact path

- Request target -> static_path -> root.join(absolute Windows path) -> fs::read -> HTTP response.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm Rust std::path behavior and HTTP target normalization on supported Windows builds; test drive-absolute and UNC/rooted variants.
- Validation should exercise Rust PathBuf semantics and raw HTTP target parsing on the supported Windows toolchain.
- Exact HTTP client normalization of drive/backslash targets and Path::is_absolute behavior should be reproduced on supported Windows versions.
- Requires confirmation of how the leading slash is normalized for each Windows request-target variant.
- Exact HTTP client normalization and Rust Windows PathBuf push semantics should be confirmed dynamically.
- Validate exact browser URL normalization on Windows.
- Browser URL normalization may rewrite some backslash forms; validate with a raw HTTP client and Windows Path semantics.
- Exact Windows Path::join behavior for the accepted raw request forms is the proof gap and requires platform validation.

### Preconditions

- Windows host and access to the loopback dev server.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Windows-only hypothesis
- Read-only impact
- Literal parent traversal is blocked

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (Path guard) — Rejects only substring .., strips leading slash, then joins onto build root. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1241-1253,1270-1284` (Reachable file read) — Unmatched GET path flows to static_path and fs::read. Byte-identical mirrored worktree copy was independently reviewed.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (root_control) — static_path rejects only strings containing .. and then joins an attacker path to build/.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1252-1272` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Unhandled GET paths flow into serve_static and static_path.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1283-1305` (sink) — The joined path is read and returned.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:350-377` (entrypoint) — Raw HTTP target is split but not URL-decoded or platform-normalized.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:390-404` (root_control) — Control rejects only '..' and trims only forward slashes.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:404-405` (sink) — Path::join on Windows can treat backslash-rooted or drive-prefixed rel values as rooted and replace the build base.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:832-856` (request target)
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1270-1284` (read sink)
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (broken helper)
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (root_control) — The check only rejects the substring '..' and then Path::join accepts platform-absolute children.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1270-1288` (entrypoint) — The raw request path is resolved by static_path and then read.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (incomplete path control) — Uses substring rejection and Path::join without canonical containment.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1266-1284` (file read sink) — Reads the resulting build-relative path.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1244-1284` (entrypoint) — Unmatched request paths fall through to static-file resolution and response.

## locked-dependency-integrity-bypass — Locked builds use mutable dependency sources without content verification

### Source

- A local attacker, compromised build step, or mutable path dependency can change dependency files after the lock was generated; a writable git cache is likewise mutable.

### Closest control

- Non-locked resolution calls Store::verify_entry, and Source/Store.rs provides verify_content_hash, but locked mode does not use those controls.

### Sink or broken control

- --locked checks lock metadata but neither records dependency content hashes nor calls Store verification before returning the source directories used by the build.

### Impact

- Dependency code can be replaced and compiled under an unchanged lock file, defeating reproducibility and supply-chain tamper detection.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Write access to a path dependency or the per-user git cache is required; that is a realistic local/CI boundary rather than a remote-only primitive.

### Preconditions

- High: content_hash is explicitly set to None and the locked branch bypasses both ensure_* and verify_entry.

### Affected locations

- `Source/Fetch.rs:48-73` (locked-mode resolution) — locked mode validates manifest metadata then returns mutable path or git-cache directories
- `Source/Fetch.rs:182-197,309-318,408-416` (content hashes discarded) — dependency lock entries receive content_hash None even after store installation computes a hash
- `Source/Fetch.rs:540-578` (unverified locked paths) — build_dep_dirs_from_lock selects path dependency and git cache directories without store verification

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently: recording and verifying immutable dependency content in locked mode fixes every absorbed path/git-cache subcase. ## package-store-incomplete-content-hash — Package store integrity hashes omit copied non-.jet files

### Source

- A package publisher, compromised cache process, or local store attacker controls non-.jet package files such as assets, metadata, scripts, or native artifacts.
- A package author supplies non-.jet build inputs, assets, configuration, generated metadata, or native-support files, or an attacker later modifies those files in a store entry.
- Dependency-controlled or post-ingestion modified C/Rust sources, scripts, binaries, assets, headers, build inputs, and other non-.jet files
- Mutable or malicious non-Jet dependency files such as native libraries, assets, scripts, or foreign sources.
- A local or supply-chain attacker modifies a non-.jet asset, native library, script, or other copied package file after the lock/store content hash is recorded.
- Manual full-file review of package hashing and store verification.
- Package store content may be modified after fetch by a same-user process, compromised cache, or other local tooling.
- Files in a fetched package or an attacker/process able to modify a cached package entry, especially native sources, build scripts, FFI artifacts, and data files.

### Privileged boundary

- Fetched/local package bytes to trusted content-addressed store and build inputs.

### Closest control

- tree_hash sorts paths and hashes Jet source bytes deterministically, but its file-selection boundary is narrower than the installed tree.
- SHA-256 and Ed25519 are strong primitives and paths/build/target are intentionally excluded, but the omission of all other extensions is broader than those exclusions and is not compensated by a manifest of auxiliary files.
- verify_entry compares a recorded content hash, but the hash domain excludes the files that ingestion retains.
- verify_entry recomputes tree_hash, but that hash deliberately ignores all non-.jet content.
- The store recomputes and compares a SHA-256 tree hash, but that hash deliberately omits all non-.jet content even though ingestion and linking retain it.
- A SHA-256 digest is computed and verified, but only over the filtered subset.
- E1204 compares an expected tree hash to a recomputed value, but the hash input deliberately excludes manifests, native sources, build recipes, and assets.
- The lock/store digest authenticates only .jet paths and bytes.
- Store insertion and verification both compute a SHA-256 tree digest, but the collector filters the integrity domain to Jet-extension files.

### Sink or broken control

- The integrity verifier recomputes a hash that omits every non-.jet file even though those files are copied and linked as part of the installed package.
- tree_hash recursively includes only files whose extension equals Jet's source extension, while the store copies all nonhidden files and publishing signs/records that incomplete hash.
- Build/runtime/package consumers can use unverified non-Jet bytes from an otherwise successfully verified store entry.
- Integrity verification accepts store content whose non-Jet bytes changed.
- verify_entry reports success while unmeasured package files differ from the fetched/locked content and remain available to later build, FFI, resource, or packaging paths.
- Integrity identity and later verification omit non-.jet bytes even though package copying and downstream builds can consume them.
- A modified non-.jet package input leaves tree_hash unchanged and therefore passes verify_content_hash/verify_entry.
- The full store tree is linked after verifying only its .jet subset.
- The global package store accepts and later verifies a whole copied tree using a digest that does not authenticate most of that tree.

### Impact

- Covered package files can be added or modified without changing the recorded content identity or triggering store tamper diagnostics, allowing unverified runtime data or native/support artifacts to reach consumers.
- Non-.jet package content can change without changing the signed content hash, lock fingerprint, or E1204 store-verification result, undermining package/store integrity for build-consumed auxiliary files.
- Package/store tampering or cache poisoning of non-Jet build and runtime inputs is accepted as intact, enabling substituted code/data to reach builds or execution without changing the lock-visible hash.
- Tampered executable or runtime-relevant dependency content can survive lock/store verification.
- Package/store tampering can persist undetected and influence native linking, build behavior, resources, or shipped artifacts despite a successful integrity check.
- Undetected modification or substitution of security-relevant package content while the store reports the expected tree hash.
- Executable build inputs or package metadata can be substituted without detection, defeating the store's stated tamper guarantee and enabling dependency code execution or artifact compromise.
- Security-relevant dependency content can be substituted without changing the recorded hash/fingerprint.
- Package provenance and cache-integrity checks can report success while security-relevant non-Jet bytes differ, allowing undetected dependency/build-input substitution or persistence.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validation should inventory executable and runtime-read non-.jet file types to calibrate impact beyond the demonstrated integrity gap.
- Central validation should enumerate concrete non-Jet consumers and mutation authority.
- Validation should demonstrate a concrete consumed native/resource file, mutate it, and confirm verify_entry still succeeds.
- Some current packages may be Jet-only, but the copy and build model does not enforce that invariant.
- Validation should identify the shortest default downstream consumer.
- Downstream execution/consumption of each omitted file type depends on package workflows; centralized validation should demonstrate one native/build artifact path.

### Preconditions

- High for integrity bypass; security impact depends on whether a consuming package loads the altered non-.jet artifact.
- The package uses security-relevant non-.jet content or an attacker can modify a writable store/cache entry after initial resolution.
- Dependency behavior consumes a non-Jet file.
- Attacker can alter that file before or within store reuse.
- A dependency contains a security-relevant non-.jet file.
- An attacker can alter that store file or substitute it before a later verification/use.
- A package contains security-relevant non-.jet files
- An attacker can alter those omitted files without altering hashed .jet files
- An attacker or compromised tool can alter an existing store entry but cannot update the lock's expected hash.
- A dependency has security-relevant non-.jet content.
- The attacker changes it before import or tampers with the store.
- A package contains security-relevant non-Jet content, and that content changes independently of its Jet sources or is tampered with in the store.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Reachability and impact require centralized validation; no final severity is assigned here.
