## comptime-fetch-ssrf — Hash-pinned compile-time fetch permits arbitrary outbound requests before verification

### Source

- Untrusted project or dependency source evaluated during compilation controls the complete core.net.fetch URL and expected hash.
- Attacker-controlled Jet source supplies a core.net.fetch URL targeting loopback, private, link-local, metadata, or other internal HTTP services
- Untrusted source controls a core.net.fetch HTTP(S) URL and expected hash.
- Untrusted compile-time URL at dispatch.rs:774-801
- Untrusted Jet project source supplies compile-time fetch URL and expected hash.
- Untrusted Jet source controls the literal URL supplied to compile-time `core.net.fetch`.
- A compiled project or dependency supplies a URL to core.net.fetch.
- Untrusted Jet source supplies a literal core.net.fetch URL during ordinary checking/build evaluation.

### Closest control

- A 30-second connect/read timeout and post-fetch SHA-256 verification protect content identity, not destination authorization or request side effects.
- Scheme checks, timeouts, and post-download SHA-256 verify content only after the network request/response; they do not restrict destination authority.
- Scheme restriction and post-fetch content hash verify bytes but do not prevent the request, redirect, or blind side effect.
- The fetch route is treated as hermetic and hash verification occurs only after the request.
- Only scheme filtering and connect/read timeouts are present. The post-fetch SHA-256 comparison authenticates returned bytes but does not authorize the destination or redirects.
- Required SHA-256 is checked only after local/network access completes; no scheme/host/IP/redirect boundary.
- The evaluator requires a SHA-256 pin, but destination scheme/address policy is only a file/http/https allowlist; the request/read occurs before the content hash comparison and redirects are not revalidated.
- A required SHA-256 validates returned content only after the request or file read has occurred.
- http/https/file scheme allowlist plus post-response SHA-256 pin; no destination allowlist, IP-range denial, or pre-request authority boundary.

### Sink or broken control

- The compiler performs the HTTP request before validating the content hash and does not require the impure-effect gate or restrict loopback, private, link-local, or metadata destinations.
- ureq Agent sends a blocking GET to the selected URL
- The compiler performs the outbound request without private/loopback/link-local destination restrictions.
- `ureq::AgentBuilder::get(url).call()` can reach arbitrary HTTP(S) destinations; no loopback, link-local, private-address, DNS-rebinding, or redirect boundary is enforced.
- std::fs::read or ureq outbound request to attacker-selected destination.
- `file://` calls unrestricted `std::fs::read`; HTTP(S) uses ureq for attacker-selected hosts, loopback/private addresses, and redirect targets.
- std::fs::read handles file URLs and ureq performs HTTP(S) requests without blocking loopback, link-local, RFC1918, metadata, or redirect destinations.
- Blocking ureq GET to attacker-selected network destinations during compilation.

### Impact

- Compiling attacker-controlled code can scan or trigger internal HTTP services, reach cloud metadata endpoints, and potentially disclose responses when their hash is known or learned from the mismatch diagnostic.
- Compiler-host SSRF enabling internal-service probing and GET side effects under host network authority.
- Blind SSRF from a developer/compiler host into internal services during routine check/build/editor compilation.
- Compilation can scan or trigger internal services and cloud metadata endpoints.
- Compiling or checking hostile Jet source can issue blind requests to localhost or internal services under the developer/CI network identity, including state-changing GET endpoints or metadata services.
- Compiling an untrusted project can send GETs to internal services and probe local files under compiler authority.
- Building an untrusted project can perform local file probes and server-side requests from the developer host, including access to loopback/private services, before failing or embedding hash-matching content.
- Compilation, IDE evaluation, or CI can be induced to probe/read local files or send requests to internal services; request side effects occur even if the hash later fails.
- Malicious project can cause requests to loopback/private/cloud metadata or state-changing internal GET endpoints from the developer/CI network even when the hash later fails.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Some build environments restrict egress; redirects and DNS rebinding behavior should be checked during validation for severity calibration.
- Response bytes reach the program only on hash match; redirects and exact diagnostics side channels require validation, but request issuance precedes hashing.
- Response contents are not returned with an unknown hash, so this is primarily blind SSRF unless a predictable response hash is known.
- Redirect and DNS-rebinding behavior need centralized validation.
- Validate ureq redirect behavior and whether higher-level package policy independently denies dependency-originated compile-time network effects.
- Central validation should confirm sema/effect gates and redirect behavior.
- Validation should determine whether build trust prompts or higher-level policy intercept this path and quantify exploitability of hash matching/mismatch diagnostics.
- Validation should confirm exact ureq redirect defaults and whether file responses become observable when a matching digest is unavailable.
- Concrete internal target and deployment-specific network reachability require centralized validation; request emission is direct.

### Preconditions

- A victim evaluates attacker-influenced Jet source using core.net.fetch and the process can reach the target resource.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Private-network and loopback destinations are not filtered.
- The threat model explicitly treats untrusted URL evaluation as SSRF-sensitive.

## git-revision-cache-path-traversal — Manifest Git revisions escape the cache root and shape recursive deletion

### Source

- A malicious pkg.jet dependency controls the direct Git rev string.
- Attacker-controlled rev string in an untrusted pkg.jet manifest or lock record.

### Closest control

- The URL portion is SHA-256 hashed before path use, but the revision portion is not encoded or normalized.
- URL is hashed, but rev is not validated or hashed before PathBuf::join; git checkout validation occurs only after filesystem paths are selected.

### Sink or broken control

- The revision is treated as a raw PathBuf component rather than a digest-safe cache key; absolute or ../ values escape the intended per-user git-cache directory and drive create_dir_all and remove_dir_all.
- git_cache_dir returns cache_dir.join(rev_prefix), then git_clone creates/removes/renames at paths derived from it.

### Impact

- Fetching the dependency can create directories outside the cache and recursively delete an attacker-shaped sibling path within the build user's filesystem permissions; an already-existing escaped directory may also be consumed as dependency source without cloning.
- A crafted absolute or parent-relative revision can redirect package-cache filesystem operations outside ~/.jet/git-cache, enabling creation of attacker-controlled checkout trees at unintended writable locations and locked-mode local path confusion.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validation should use a disposable filesystem tree to map exact PathBuf::with_extension target shapes and confirm which escaped existing directories can reach manifest loading.
- Exact overwrite/deletion reach depends on target existence and with_extension("_tmp") behavior; validation should test absolute and ../../../ revision strings.

### Preconditions

- High for cache-root escape and arbitrary directory creation; deletion targets are constrained to the derived ._tmp suffix and the first 16 revision bytes but remain attacker-influenced.
- Victim fetches or builds an untrusted project containing the crafted git dependency; selected destination or parent is writable.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/PackageManifest/ParseBlocks.rs:167-207` (unvalidated direct revision) — rev accepts arbitrary unquoted text with no path-component validation
- `Source/Fetch.rs:341-354,492-500,589-599` (cache path construction) — a direct rev is joined into the cache path; absolute components replace the prefix and traversal components are retained
- `Source/Fetch.rs:632-649,675-686` (filesystem mutation sink) — git_clone creates dest and recursively deletes dest.with_extension('_tmp') before cloning and later renaming
- `Source/Fetch.rs:499` (source) — Manifest GitSelector::Rev is accepted verbatim.
- `Source/Fetch.rs:589-597` (root_control) — Revision prefix is joined as a path component without rejecting absolute paths or separators.
- `Source/Fetch.rs:614-641` (sink) — Derived path controls directory creation, temp-path deletion, and clone destination.
- `Source/Fetch.rs:549-557` (source) — Locked-mode revision also reaches the same cache path builder.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently: encoding the revision as a safe cache key and enforcing containment fixes directory creation, consumption, and derived temporary deletion paths. Current reduction: carried forward with its original source-ledger identities and no cross-root collapse. Reducer dedup-0005: The new manifest/lock trace reaches the same raw revision-derived cache key and filesystem operations. Encoding the revision and enforcing cache-root containment fixes every mapped source. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## git-revision-utf8-slice-panic — Multibyte Git revisions panic dependency resolution at a byte boundary

### Source

- A malicious project or transitive dependency manifest supplies a valid UTF-8 revision whose 16th byte lies inside a multibyte character.

### Closest control

- The slice limits length to 16 bytes for path size but does not preserve UTF-8 boundaries.

### Sink or broken control

- Rust string byte indexing is performed without is_char_boundary or digest/encoding conversion and therefore panics in normal dependency resolution.

### Impact

- A crafted manifest deterministically terminates jet fetch/build resolution, causing a developer or CI denial of service.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Process-wide impact depends on panic configuration and whether the caller catches unwinding; the operation at minimum fails the requested build.

### Preconditions

- High: the panic condition follows directly from Rust str slicing semantics and occurs before git invocation.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/PackageManifest/ParseBlocks.rs:167-207` (arbitrary UTF-8 revision) — rev is any manifest string
- `Source/Fetch.rs:589-599` (unchecked UTF-8 byte slice) — rev[..16.min(rev.len())] panics when byte 16 is not a UTF-8 character boundary
- `Source/Fetch.rs:341-350,492-500` (direct rev route) — direct revisions reach git_cache_dir before external Git validation

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently: replacing byte slicing with a character-safe or digest-derived cache key fixes the panic without subsuming path traversal. Current reduction: carried forward with its original source-ledger identities and no cross-root collapse. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

## tower-owner-payload-forgery — Tower trusts caller-supplied owner attribution for privileged mutations

### Source

- Remote POST payload supplies decisionId/outcome plus by:"owner" or an arbitrary nonempty quote.
- Remote POST payload chooses card, outcome/title, and by:"owner".
- Remote POST supplies by:"owner" and optional completion cursor timestamp.
- A network client supplies POST /api/clearance JSON, including decisionId, outcome, by, quote, and comment.
- A network client supplies POST /api/clearance/batch with an attacker-selected list of decisions and shared by/quote values.
- A network client supplies POST /api/verdict with a card reference, outcome, title, and by=owner.
- A network client submits POST /api/card/update for a frozen card with by=owner and attacker-selected card fields.
- A network client submits POST /api/card/update with phase=done and by=owner for a card whose criteria are not verified.
- A network client submits POST /api/message/done with a message id and by=owner.
- A network client submits POST /api/done/clear with by=owner and an optional attacker-selected cursor timestamp.
- A network client submits POST /api/clearance/reopen for an attacker-selected decision id.
- Remote card update JSON with `by:"owner"`.
- Remote POST `/api/clearance` with `by:"owner"`, decision id, and outcome.
- Remote verdict POST with `by:"owner"` and chosen outcome.
- Any client accepted by the server, including a local agent process.
- A POST payload supplies by:"owner" or an arbitrary quote.

### Closest control

- Acceptance ballots are blocked from generic clearance, but ordinary owner decisions accept by:"owner" or any quote.
- Store rejects non-owner strings, but the caller freely supplies the exact owner literal.
- Store checks by exactly equals owner, but caller controls that value.
- Acceptance ballots have a distinct transport guard, but ordinary decisions rely only on optional server authentication plus caller-asserted identity or quote text.
- The acceptance-family filter rejects acceptance IDs, but it does not authenticate or authorize batch ratification of ordinary owner ballots.
- The store rejects by values other than owner, but that value is supplied by the same untrusted request rather than derived from authentication.
- Shape and enum validation constrain field syntax, but do not authenticate the claimed owner identity.
- The dedicated acceptance guard prevents by=owner from closing needsAcceptance cards, but ordinary unverified criteria still use the spoofable owner string.
- doneMessage() rejects non-owner strings, but the client controls that exact string.
- The function checks by === owner, but there is no authenticated identity binding at point of use.
- The UI sends by=owner, but this is only a frontend convention and the server/store do not enforce it.
- Special acceptance flags/done transition have extra checks; general frozen owner bypass remains.
- Configured auth token protects non-local callers, but token is optional; acceptance-group decisions use separate route.
- Optional shared auth token.
- mintVerdict checks by == owner, but the server does not derive that value from an authenticated owner identity.
- assertOwnerOr trusts payload fields rather than a transport-authenticated owner principal.

### Sink or broken control

- assertOwnerOr trusts caller-controlled fields rather than transport-authenticated owner identity.
- mintVerdict checks only the untrusted JSON by field.
- Owner-only check trusts caller-controlled by then advances the completion cursor.
- Authentication is disabled whenever auth.token is unset, and authorization trusts caller-controlled by=owner or any nonempty quote before ratifying the decision.
- The independently reachable batch route maps every supplied decision into ratify() while optional authentication and caller-controlled owner evidence remain the only gates.
- mintVerdict() checks only the caller-controlled by string, while the server has no authenticated-principal binding and accepts all requests when auth.token is unset.
- The frozen owner-lane guard returns immediately for the caller-controlled string by=owner.
- applyDoneGate() logs an owner bypass and permits completion solely because the untrusted body string equals owner.
- The owner-only message completion check trusts the body field by instead of an authenticated principal.
- clearDoneQueue() authorizes solely on the caller-controlled by string.
- reopenDecision() has no owner authorization check and accepts a caller-controlled by value while resetting a ratified decision to open.
- Owner lane authorization trusts body field rather than authenticated principal.
- Owner-only governance action trusts request body identity and optional auth defaults off on an all-interface listener.
- Caller-provided identity is sole owner-only check.
- Owner-only verdict creation accepts a caller assertion.
- Decision clearance/verdict paths ratify outcomes and advance cards.

### Impact

- Unauthorized ratification can select design/syntax/security outcomes and advance implementation cards as if the owner decided.
- Attacker can create durable, already-ratified owner rulings and alter downstream engineering authority.
- Completed work can be hidden from owner review and prematurely eligible for retirement.
- An unauthenticated reachable client can record an owner decision, advance blocked cards, and persist forged owner governance state.
- One request can forge and persist several owner decisions and unblock or redirect multiple cards.
- An unauthenticated reachable caller can create a durable, already-ratified owner ruling attached to a card.
- An unauthenticated reachable caller can unfreeze or rewrite owner-paused work and alter protected workflow state.
- An unauthenticated reachable caller can mark technically incomplete work done and persist false completion state.
- An unauthenticated reachable caller can hide pending agent messages from the owner and alter persistent completion state.
- An unauthenticated reachable caller can advance the owner's completion cursor and hide completed cards from the review queue.
- An unauthenticated reachable caller can revoke recorded governance state and re-block dependent work.
- Attacker can unfreeze, reassign, or alter owner-controlled work items and criteria.
- Network attacker can ratify binding decisions and advance blocked cards.
- Attacker can create durable owner rulings and alter project governance history.
- Unauthorized owner rulings and ratified decisions.
- Remote callers can choose owner decisions and alter protected project governance.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate against a fresh ordinary ballot; acceptance ballots are intentionally excluded and covered separately.
- Validate a verdict POST on a no-token instance and confirm persistence/event attribution.
- Validate queue visibility and retirement consequences after forged done/clear.
- Acceptance-specific completion remains protected by separate protocol, covered separately.
- Deployment reachability varies, but `listen(port)` is not loopback-scoped.
- None material beyond deployment exposure.
- Acceptance ballots use a separate flow; validate an ordinary ballot.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Reachability and impact require centralized validation; no final severity is assigned here.
- Reachable no-token Tower.
- Target card identifier, disclosed by state API.
- Tower server reachable over LAN/tailnet/network.
- No `auth.token` configured, which is documented default.
- Reachable Tower with default no-token config.
- Known card id or number, obtainable from unauthenticated state API.

## package-git-fetch-option-injection — Package Git revision fragments can inject fetch options

### Source

- Package upstream URL fragment controls remote.rev and may begin with --.
- An attacker-controlled permitted Git source supplies an option-like #revision such as an upload-pack override.
- A hostile package/workspace upstream such as a permitted git URL with an attacker-chosen #revision.
- A package-controlled core-provider upstream fragment after `#` becomes `remote.rev` without validation.

### Privileged boundary

- Remote package metadata crosses into a host Git subprocess.

### Closest control

- Git option parsing after repository argument must be confirmed for supported Git versions; candidate is medium confidence.
- Scheme restrictions constrain the URL but do not constrain revision option syntax.
- Network authority and URL scheme checks do not constrain revision to a ref and do not terminate git option parsing.
- `parse_remote_source` restricts URL scheme prefixes, but `split_ref` accepts any nonempty revision and the fetch command has no `--end-of-options` boundary.

### Sink or broken control

- git fetch argv places attacker-controlled rev after origin without -- or refspec validation, allowing Git option interpretation such as upload-pack selection if accepted in that position.
- git fetch interprets the project-controlled revision as an option capable of selecting upload-pack behavior.
- Command::new("git") executes fetch with attacker-controlled rev in option-parsed argv position.
- `git fetch --quiet --depth 1 --filter=blob:none origin <rev>` passes the attacker string after `origin`; Git still parses option-looking refspecs there.

### Impact

- Potential helper-command execution, network behavior change, or source-fetch policy bypass during package realization.
- Package source resolution may execute attacker-selected helper behavior with developer authority.
- Git option injection; options such as upload-pack may change invoked helper behavior and could cross the intended fetch authority boundary.
- Building or realizing a malicious package can run an attacker-selected upload-pack shell command with the developer's authority.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate with harmless fake upload-pack helper in isolated temp repo.
- Central validation should reproduce the complete application path rather than only the bounded Git CLI shape.
- Exact exploitable git option and local/remote transport behavior require validation; discovery does not claim confirmed command execution.
- Validation should reproduce through a minimal package manifest and confirm the exact provider syntax reaches sparse fetch on supported Git versions.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Shard-local bounded CLI reproduction observed the option reaching upload-pack behavior.
- Transport and Git version affect exploitability.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:463-492` (source) — split_ref preserves arbitrary fragment as rev
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:202-214` (sink) — rev appended to git fetch without option terminator
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:463-505` (source) — Untrusted upstream text after # becomes remote.rev without validation.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:483-493` (closest_control) — URL schemes are allowlisted, but revision syntax is unrestricted.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:202-214` (sink) — rev is appended to git fetch with no -- separator, allowing option interpretation.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:463-505` (source)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:202-214` (sink)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:463-505` (root_control) — split_ref accepts an arbitrary fragment as rev while validating only the base URL scheme
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:202-214` (sink) — rev is appended to git fetch without -- option termination
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:560-565` (sink) — the same rev is also passed to git checkout without --

## package-git-checkout-option-injection — Package Git revision fragments can inject checkout options

### Source

- Package upstream fragment controls checkout revision and may start with --.

### Closest control

- Exact pin-bypass options need Git-version validation; availability impact is clearer than code execution.

### Sink or broken control

- git checkout parses attacker-controlled revision as an option because no --end-of-options or validated ref syntax is used.

### Impact

- Checkout semantics/source selection can be altered, potentially defeating intended revision pin or causing controlled build failure.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate option parsing and whether any accepted option causes checkout of unintended source.

### Preconditions

- Clone occurs in a fresh temp cache and URL is scheme-validated, containing direct filesystem impact; revision syntax remains unchecked.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:463-492` (source)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:560-566` (sink) — rev passed after --quiet without --end-of-options

### Remediation subsumption

## trust-prefix-sibling-overmatch — Trust path prefix matching authorizes sibling project names

### Source

- Attacker places a project at a sibling path whose text begins with an already trusted project path, e.g. /work/app-evil after /work/app

### Closest control

- Canonicalization removes lexical aliases but the canonical result is still compared using string-prefix semantics rather than equality or Path::starts_with on components with explicit wildcard scope.

### Sink or broken control

- is_trusted/grant_matches_project_or_hash returns true and suppresses the intended project trust prompt

### Impact

- A malicious sibling project can inherit trust intended for another project and exercise build, hook, environment, service, secret, or managed-file effects under the user account.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exact reachable effects depend on the grant type and caller; both legacy and typed trust decisions share the overmatch.

### Preconditions

- A path-pattern or typed subject grant exists for a project prefix; Attacker can cause the user/tooling to open a sibling-prefix project path; The project declares trust-sensitive effects

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:401-427` (legacy trust decision) — is_trusted accepts pattern and canonical-pattern matches for the project directory.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:521-539` (typed environment grant decision) — Typed grants reuse the same project matcher.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:541-563` (broken boundary check) — Both wildcard and non-wildcard paths use raw string starts_with without a path-component boundary.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently: component-aware path ancestry replaces string-prefix authorization and fixes the sibling overmatch. Current reduction: carried forward with its original source-ledger identities and no cross-root collapse. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## signing-key-permission-fail-open — Signing-key generation writes the seed before fail-open permission tightening

### Source

- jet publish key generation on a permissive umask, filesystem with chmod failure, non-Unix platform, or attacker-influenced key path state
- A publisher generates a registry signing key on a multi-user or shared-filesystem host.

### Closest control

- The code intends mode 0600 and zeroizes memory, but does not create the file atomically with restrictive mode and does not fail if privacy cannot be established.
- The intended 0600 permission is neither established atomically at file creation nor verified before the function reports success.

### Sink or broken control

- Private Ed25519 seed remains at creation/default permissions while keygen reports success
- The Ed25519 seed can briefly be umask-readable and can remain exposed when chmod fails.

### Impact

- Another local account may read the package signing seed and forge artifacts trusted under the victim publisher identity.
- A local or shared-filesystem attacker who obtains the seed can forge packages or registry metadata under the publisher identity.

### Impact path

- Key generation -> fs::write default mode -> observation before chmod or retained permissions after ignored failure.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Default umask commonly narrows exposure; exploitability is platform/filesystem dependent and needs runtime permission validation.
- Practical race width, key-directory mode, and filesystem behavior require centralized validation.

### Preconditions

- Key generation runs where default creation permissions are broader than 0600 or permission tightening fails; A local adversary can access the resulting key path or exploit the exposure window
- Key generation runs
- Filesystem/umask permits another principal to read initial mode or chmod fails
- Attacker can inspect the key path during/after creation
- Another principal can traverse/read the keys directory during creation, or chmod fails on the backing filesystem.
- The publisher relies on this generated key for a trusted registry.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Long-lived signing authority
- Local/shared-filesystem adversary required
- Best-effort chmod failure is silent
- Private seed is written before mode hardening

### Affected locations

- `Source/Publish/Sign.rs:82-124` (secret creation) — std::fs::write creates or truncates the signing seed using umask-derived permissions, then calls set_mode.
- `Source/Publish/Sign.rs:399-406` (ignored permission failure) — Unix set_permissions errors are discarded; non-Unix implementation is a no-op.
- `Source/Publish/Sign.rs:110-118` (sink) — std::fs::write creates the seed before set_mode(0600).
- `Source/Publish/Sign.rs:399-406` (root_control) — Unix chmod errors are discarded; non-Unix set_mode is a no-op.
- `Source/Publish/Sign.rs:82-108` (source) — Registry key generation produces a fresh Ed25519 private seed.
- `Source/Publish/Sign.rs:110-122` (sink) — The seed is written to its final path before mode 0600 is applied.
- `Source/Publish/Sign.rs:396-406` (broken_control) — The separate Unix chmod ignores failure, and the non-Unix implementation does nothing.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently: atomically creating the seed with restrictive permissions and propagating permission failures fixes the disclosed key path. ## devserver-static-symlink-escape — Devserver static reads follow symlinks outside the build directory

### Source

- Attacker-controlled project/build tree contains a symlink to a developer-readable host file and attacker requests its static URL
- Symlink placed in generated `build/` tree by project source, dependency, or build hook; request path selects it.
- A project or build step places a symlink under build and a caller requests it.
- Attacker-controlled project build output containing a symlink plus a request path selecting that symlink.
- A request path selects a file under an attacker-influenced project build tree that may be a symbolic link.

### Closest control

- Literal traversal filtering keeps the lexical path under build but does not canonicalize the selected file or verify its resolved target remains beneath the root.
- Literal `..` paths are rejected and server binds loopback.
- The helper rejects literal '..' only; that is not a filesystem-resolution control.
- path.contains('..') blocks direct dot-dot spelling only and does not address symlink traversal.
- The path check is lexical and never verifies the resolved target remains under build.
- Lexical '..' rejection blocks direct parent traversal but does not stop filesystem symlink resolution.
- The resolver rejects a literal '..' substring and joins beneath the root, but performs no realpath containment or symlink check.

### Sink or broken control

- fs::read on a symlink-resolved path outside the static root
- Lexical join is treated as containment, then normal file read follows symlink.
- fs::read follows the symlink to a host file.
- fs::read follows a build-root symlink to an arbitrary host file without canonical-root verification or no-follow semantics.
- fs::read follows the selected symlink to an arbitrary readable local target.

### Impact

- Disclosure of arbitrary developer-readable host files through the devserver response.
- Remote webpage/local client can retrieve developer-readable files outside project through devserver.
- Malicious project web code can read and exfiltrate host files accessible to the developer.
- A malicious project opened with jet dev can read host files and exfiltrate them from its same-origin page.
- The response discloses arbitrary developer-readable files.
- Disclosure of developer-local files to attacker-controlled project code served from the same development origin, with possible exfiltration.
- Arbitrary local-file disclosure through the dev server.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Centralized validation should confirm build cleanup/preservation behavior for committed or prebuilt symlinks.
- Whether normal Jet build emits/copies symlinks needs end-to-end confirmation; malicious build hooks can create them.
- Some build modes may replace selected fixed assets; arbitrary additional build entries are not rejected here.
- A separate build step may clear build/ in some modes; this implementation itself does not clear arbitrary entries.
- Confirm normal build preparation preserves the chosen symlink.
- Confirm build pipeline symlink preservation and served-root placement on each supported platform.
- Validate the exact served root and whether the normal build pipeline preserves attacker-supplied symlinks.

### Preconditions

- The user runs jet dev in an attacker-supplied repository containing a build-tree symlink.

### Severity-relevant facts

- A symlink exists under build pointing to readable external file.
- Devserver serves that build tree.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (lexical-only path control) — static_path rejects literal dot-dot and joins lexically without resolving symlinks.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1270-1284` (static route and read sink) — serve_static joins the URL path and fs::read follows the resulting symlink target.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:350-387` (entrypoint) — Loopback HTTP request target selects the static relative path.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:390-404` (root_control) — The only containment check rejects textual '..'; it does not canonicalize or reject symlinks.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:404-405` (sink) — std::fs::read follows a project-supplied build/<name> symlink to its host target.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1270-1284` (static route)
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (lexical helper)
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (root_control) — static_path rejects only lexical '..' and then joins the request path to build_root without canonical containment.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1270-1283` (sink) — The resolved path is read from disk and returned as the HTTP response.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:91-94` (path control) — static_path rejects '..' lexically but does not canonicalize or reject symlinks.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:1276-1285` (file-read sink) — The resolved static path is read from disk and returned.

## lldb-breakpoint-command-injection — Generated filenames are interpolated into LLDB command text

### Source

- Attacker-controlled Jet source filename/basename used when a developer runs native debug or DAP
- A developer debugs a Jet file whose basename contains LLDB metacharacters or a newline.
- The basename of the user-selected Jet source file; Unix filenames may contain newlines and LLDB metacharacters.

### Closest control

- LLDB process launch uses safe argv, but the later command interpreter string has no quoting/escaping for the filename.
- lldb process argv is separated safely, but stem() preserves most filename bytes and the command-language argument is unquoted.
- stem() only replaces dots; the debugger performs no rejection or LLDB quoting/escaping before interpolation.

### Sink or broken control

- Inferior::cmd writes attacker-influenced text to the LLDB command interpreter
- set_breakpoint writes breakpoint set -f <filename> into LLDB stdin.
- set_breakpoint formats the filename into `breakpoint set -f ...`, and write_lines writes it verbatim to LLDB's command interpreter followed by a newline.

### Impact

- Potential LLDB option/command injection or debugger-control manipulation in the developer context.
- A malicious repository filename can inject debugger options or commands in the developer context.
- Debugging a maliciously named project file can execute attacker-chosen LLDB commands in the developer's debugger process, potentially including debugger-supported shell/script commands.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exact arbitrary-command syntax and supported LLDB parsing behavior require validation; drop if all attainable basenames are inert -f data.
- Confirm an attainable filename payload on supported filesystems and LLDB versions.
- The user explicitly chooses to debug the file, and exploitation beyond debugger state manipulation depends on LLDB command availability; malicious repositories can nevertheless supply such names.

### Preconditions

- Victim debugs a maliciously named Jet file with native LLDB path; Attainable filename bytes are interpreted specially by the installed LLDB command parser
- victim invokes native debug/DAP with LLDB
- Victim runs jet debug/native or DAP on an attacker-influenced filename
- LLDB is installed
- Filesystem permits control characters in the filename

## package-store-install-symlink-escape — Package-store installation follows dependency symlinks outside the source tree

### Source

- A malicious Git or path dependency can contain symlink entries targeting host files or directories.
- Symlink node in an attacker-controlled git dependency checkout.
- A malicious Git dependency or project path dependency contains a file or directory symlink targeting a developer/CI host path.
- A malicious Git or path dependency contains a file or directory symlink resolving outside its source root.
- Files and symlinks from a fetched Git dependency or selected path dependency.
- A malicious Git or path dependency containing a symlink to an absolute or parent-relative host path
- An untrusted path or git dependency contains a symlink outside its source root.
- Attacker-controlled Git dependency tree containing file or directory symlinks.
- A git or path dependency tree can contain symlinks to files or directories outside that dependency.
- A malicious path or Git dependency includes a file or directory symlink to a victim-readable location outside the dependency checkout.
- A project dependency tree controlled by a collaborator contains a symlink whose target is outside that tree.
- A remote Git dependency includes an absolute or escaping relative symlink.
- A malicious path or git dependency tree containing a file or directory symlink to an absolute or escaping host path.
- A malicious Git dependency or path dependency contains a symlink whose target resolves to a victim host file or directory.
- Manual full-file review of package store ingestion.
- A malicious Git/path dependency controls directory entries, including symlinks, in the tree passed to ensure_git_dep or ensure_path_dep.
- Symlink entries committed to an attacker-controlled Git dependency.
- A hostile path or git dependency tree contains file or directory symlinks targeting predictable host locations.

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted dependency filesystem entries cross into the shared store and project dependency tree.
- Untrusted package filesystem graph to trusted user-level package store.

### Closest control

- copy_jet_tree uses Path::is_dir and fs::copy, both of which follow symlink targets, without symlink_metadata or source-root containment.
- Tree hash and store content verification; both follow the same link and therefore bless copied host bytes.
- The copy skips dot names/build/target and later compares tree_hash, but both copying and hashing follow the same attacker-selected symlinks and no canonical-root check or symlink rejection occurs.
- Hidden/build directories are skipped and Jet source is hashed, but neither traversal rejects symlinks or canonicalizes descendants against the package root.
- Destination paths are constructed internally, but source entries are not rejected when they are symlinks.
- Hidden/build/target names are skipped, but link type and resolved containment are never checked.
- copy_jet_tree uses is_dir and fs::copy without canonical containment or symlink rejection.
- Lexical dot/build/target filtering and post-copy tree hash; neither rejects symlinks or proves canonical containment.
- Dot directories and build/target names are skipped, but file type and canonical containment are never checked before recursive copy.
- The copier filters dot/build/target names and later hashes selected source files, but it never rejects symlink file types or proves canonical containment.
- Git pins a revision and the resulting store tree is hashed, but neither control validates that every copied object is a regular in-tree file.
- The git revision and resulting tree hash pin source identity, but the hash routine itself follows symlinks and therefore authenticates copied host content rather than rejecting an out-of-tree target.
- Dot directories, build, and target are skipped and content hashes are verified after copying, but symlink nodes are neither rejected nor confined.
- Hidden basenames are skipped, but symlinks with non-hidden names remain traversable.
- Hidden/build/target names are skipped, but entry metadata is not checked with symlink_metadata and targets are not constrained beneath source_dir.
- Name exclusions exist, but file_type/symlink_metadata and canonical containment checks do not.
- The copier excludes hidden names and build/target directories, but does not inspect symlink_metadata, reject links, or enforce canonical containment beneath source_root.
- copy_jet_tree filters dotfiles/build/target by lexical child name and later verifies copied content hash, but does not reject symlinks or prove canonical source containment.

### Sink or broken control

- Recursive reads and copies import the symlink target into the trusted package store.
- fs::read/fs::copy recursion through symlink targets.
- copy_jet_tree uses Path::is_dir and fs::copy, both of which follow symlinks, and tree_hash likewise traverses/reads through them without lstat containment.
- Recursive reads and copies dereference attacker-supplied symlinks outside the dependency root.
- Recursive copy dereferences file and directory symlinks outside the dependency root.
- copy_jet_tree recursively reads the symlink target and copies its contents into the global package store.
- External targets are copied into the global store and linked into the build.
- copy_jet_tree recursively follows dependency symlinks into the user package store.
- Store ingestion recursively copies the external symlink target into the persistent package store and then links/copies it into the project dependency tree.
- Recursive installation dereferences the symlink and copies the target bytes into the user-global package store.
- Installation dereferences repository symlinks and copies victim-local target bytes as regular store files.
- copy_jet_tree, link_or_copy_tree, and copy_dir_recursive follow Path::is_dir and fs::copy/hard_link targets without symlink_metadata or canonical containment checks.
- copy_jet_tree follows symlinked directories/files and copies their host targets into ~/.jet/store and project dependency trees.
- Recursive store copy dereferences file symlinks and follows directory symlinks outside the declared package root.
- copy_jet_tree follows file and directory symlinks and copies host files or recursively traverses host directories into the package store.
- copy_jet_tree imports host file contents or recursively copies a host directory into the store.
- Hashing and recursive copying dereference package-controlled links and can read/copy host paths outside the cloned package.
- src_path.is_dir recursively follows directory symlinks and fs::copy follows file symlinks into the shared store/build tree.

### Impact

- Fetching a malicious dependency can copy host files or directory trees into the global store, exposing sensitive content to later package/build/vendor workflows and causing unbounded host traversal.
- Local file disclosure into artifacts/diagnostics, unintended recursive copying, and integrity confusion tied to victim-specific host state.
- Dependency resolution can ingest host file contents into the global trusted store and project dependency tree, enabling disclosure or persistent build-input contamination.
- Developer-readable host files or directories can be copied into the shared store and linked build tree, enabling disclosure through later malicious package behavior and possible resource exhaustion.
- Host files can be read and copied into the Jet store, and directory links can trigger broad traversal or resource exhaustion.
- Untrusted dependencies can import host files or whole directories into the Jet store and project dependency projection, exposing sensitive local data to later build/package operations and violating workspace isolation.
- Building a dependency can copy host files into persistent store or build artifacts.
- Host files reachable through crafted symlinks can be copied into trusted dependency/store or vendor trees.
- Fetching a malicious dependency can copy developer secrets or arbitrary host trees into package/store artifacts, enabling later disclosure or use as build input; cycles can also exhaust resources.
- Host files, including credentials or private source, can be imported into package/build trees where later tooling, packaging, or dependency code can read or disclose them.
- Files readable by the victim can be copied across the project boundary into dependency storage and then consumed or redistributed as package assets/source.
- A malicious dependency can cross the checkout boundary, capture victim-local files into package storage, and make them available to later package processing.
- Fetching, linking, or vendoring a crafted dependency can read arbitrary files or recursively copy readable host directories into the Jet store, build dependency tree, or project vendor directory, exposing local secrets and expanding trusted compilation input.
- Local files can be copied into build inputs and may be exposed by diagnostics, artifacts, vendoring, or later publication.
- Copying developer-readable host files into the package store, possible later disclosure/consumption, and recursive-cycle denial of service.
- Fetching a malicious dependency can disclose host files through copied store/project content and can exhaust disk or recurse through large external trees.
- Host-file disclosure into package material and possible disk exhaustion.
- Fetching a dependency can ingest local host files into the package store, expose them to later package processing, or cause package-triggered denial of service through recursive/special filesystem traversal.
- Fetching a hostile dependency can copy sensitive host file contents or large host directory trees into Jet's store and project build inputs, enabling disclosure through build artifacts or causing resource exhaustion.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exact downstream disclosure path depends on later use of the copied store content; symlink-following behavior was established statically, not via PoC.
- Windows/git configurations that materialize symlinks as text reduce exploitability; Linux/macOS default checkouts are relevant.
- Central validation should demonstrate file and directory symlink behavior and the clearest downstream disclosure channel.
- Downstream exposure of copied host data depends on later store/package publication behavior; platform-specific symlink behavior should be exercised.
- Runtime platform symlink behavior and later exposure should be confirmed centrally.
- Validate how each supported git/filesystem platform materializes symlinks and where copied non-.jet files are later published or executed.
- Validate the end-to-end fetch/store/link flow on Unix and identify the first normal build/runtime consumer that can exfiltrate an imported non-.jet file.
- End-to-end validation should demonstrate which package APIs expose the copied asset and calibrate confidentiality impact.
- Validate the exact checkout configuration and the best post-copy exfiltration primitive before final severity assignment.
- Validate with a temporary git dependency containing both file and directory symlinks; Windows behavior may differ when git does not materialize symlinks.
- Actual exfiltration depends on a later consumer surfacing the copied content; the containment violation itself occurs during ingestion.
- Windows symlink creation/preservation differs, but Unix developer and CI environments are directly affected.
- A full exfiltration PoC should show package code or later tooling exposing the copied bytes.
- A confidentiality demonstration should identify a normal downstream route that exports or exposes copied bytes; denial-of-service reachability is more direct.
- Downstream exfiltration depends on how dependency source/build artifacts are exposed. Registry artifact extraction may have separate symlink controls; this candidate targets path/git ingestion.

### Preconditions

- The victim fetches or builds a path dependency containing the crafted symlink; the symlink target exists and is readable.
- The victim resolves the crafted Git dependency on a system where the symlink target exists and is readable.
- The dependency checkout contains a symlink whose target is readable by the victim.; Victim performs package fetch/store installation.
- Victim platform checks out git symlinks.
- Target path is readable by the victim.
- Victim fetches the malicious dependency.
- Victim realizes an attacker-controlled dependency.
- The platform materializes symlinks and the target is readable by the developer process.
- User fetches or stores an attacker-controlled dependency tree containing symlinks
- A linked host path exists and is readable
- Platform supports symlinks and victim fetches a dependency containing a link whose target exists on the victim host.
- The dependency contains symlinks and targets are readable.
- Victim fetches a malicious Git dependency.
- Checkout platform materializes symlinks.
- A fetched repository preserves a crafted symlink and the link target is readable by the developer.
- Victim fetches/builds a hostile dependency on a platform that materializes symlinks.
- The symlink target is readable by the victim.
- A dependency source includes attacker-controlled symlinks
- Filesystem permits symlinks
- The victim fetches or installs an attacker-controlled dependency containing a symlink to a readable host path.
- Git preserves symlinks.
- The target exists and is readable.
- The victim fetches the dependency.
- The platform materializes repository symlinks, as on typical Unix git checkouts.
- The developer fetches or vendors an attacker-controlled git dependency, or resolves an untrusted path dependency.
- The symlink target is readable by the developer process.
- Victim fetches or builds an attacker-controlled dependency containing symlinks
- Symlink target is readable
- The package source preserves attacker-created symlinks and the resolved target is readable by the Jet process.
- Dependency checkout preserves symlinks; target path exists and is readable by the developer/CI account; user runs fetch.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Reachability and impact require centralized validation; no final severity is assigned here.
- Git can materialize repository symlinks on supported Unix hosts.
- The final exfiltration channel depends on subsequent package behavior.
- The threat model forbids project collaborators from gaining authority outside the project.
- The global store can outlive the original dependency tree.
- No local collaborator access is required when the dependency is remote.
- The effect occurs during dependency installation.

## vendor-symlink-escape — Vendoring follows dependency symlinks outside the source tree

### Source

- A malicious resolved dependency tree can contain symlinks targeting host files or directories.
- A resolved malicious dependency contains a symlink to a host file or directory.

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted dependency filesystem graph to developer-controlled vendored output.

### Closest control

- copy_dir_recursive follows symlinks through Path::is_dir and fs::copy without symlink rejection or source-root containment.
- copy_dir_recursive uses is_dir/fs::copy without rejecting symlinks or enforcing a resolved source root.

### Sink or broken control

- jet registry vendor copies the resolved target content into the project vendor tree.
- The vendor operation copies resolved target content into the project vendor tree.

### Impact

- An opt-in vendor operation can copy developer/CI host secrets into a project tree that may later be committed or published.
- Developer or CI secrets can be copied into a tree later committed or published.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Opt-in workflow lowers likelihood; downstream commit/publish and exact source-dir selection require centralized validation.
- Downstream disclosure depends on commit/publish workflow.

### Preconditions

- Victim vendors a resolved malicious dependency.; A dependency symlink target is readable.
- victim opts into registry vendor
- symlink target is readable
- Victim vendors a dependency containing attacker-controlled symlinks
- Filesystem permits symlinks
- The victim invokes jet registry vendor.
- A dependency contains a symlink.
- The target is readable.

### Affected locations

- `Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:17-46` (entrypoint/wrapper)
- `Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:110-118` (root_control)
- `Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:117-120` (sink)
- `Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:17-56` (entry)
- `Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:110-123` (copy sink)
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:39-55` (entrypoint) — The vendor command recursively copies each dependency into its destination.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:110-123` (recursive copy sink) — copy_dir_recursive follows is_dir and fs::copy without a symlink or canonical-root policy.
- `Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:9-22,39-62` (vendor roots) — Resolved dependency directories are recursively copied.
- `Source/Publish/Vendor.rs:110-123` (symlink-following copy) — is_dir/fs::copy dereference links.
- `Source/Fetch.rs:535-578` (path/git sources) — dep_dirs can point directly to path dependencies or Git caches.

## web-codegen-template-injection — Jet string literals are emitted raw into generated JavaScript templates

### Source

- Attacker-authored safe Jet literal text in an interpolated string.

### Closest control

- The interpolation branch appends literal parts directly between JavaScript backticks; unlike the non-interpolated branch, it does not escape backticks, backslashes, or JavaScript interpolation delimiters.

### Sink or broken control

- The resulting text is written as executable app.js and loaded by the web target.

### Impact

- Safe Jet source can break out of the intended string literal and inject arbitrary JavaScript into the generated web application, bypassing language capability/type controls.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Parser character preservation and an end-to-end web build were not dynamically validated; the raw emitter mismatch is direct static evidence.

### Preconditions

- Victim builds or serves attacker-authored Jet source for the web target.; The parser permits relevant literal characters in an interpolated string.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:4363-4371` (entrypoint/wrapper)
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:4609-4617` (root_control)
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:4615-4617` (sink)

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently: JavaScript-string/template escaping at web code generation fixes every absorbed interpolation path. Current reduction: carried forward with its original source-ledger identities and no cross-root collapse. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## rustc-build-profile-env-injection — Project build-profile environment reaches the rustc process

### Source

- Attacker-controlled pkg.jet named-profile environment key/value pairs.

### Closest control

- ProfileConfig copies arbitrary environment names and values without denying process-loader/tool-resolution variables or separating build-time compiler environment from program runtime environment.

### Sink or broken control

- apply_env installs the values on the rustc Command immediately before spawning the compiler.

### Impact

- A cloned malicious project can influence executable lookup or dynamic-loader behavior of rustc and plausibly execute attacker-controlled native code with developer/CI privileges when that profile is built.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Platform-specific executable/loader behavior and named-profile selection flow require centralized validation; no payload was executed.

### Preconditions

- Victim selects a malicious named build profile from the project.; The platform honors an injected compiler-process environment variable such as a loader or path control.

### Affected locations

- `Source/main.rs:192-201` (entrypoint/wrapper)
- `Source/main.rs:272-275` (root_control)
- `Source/CmdCompile.rs:3036-3048` (sink)

## dependency-name-path-traversal — Unvalidated package identifiers escape store, project, and registry roots

### Source

- Attacker-controlled dependency keys and package version strings from root or fetched manifests.
- An attacker-controlled manifest uses a rooted, separator-containing, or parent-component dependency key.
- Attacker-controlled pkg.jet dependency key such as ../../outside/name
- A fetched dependency controls its quoted payload version; the parser copies it without path-component validation.
- Project dependency aliases and dependency package version strings come from pkg.jet and may contain path separators or parent components.
- The dependency alias is the raw key from a cloned project's deps block.
- A hostile root or transitive package manifest supplies a dependency key containing ../ components or an absolute path.
- A malicious root or transitive package manifest controls dependency alias names and dependency package version metadata.
- full-file discovery review
- A Git or path dependency package manifest supplies its package version (and potentially name).
- The package version field in an attacker-controlled dependency manifest.
- A hostile Jet package manifest controls dependency-map keys, which become dep_name.
- A hostile project manifest controls a dependency name propagated as a dep_dirs map key.

### Privileged boundary

- Manifest identifiers cross into developer filesystem path construction.

### Closest control

- Manifest parsing and path construction do not require dependency names or versions to be single safe path components, and destination joins lack containment enforcement.
- Version and fingerprint suffixes shape store names but no parser or sink check enforces a single safe component or post-join containment.
- Manifest parsing validates dependency value shape but never requires dependency keys to be a single safe identifier/path segment.
- Dependency values and Git shapes are parsed, but dependency key names are only trimmed; neither the parser nor Fetch validates them as a single safe path component.
- Manifest parsing checks dependency value shape but never restricts names/version to one safe path component; normalize_path applies only to path dependency source paths, not destination names.
- The registry base directory is selected by trusted configuration, but Path::join does not sanitize parent components in the appended name.
- The fingerprint prefix is stripped, but no component, separator, canonical-containment, or semantic-version validation is applied before joining.
- The store suffix contains a hex fingerprint, but package version characters and path components are never validated or encoded.
- Dependency source values and hashes are validated, but no control constrains dependency names to one safe path component before Path::join.
- Vendor base directory is resolved by the CLI, but each dependency name is joined without rejecting absolute paths, separators, `.` or `..`.

### Sink or broken control

- Store creation/copy and project dependency linking use paths derived from raw dependency names or versions.
- Path joining and directory creation may resolve outside intended store or project dependency roots.
- PathBuf::join on raw dependency names selects store and project materialization destinations.
- PathBuf::join accepts parent traversal and replaces the prefix for absolute operands, after which create_dir_all and recursive link/copy write the dependency tree outside the intended roots.
- Store::ensure_path_dep derives ~/.jet/store paths from name/version, and Store::link_into_project recursively copies package files to project_root/.jet-build/deps/<dep_name>.
- index_entry_path joins the raw name into a filesystem path, and write_index_entry creates parents then writes it without canonical containment enforcement.
- fs::create_dir_all and copy_jet_tree operate on the derived store path, so separator and parent components can move the destination outside ~/.jet/store.
- create_dir_all and copy_jet_tree operate on store_dir().join(format!(name-version-fingerprint)), allowing slash and parent components from version to redirect writes outside the store.
- create_dir_all plus recursive copy/hardlink operations write dependency-controlled trees to store_path and project_root/.jet-build/deps.join(dep_name).
- std::fs::remove_dir_all(dest) followed by recursive copy at the escaped destination.

### Impact

- Routine dependency fetch can create or overwrite attacker-selected developer-writable paths outside package roots.
- Fetching a malicious project may create or populate attacker-selected writable directory trees outside intended package locations.
- Running jet fetch on a malicious project can create and populate attacker-chosen directories outside the package store and .jet-build/deps, potentially modifying project or host files.
- A malicious dependency manifest can redirect package installation outside ~/.jet/store and overwrite/create attacker-chosen user-writable paths with dependency content.
- Ordinary dependency fetch can create directories and overwrite files outside ~/.jet/store, including trusted configuration or executable locations writable by the developer.
- Fetch can hard-link or copy dependency content to attacker-selected writable paths outside the project build directory.
- Building a malicious manifest can create and populate attacker-selected directories outside the project build tree or package store under the victim account.
- A supply-chain package can place attacker-controlled source files in newly created directories outside ~/.jet/store or .jet-build/deps, including elsewhere in the project, home, or parent directories.
- Running registry publish on a malicious project can create or overwrite a .jsonl-suffixed file outside the registry clone with the user's permissions.
- A malicious dependency can make fetch create directories and copy its source tree outside the intended package store, overwriting files where derived names collide.
- Fetching a malicious package can create directories and copy attacker-controlled files outside the intended global package store under the user's account.
- Running `jet fetch` on a hostile project can create attacker-controlled directories/files at writable paths outside the package store and project build root.
- When a developer runs `jet registry vendor`, a crafted dependency name can select and recursively delete an arbitrary existing writable directory outside vendor, then attempt to replace it with dependency content.

### Impact path

- malicious transitive manifest key -> Dep.name -> resolve_dep -> store_path/link join -> filesystem writes outside root
- malicious transitive deps key containing ../ -> parse_deps/Convert -> Resolver dep_name -> .jet-build/deps.join(dep_name) and store_path(name,version,fp) -> recursive filesystem copy outside intended root

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Existing destination directories may cause early reuse; attacker can choose a fresh destination.
- Central validation should establish accepted key syntax and actual escaped writes on each supported platform.
- Parser-to-store dataflow is static and direct; filesystem effects were not dynamically validated in this no-PoC shard.
- Validate exact manifest spelling accepted by the current parser and target-platform path semantics.
- Validate one accepted crafted key against the current parser without writing outside a temporary test root.
- Validate exact accepted manifest spelling for ../ and absolute aliases and bound the write primitive on Unix and Windows.
- Existing-directory early return limits overwrite of established directories, but creation and file placement outside the intended roots remain direct.
- The suffix limits exact filename choice, but does not restore store-root containment or prevent escaped directory writes.
- Central validation should construct the shortest accepted manifest and determine the most security-relevant reliably writable destination.
- A higher-level manifest grammar or command path may reject slash/absolute keys before these helpers; discovery found no such validation. Exact platform path semantics need reproduction.
- A higher-level parser may reject path-shaped names; none was found in the dependency parser. remove_dir_all behavior for parent-component paths is platform-dependent, while absolute-path selection is direct.

### Preconditions

- Victim fetches/builds a malicious git/path dependency containing a crafted transitive dependency name.
- Escaped destination is writable or does not yet exist.
- Victim fetches an attacker-controlled manifest.
- The crafted key is accepted and the escaped target is writable.
- Victim runs jet fetch/update for an attacker-controlled project manifest and the chosen destination does not already exist as a directory.
- Developer fetches an attacker-controlled project or dependency manifest with crafted alias/version text.
- Manifest grammar accepts a crafted dependency key containing separators/parent components on the target platform.
- Victim resolves/builds a manifest containing a malicious dependency alias.
- The chosen destination is writable and does not already cause link_into_project to return early.
- Victim runs jet registry publish in an attacker-controlled project
- A useful writable target can be addressed with the forced .jsonl suffix and repeated name components
- The victim fetches a package with crafted identity fields and has write permission to the escaped destination.
- A fetched dependency controls its manifest version and supplies enough slash/parent components to escape the store root; target placement must satisfy existing-file and hidden-file constraints.
- Developer or CI runs fetch on a crafted manifest; the dependency resolves; escaped destination is writable and not already short-circuited as an existing directory.
- Developer or CI runs the vendor command on a crafted manifest; dependency resolution succeeds; selected destination exists and process has write permission.

## canvas-project-revision-not-enforced — Canvas project transactions parse but do not enforce project_revision

### Source

- A Canvas project transaction supplies project_revision and touched-file revisions.

### Closest control

- Touched files are checked individually, but the required project_revision is assigned to an unused variable.

### Sink or broken control

- The operation dispatch persists dependency, package, workspace, target, field, or service changes.

### Impact

- A stale client can commit a project-wide transaction against a different projected state and violate optimistic concurrency.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate a multi-file stale-state conflict where touched files remain unchanged.

### Preconditions

- Project state changes after the client projection while the operation's listed touched-file checks still pass.
- valid current revisions for named touched files

### Affected locations

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/schema_api.rs:399-420` (root_control) — The requested project_revision is assigned to an underscore-prefixed variable and never compared with ctx.project_revision.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/project_transactions.rs:1028-1088` (sink) — Accepted project changes are written to source-truth files.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/schema_api.rs:399-425` (broken control)

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because enforcing the advertised project_revision before transaction dispatch fixes this stale-project snapshot control; request authentication and symlink containment are separate controls. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## gzip-runtime-unbounded-output — Gzip decompression has no output budget

### Source

- Jet application or build/comptime-adjacent flow passing attacker-supplied gzip bytes to core.compress.gzip.decompress.
- Compressed gzip bytes supplied to the exported runtime API.
- Attacker-controlled gzip bytes reaching core.compress.gzip.decompress
- Jet program input supplies highly compressible gzip bytes to the decompression API.
- Jet application passes attacker-controlled compressed bytes to core.compress.gzip.decompress on AOT or JIT tier.

### Privileged boundary

- Compressed runtime input to Jet application process memory and CPU

### Closest control

- Malformed-stream errors only; no take(), byte counter, decompressed-size ceiling, or configurable budget in AOT/JIT.
- Malformed-stream errors are handled, but decoded byte count and expansion ratio are not bounded.
- Malformed-stream errors are returned, but read_to_end grows an unbounded Vec; the interpreter archive implementation separately demonstrates a 64 MiB policy cap
- Decoder errors are propagated, but output size or expansion ratio is not limited.
- Malformed-stream Result handling only; no compressed size, expansion ratio, or maximum output check. Interpreter sibling has a 64 MiB cap, proving intended bounded behavior elsewhere.

### Sink or broken control

- flate2::read::GzDecoder::read_to_end grows Vec until stream end.
- GzDecoder::read_to_end grows a Vec until end of stream.
- GzDecoder::read_to_end(&mut Vec)
- read_to_end materializes the entire decompressed stream in memory.
- GzDecoder::read_to_end allocates until stream completion.

### Impact

- A small gzip bomb can exhaust memory or terminate a Jet service/process; JIT then allocates a second list representation, increasing amplification.
- Memory exhaustion and process denial of service.
- Memory and CPU exhaustion from a compact high-ratio gzip stream
- A small compressed payload can exhaust process memory or cause prolonged CPU use in an application/service using the API.
- Small gzip bomb can exhaust process memory or CPU in Jet services processing untrusted compressed content.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Impact depends on caller-side limits and deployment memory controls; public API itself provides no safe bound.
- Application reachability and a practical compressed-to-expanded ratio need centralized validation.
- Severity depends on whether the embedding application separately limits compressed input/output.
- Generic decompression APIs sometimes delegate limits to callers, but Jet API exposes no bounded variant and tier sibling enforces a cap.

### Preconditions

- An application passes attacker-influenced compressed bytes to gzip decompression.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Runtime consumer exposure is application-dependent
- No expanded-output cap
- Shared runtime wrapper returns the full allocation
- Expansion ratio can be attacker-controlled.
- The API returns a fully materialized byte vector.

## zstd-runtime-unbounded-output — Zstandard decompression has no output budget

### Source

- Jet application passing attacker-supplied zstd bytes to core.compress.zstd.decompress.
- Compressed zstd bytes supplied to the exported runtime API.
- Attacker-controlled zstd bytes reaching core.compress.zstd.decompress
- Jet program input supplies highly compressible zstd bytes to the decompression API.
- Jet application passes attacker-controlled zstd frames to core.compress.zstd.decompress on AOT or JIT tier.

### Privileged boundary

- Compressed runtime input to Jet application process memory and CPU

### Closest control

- Decode errors only; AOT/JIT do not apply the resident evaluator's existing output/window bounds.
- Malformed-stream errors are handled, but decoded byte count and expansion ratio are not bounded.
- decode_all has no surrounding output/window budget, while the interpreter archive decoder separately limits output and window sizes
- Library decode errors are mapped, but no output cap or expansion-ratio policy is supplied.
- Decode errors only; no maximum frame/output/ratio guard. Interpreter implementation caps window at 128 MiB and output at 64 MiB.

### Sink or broken control

- zstd::stream::decode_all consumes and allocates the entire expanded stream.
- zstd::stream::decode_all grows a Vec until end of stream.
- zstd::stream::decode_all(data)
- decode_all materializes all decompressed bytes.
- zstd::stream::decode_all expands the complete stream into memory.

### Impact

- Memory exhaustion and process/service denial of service from high-ratio zstd input, with extra JIT heap-copy amplification.
- Memory exhaustion and process denial of service.
- Memory or CPU exhaustion from a high-expansion or large-window zstd frame
- Memory exhaustion or CPU denial of service in an application/service using the API.
- Compressed bomb can exhaust memory/CPU in a Jet process handling untrusted zstd input.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Caller/deployment limits can mitigate impact; API-level behavior remains unsafe-by-default for untrusted streams.
- Decoder library defaults and a compact practical trigger need centralized validation.
- Severity depends on external request/input limits in the embedding application.
- Final reportability depends on whether API contract assigns output budgeting to callers.

### Preconditions

- An application passes attacker-influenced compressed bytes to zstd decompression.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Runtime exposure depends on application use
- No explicit cap
- Full decoded allocation is copied into the JIT heap representation
- The output allocation is controlled by decompressed size.
- No local resource budget is enforced.

### Affected locations

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Compress.rs:49-52` (concrete_implementation) — Canonical zstd runtime implementation decodes the entire frame into memory.

- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Compress.rs:47-51` (root_control) — zstd::stream::decode_all allocates the full decompressed stream with no API ceiling.
