## tower-docs-symlink-walk — Tower docs inventory recursively traverses symlinked directories

### Source

- A malicious checked-out repository containing a directory symlink under docs, including a self-referential or external-tree link.
- A repository/workspace supplies a symlink under docs/, or a same-user process creates one before enumeration.
- An attacker-controlled project contains a symlinked directory beneath docs pointing to an external host directory.

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted project directory graph to host filesystem contents and long-lived Tower process availability.

### Closest control

- Hidden-name filtering and .md suffix filtering; neither constrains the resolved directory graph.
- Hidden-name filtering and lexical prefix construction do not inspect link targets.
- walkMd skips dot names and filters .md suffixes but uses statSync rather than lstatSync/realpath confinement, so it treats a directory symlink as an in-root directory.

### Sink or broken control

- statSync/readFileSync plus recursive walkMd calls follow symlink targets with no containment or cycle detection.
- Recursive readdir/stat/read outside the docs root.
- Recursive traversal reads external markdown metadata/content for title extraction and exposes discoverable paths through the docs API.

### Impact

- Disclosure of markdown contents/titles outside the project and deterministic process crash or resource exhaustion through symlink cycles or very large external trees.
- External markdown metadata/title disclosure and denial of service through cycles or large trees.
- Enumeration of external markdown filenames, titles, sizes, and timestamps, enabling subsequent targeted showDoc reads through the same symlink path.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exact crash depth and external-file exposure depend on platform and accessible tree contents.
- Low.
- Validation should test cycles as well as external traversal; symlink loops may additionally cause resource exhaustion or caught recursion errors depending on platform.

### Preconditions

- Victim runs Tower in a repository with a malicious docs directory symlink.
- Platform supports checked-out symlinks.
- Tower operates on an untrusted or locally tampered workspace containing a docs symlink; API reach is separate.
- Victim runs Tower in a project containing an attacker-planted directory symlink; external directory is readable.

### Affected locations

- `plugins/tower/app/docs.mjs:142-161` (root_control) — walkMd uses statSync, follows directory symlinks, and recurses without realpath containment or a visited-directory set.
- `plugins/tower/app/docs.mjs:149-158` (sink) — Traversal recursively reads .md files and returns their metadata/title.
- `plugins/tower/app/docs.mjs:182-207` (entrypoint/wrapper) — listDocs invokes walkMd for the whole docs tree.
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:256-263` (entrypoint/wrapper) — GET /api/docs without path returns the recursive inventory.
- `plugins/tower/app/docs.mjs:142-160` (root_control) — statSync follows symlinks and walkMd recursively enters directory targets without realpath containment or cycle tracking
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:257-263` (entrypoint/wrapper) — GET /api/docs invokes listDocs
- `plugins/tower/app/docs.mjs:182-206` (sink) — listDocs returns external markdown metadata/titles and can recurse unbounded symlink graphs
- `plugins/tower/app/docs.mjs:142-161` (root_control) — walkMd uses statSync, recursively follows directory symlinks, and reads discovered .md files.
- `plugins/tower/app/docs.mjs:182-187` (entrypoint/wrapper) — listDocs traverses the docs root.
- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:257-263` (sink) — GET /api/docs returns discovered external paths, titles, sizes, and timestamps.

## processspec-output-limit-late — ProcessSpec output_limit is enforced only after unbounded capture

### Source

- A spawned child process writes attacker-influenced or unbounded stdout/stderr.

### Closest control

- ProcessSpec exposes timeout_ms and output_limit.

### Sink or broken control

- read_to_string consumes the complete streams before output_limit is evaluated.

### Impact

- Memory exhaustion of the JIT host despite the caller configuring an output limit.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Reachability depends on the authority granted to process execution, but the advertised limit is ineffective whenever reached.
- External OS limits may terminate first; the code provides no bound.
- The memory threshold should be calibrated during validation.

### Preconditions

- A Jet program can spawn a process whose output volume is attacker-controlled or otherwise unbounded
- Output capture is enabled
- Captured output is enabled.
- The child is attacker-controlled or faulty.
- The caller relies on output_limit.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Reachability and impact require centralized validation; no final severity is assigned here.

## build-action-unbounded-output — Local build actions capture unbounded output without a timeout

### Source

- A project-controlled BuildAction launches an approved tool/executable that emits unbounded stdout or stderr or never exits.

### Closest control

- Remote execution has timeout_ms, and local actions require capability/tool resolution and bubblewrap; none of those controls limit local output or duration.

### Sink or broken control

- The local action path calls std::process::Command::output(), which buffers both streams completely and has neither a byte limit nor a local timeout.

### Impact

- A malicious workspace/build package can hang a developer or CI build indefinitely or exhaust host memory.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Reachability and impact require centralized validation; no final severity is assigned here.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Build/execution_runtime.rs:212-255` (entrypoint/wrapper)
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Build/execution_runtime.rs:397-448` (root_control)
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Build/execution_runtime.rs:448-456` (sink)

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because bounding and timing out local build-action capture fixes this subprocess sink; the separate ProcessSpec post-capture limit does not cover this implementation. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## notebook-preauth-slowloris — Notebook server authenticates only after a blocking read on its sole connection loop

### Source

- A remote client connects to a notebook explicitly exposed with --bind and sends no request bytes.

### Closest control

- Request storage is capped at 4096 bytes, but that does not bound time waiting for bytes.

### Sink or broken control

- The single-threaded listener performs a blocking stream.read() with no read deadline before parsing or checking the bearer token.

### Impact

- One connection can indefinitely deny health/UI access and notebook service until restart.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Default loopback binding lowers remote exposure; non-loopback mode explicitly exists and bearer auth does not protect the pre-auth socket.

### Preconditions

- Attacker can reach loopback locally or an explicitly non-loopback notebook bind.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Reachability and impact require centralized validation; no final severity is assigned here.

### Affected locations

- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:48-59` (entrypoint/wrapper)
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:117-128` (root_control)
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:118-167` (sink)

### Remediation subsumption

- Merged duplicate notebook reports of the same single accept-loop blocking read before authentication. A pre-auth read deadline plus concurrent/bounded connection handling fixes every absorbed source. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## jetpack-self-authorized-build-script — Project policy can self-authorize unsandboxed dependency build script

### Source

- Malicious project manifest sets trust allow and points to package containing Cargo build script.

### Closest control

- UI describes policy as source-reviewed; sandbox warning is emitted, and operator can preconfigure `sandbox require`.

### Sink or broken control

- Untrusted metadata supplies its own trust decision, after which cargo executes package build.rs without a jail under default policy.

### Impact

- Opening/running attacker project can execute arbitrary build-script code with developer privileges without an independent user grant.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Need validate exact top-level command ordering for every entry path and whether product treats source-reviewed `allow` as intentional independent consent.

### Preconditions

- User invokes trust-sensitive Jet env/build flow in attacker project.
- Project `policy.trust` parser accepts default allow.
- Package is realized as library with Cargo.toml/build.rs.
- Default sandbox fallback remains enabled.

### Severity-relevant facts

- User invokes trust-sensitive Jet env/build flow in attacker project.
- Project `policy.trust` parser accepts default allow.
- Package is realized as library with Cargo.toml/build.rs.
- Default sandbox fallback remains enabled.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:712-748` (attacker-defined authorization) — Project manifest `policy.trust.default = allow` returns success before user prompt or stored grant.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/PackageManifest/mod.rs:110-134` (manifest-controlled trust value) — Trust policy and Allow decision are parsed from project-controlled package metadata.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider.rs:621-704,740-779` (untrusted package materialization) — Remote package tree including Cargo.toml is copied then automatically compiled for library packages.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider.rs:992-1020` (process execution sink) — Pinned cargo executes package Cargo.toml and build.rs with inherited host authority.
- `crates/jetpack/src/RuntimePolicy.rs:214-218,246-351` (sandbox fallback) — Default policy explicitly permits unsandboxed fallback; detector never reports Strong.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because project-controlled policy and the dependency build script cross the same trust decision; requiring authority external to the dependency fixes this self-authorization path. ## jit-http-crlf-injection — JIT generic HTTP request serialization permits CRLF request injection

### Source

- JIT code supplies request method, URL, or cookie strings.

### Closest control

- The canonical HTTP implementation validates method and header control characters at crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/HTTP.rs:3055-3065, but the JIT cleartext helper does not apply equivalent validation and does not enforce its accumulated header_error.
- Explicit headers have a validator, but these independent fields are concatenated without control-character checks.
- The destination must use http:// and connect successfully; URL scheme/host parsing occurs, but it does not sanitize CRLF-bearing request components.

### Sink or broken control

- Raw request-line and Cookie bytes are written to TcpStream.
- Those strings are inserted verbatim into a cleartext HTTP/1 request and written to the destination socket.

### Impact

- An attacker who influences a forwarded request field can smuggle request bytes to an upstream cleartext HTTP service, potentially injecting headers, splitting requests, or confusing intermediary/backend message boundaries.
- Untrusted values can inject headers or additional HTTP framing toward a chosen origin.
- HTTP request splitting, injected headers, or an extra request to the selected origin/proxy, potentially confusing downstream authorization and request boundaries.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Semantic-layer constraints may reduce which source fields typical Jet programs expose; validate with a minimal JIT program containing CRLF in each field.
- Confirm safe Jet URL construction preserves CR/LF; method and cookie strings are directly controllable.
- Public API conversions may reject some malformed field forms before this host function; validation should enumerate each reachable field independently.

### Preconditions

- Jet program forwards attacker-controlled strings into generic request method/URL/cookie
- JIT/dev execution is used
- Destination accepts cleartext HTTP
- Code runs through the JIT host implementation.
- The destination uses cleartext http://.
- Untrusted input reaches method, URL, or cookie fields.
- generic request API under JIT
- cleartext HTTP destination
- Application code uses the JIT HTTPRequest.send path over cleartext HTTP.
- Less-trusted data reaches a serialized request field.
- A downstream server or proxy interprets injected delimiters.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Code runs through the JIT host implementation.
- The destination uses cleartext http://.
- Untrusted input reaches method, URL, or cookie fields.
- An attacker who influences a forwarded request field can smuggle request bytes to an upstream cleartext HTTP service, potentially injecting headers, splitting requests, or confusing intermediary/backend message boundaries.
- Uncertainty: Semantic-layer constraints may reduce which source fields typical Jet programs expose; validate with a minimal JIT program containing CRLF in each field.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1318-1323,1357-1365` (attacker_source) — JIT request constructor accepts method/URL and cookie builder accepts name/value as runtime strings.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1406-1469` (root_control) — Method, URL-derived path/authority, and cookie strings are concatenated without CR/LF validation.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1464-1483` (sink) — Constructed bytes are written directly to TCP stream.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/HTTP.rs:3050-3070` (negative_control) — Canonical AOT send path validates method token and rejects CR/LF/NUL in headers.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1407-1416, 1441-1453` (untrusted request fields) — Cookie name/value and raw URL-derived authority/path are copied without control-character validation.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1463-1483` (raw HTTP serialization sink) — Method, path, authority, cookies, and headers are interpolated directly into an HTTP/1.1 byte stream.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1557-1564` (JIT host entrypoint) — The request host function calls the vulnerable cleartext helper.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1318-1365` (sources)
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1406-1483` (serialization sink)
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:1406-1482` (Raw request construction) — Concatenates method, path, authority, cookies, and custom header names/values with CRLF separators without rejecting embedded CR/LF.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-jit/src/jit/lower_ctx.rs:18159-18165` (JIT reachability) — Lowers HTTPRequest.send to the affected host function.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/HTTP.rs:3056-3065` (Contrasting validation) — The canonical transport validates the method token and rejects CR/LF/NUL in headers, showing the JIT path bypasses an expected control.

## devserver-build-symlink-overwrite — Project-controlled build symlink redirects finalized web outputs to host paths

### Source

- An attacker-supplied repository can make build a symlink to another writable host directory before the user runs jet dev.

### Closest control

- The staging root is recreated, but the real output root is merely create_dir_all'd; that accepts an existing directory symlink.

### Sink or broken control

- Final destination ownership and canonical project containment are not verified before rename.

### Impact

- Routine dev startup can overwrite predictable files (including index.html/app.js/manifest names) outside the project with attacker-generated content.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Repository checkout policy may reject symlinked build on some platforms; Unix Git worktrees normally preserve it.

### Preconditions

- Malicious project controls a build symlink and the user runs its dev entry with write permission to the target.

### Affected locations

- `Source/CmdCompile.rs:721-740` (entrypoint) — jet dev runs the generated program in the project working directory with JET_DEV_FILE/JET_BIN.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:230-235,302-307` (root_control) — Staging is isolated, but the final build directory is accepted without symlink/canonical containment checks.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:308-315,325-336` (sink) — Six staged files are renamed to build/<fixed-name>, following a symlinked build parent.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because descriptor-bound, no-follow finalization beneath the build root fixes the generated-output write sink; static-file read containment does not fix it. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## package-git-kind-probe-option-injection — Jetpack provider-kind probe parses an untrusted revision as a Git option

### Source

- An attacker-controlled package upstream supplies an option-like Git revision.

### Privileged boundary

- Remote source metadata crosses into a host subprocess before provider kind is known.

### Closest control

- Network policy and Git-availability checks do not constrain the revision argv element.

### Sink or broken control

- The provider classification fetch interprets the revision as a Git option.

### Impact

- Lightweight remote classification may execute attacker-selected helper behavior with developer authority.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Central validation should reproduce the application-level probe and supported transport set.

### Preconditions

- Online provider-kind inference runs for an attacker-controlled source.
- Git and an applicable transport are available.

### Severity-relevant facts

- This probe is independently reachable from sparse realization.
- It shares the Git CLI shape observed in shard-local bounded reproduction.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:463-509` (revision source) — The upstream #revision is preserved without option-prefix validation.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider.rs:1701-1712` (probe sink) — The revision is passed to git fetch after origin without an end-of-options control.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because terminating or validating revision arguments at the provider-kind probe invocation fixes this separately reachable Git subprocess; sparse realization and checkout invocations remain separate. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## lsp-predictable-log-symlink-write — LSP panic logging follows a predictable shared temporary symlink

### Source

- A local attacker prepositions /tmp/jet-lsp.log as a symlink and attacker-controlled project/protocol input triggers a caught handler panic.

### Privileged boundary

- A shared temporary namespace crosses into a developer-authority file append.

### Closest control

- The panic is caught, but the fixed pathname is opened with ordinary symlink-following semantics.

### Sink or broken control

- The panic line is appended through a prepositioned symlink to a developer-writable target.

### Impact

- A local attacker can append constrained log text to an arbitrary file writable by the developer.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Central validation should identify a harmless panic trigger and confirm platform-specific open semantics.

### Preconditions

- A local attacker can create the predictable /tmp path first.
- Attacker-controlled input can trigger a caught handler panic.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Requires a local attacker and a reliable caught-panic trigger.
- Content is constrained to the logging format.

### Affected locations

- `Source/LSP/Server.rs:270-288` (panic source) — A caught request-handler panic is converted to a log message.
- `Source/LSP/Server.rs:291-299` (open sink) — OpenOptions create+append opens fixed /tmp/jet-lsp.log without no-follow, ownership, or inode checks.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because secure exclusive temporary-file creation fixes the predictable LSP panic-log write sink. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## plugin-call-unbounded-resources — Sandboxed WASM plugin execution lacks time and memory budgets

### Source

- A Jet application loads an untrusted or compromised WASM component and calls an exported function.

### Privileged boundary

- Capability-denied plugin code crosses into shared host CPU and memory resources.

### Closest control

- The empty linker denies filesystem/network/process imports and traps are caught, but capability isolation does not bound computation or memory growth.

### Sink or broken control

- func.call runs synchronously in an unlimited Store, allowing non-termination or memory exhaustion.

### Impact

- A malicious sandboxed plugin can hang or terminate the host Jet process through CPU or memory exhaustion.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Central validation should confirm Wasmtime defaults and demonstrate bounded harmless CPU and memory exhaustion cases.

### Preconditions

- An application intentionally loads and calls an attacker-controlled plugin component.

### Severity-relevant facts

- The plugin cannot access host capabilities through imports.
- Resource denial remains possible inside the supposedly sandboxed compute boundary.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:52-75` (plugin load boundary) — Engine and Store are created without fuel, epoch interruption, or a Store limiter.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/Prelude/Plugin.rs:91-141` (plugin call sink) — An untrusted exported function is called synchronously with no time or memory budget.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because Wasmtime fuel, epoch interruption, and memory limits at plugin-call execution fix this sandbox resource-control gap. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## wasm-list-i64-untrusted-ownership — Generated WebAssembly integer-list ABI reconstructs and frees unchecked host pointers

### Source

- JavaScript or another embedding host can supply forged, reused, interior, or mismatched pointer/count values.

### Closest control

- Null is rejected, but no allocation identity, bounds, alignment, layout, or ownership state is verified.

### Sink or broken control

- Unchecked Box::from_raw reconstruction assumes the pointer came from the matching allocator exactly once and that len matches its layout.

### Impact

- The host can cause invalid free, double free, out-of-bounds vector ownership, traps, or corruption of Jet state within the Wasm module.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Practical impact depends on which symbols are exported in the final module and browser sandbox containment.

### Preconditions

- An untrusted embedding context can call the generated integer-list ABI or exported Jet functions that consume it.

### Severity-relevant facts

- An untrusted embedding context can call the generated integer-list ABI or exported Jet functions that consume it.
- The host can cause invalid free, double free, out-of-bounds vector ownership, traps, or corruption of Jet state within the Wasm module.
- Uncertainty: Practical impact depends on which symbols are exported in the final module and browser sandbox containment.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:1892-1917` (root_control) — A packed host pointer and element count become Box<[i64]> ownership without provenance checks.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:1919-1929` (sink) — The exported list free accepts arbitrary pointer/count pairs.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because allocation identity, bounds, layout, and consume-once checks must be enforced for the generated integer-list ABI instance. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. ## wasm-list-string-untrusted-ownership — Generated WebAssembly string-list ABI trusts host pointer ownership and embedded counts

### Source

- JavaScript or another embedding host controls the packed pointer/length and contents of the encoded list blob.

### Closest control

- Assertions check some blob offsets only after the unsafe Box conversion; they cannot establish pointer provenance or prevent double-free/invalid-free.

### Sink or broken control

- Raw Box ownership is reconstructed from untrusted integers, and the blob's count is used in Vec::with_capacity without a semantic item ceiling.

### Impact

- Forged calls can corrupt or trap the module and crafted counts can amplify memory consumption, violating memory-safe application behavior.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validation should confirm export visibility and whether glue code hides the raw symbols from ordinary page scripts.

### Preconditions

- An untrusted embedding context can invoke the generated string-list ABI or a corresponding exported Jet function.

### Severity-relevant facts

- An untrusted embedding context can invoke the generated string-list ABI or a corresponding exported Jet function.
- Forged calls can corrupt or trap the module and crafted counts can amplify memory consumption, violating memory-safe application behavior.
- Uncertainty: Validation should confirm export visibility and whether glue code hides the raw symbols from ordinary page scripts.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:1933-1970` (root_control) — A host pointer and byte length are converted to owned bytes without provenance validation.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:1971-1985` (sink) — Attacker-controlled count and lengths drive allocation/parsing after ownership reconstruction.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:1987-1997` (sink) — The exported free accepts arbitrary pointer and byte length.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because the generated string-list blob ABI has its own pointer ownership, embedded-count, and allocation-budget controls. ## wasm-map-untrusted-ownership — Generated WebAssembly string-map ABI reconstructs and frees unchecked host pointers

### Source

- JavaScript or another embedding host controls the packed pointer/length and serialized map bytes.

### Closest control

- Checked arithmetic and assertions bound offsets within the claimed slice, but no control proves that the slice itself is a live matching allocation or has not already been freed.

### Sink or broken control

- Unchecked Box::from_raw assumes unique matching allocation ownership, while serialized counts are trusted to drive repeated decoding.

### Impact

- Forged or repeated calls can cause invalid/double free, traps, or corruption of Jet application state inside the module.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validation should determine final symbol exposure and demonstrate the module-level consequence under the supported JS glue.

### Preconditions

- An untrusted embedding context can invoke the generated map ABI or a matching exported Jet function.

### Severity-relevant facts

- An untrusted embedding context can invoke the generated map ABI or a matching exported Jet function.
- Forged or repeated calls can cause invalid/double free, traps, or corruption of Jet application state inside the module.
- Uncertainty: Validation should determine final symbol exposure and demonstrate the module-level consequence under the supported JS glue.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:2001-2038` (root_control) — A packed host pointer and byte length become owned Rust bytes with no allocation provenance check.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:2039-2059` (sink) — Host-controlled entry counts and lengths drive decoding after unsafe ownership reconstruction.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:2061-2071` (sink) — The exported free accepts arbitrary pointer and byte length.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because the generated map ABI has its own pointer ownership and serialized-count decoding instance. ## wasm-string-untrusted-ownership — Generated WebAssembly string ABI reconstructs and frees unchecked host pointers

### Source

- JavaScript or another WebAssembly embedding host can call exported bindings/free functions with forged, stale, duplicated, interior, or mismatched pointer-length pairs.

### Closest control

- The only check is ptr != 0 (plus a len==0 branch); there is no allocation registry, capability handle, bounds/provenance validation, or consume-once state.

### Sink or broken control

- Box::from_raw(slice_from_raw_parts_mut(...)) assumes allocation provenance, exact layout, and unique ownership that the host values do not prove.

### Impact

- Forged calls can trigger double free, invalid deallocation, memory corruption, traps, or corruption of memory-safe Jet application state inside the Wasm module.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- WebAssembly sandboxing may contain host compromise, but application integrity and Jet's in-module memory-safety guarantee remain at risk; export visibility should be confirmed.

### Preconditions

- Untrusted or compromised JavaScript can access the instantiated module's exports, or an exported Jet function accepts a packed string argument from an embedding host.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Untrusted or compromised JavaScript can access the instantiated module's exports, or an exported Jet function accepts a packed string argument from an embedding host.
- Forged calls can trigger double free, invalid deallocation, memory corruption, traps, or corruption of memory-safe Jet application state inside the Wasm module.
- Uncertainty: WebAssembly sandboxing may contain host compromise, but application integrity and Jet's in-module memory-safety guarantee remain at risk; export visibility should be confirmed.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:1851-1876` (root_control) — A host-provided packed pointer and length are converted directly into Box ownership.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs:1878-1888` (sink) — The exported free accepts any nonzero pointer and arbitrary length and reconstructs a Box.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained independently because the generated scalar string ABI must validate allocation provenance, exact layout, and consume-once ownership. ## d0017-s1-tar-pax-allocation — PAX logical size can bypass stored-size allocation limit

### Source

- A downloaded attacker-controlled tar stream containing PAX headers and a following metadata entry.
- full-file discovery review

### Privileged boundary

- Remote registry archive bytes cross into the package manager's local validation process.

### Closest control

- MAX_ARCHIVE_ENTRY_BYTES is checked against a PAX-overridden logical size, not the raw stored size used for allocation.
- Compressed download, logical per-entry, total expanded size, and entry-count limits exist, but none bounds the raw stored size used for metadata capacity in this state.

### Sink or broken control

- Vec::with_capacity(stored as usize) allocates from the unchecked tar header size before confirming payload availability.
- A small inherited PAX logical size can pass per-entry accounting while an attacker-selected large stored size drives Vec capacity.

### Impact

- A small malicious provider archive can request extreme memory allocation and terminate or destabilize the Jet process.
- A crafted package archive can trigger excessive allocation or process termination during validation.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- A synthetic two-header tar should confirm the parser state transition and allocator behavior on supported targets.

### Preconditions

- Jet inspects an attacker-controlled provider tar archive
- Archive uses a PAX size override followed by a metadata-type entry with a large stored size
- Victim fetches a crafted tar or tar.gz package
- Allocator attempts the attacker-declared capacity before payload truncation is detected

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:315-332` (PAX size state)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:335-340` (logical-only limit check)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:342-347` (stored-size allocation sink) — Metadata entry buffer capacity uses unchecked stored as usize.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:233-246` (entrypoint) — Downloaded archives pass a compressed-size budget and enter tar preflight.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:315-342` (broken_control) — A pending PAX logical size replaces stored size for limit accounting, while metadata allocation still uses raw stored size.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:342-349` (sink) — Vec::with_capacity(stored as usize) allocates before the metadata payload is read.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0005: Retained separately: this provider TAR parser checks PAX logical size but allocates from unchecked stored size. Existing runtime TAR eager materialization uses a different parser and sink. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to d0017-s1-tar-pax-allocation: each identifies the same actionable root control and sink instance, or a broader receipt assigned once to its strongest matching canonical tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes every absorbed instance. Distinct independently reachable implementations remain separate. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## d0017-s1-aot-termios-layout — AOT terminal control uses a non-portable termios FFI layout

### Source

- Normal live/secret-input runtime operation
- Ordinary safe Jet code can enter a live terminal block or call the secret-input API on macOS, reaching the generated terminal adapter without an explicit unsafe region.

### Closest control

- The code attempts platform padding and uses repr(C), but padding cannot correct wrong field widths, offsets, and omitted fields.

### Sink or broken control

- The hand-written repr(C) Termios does not match the 64-bit Darwin ABI; tcgetattr writes a larger/differently laid-out native structure through the pointer.

### Impact

- Stack memory corruption and potentially safe-language memory-safety escape in generated AOT programs on macOS.
- Calling a safe terminal API on macOS can overwrite adjacent stack memory and later pass mislaid fields back to tcsetattr, violating Jet's memory-safety invariant and plausibly crashing or corrupting generated programs.

### Impact path

- safe live/input_secret feature -> jet_term_enter[_secret] -> jet_term_unix::enter -> tcgetattr writes native struct into undersized Rust allocation

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm size/offsets with a macOS compile-time assertion and ASan run.
- Central validation should compile on Darwin, assert size/alignment against the platform header, and run under ASan; other BSD Unix targets may have additional mismatches.

### Preconditions

- AOT runtime executes the terminal-control path on an affected non-Linux Unix ABI
- Standard input is a terminal or reaches tcgetattr
- 64-bit macOS target
- Terminal-mode operation is invoked
- Generated native program runs on macOS with terminal stdin and invokes live/direct-input or input_secret.
- generated program runs on macOS or another non-Linux Unix with an incompatible termios ABI
- stdin is a terminal and the safe terminal feature is entered

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:314-331` (custom termios layout)
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:333-360` (FFI declarations and write) — tcgetattr writes the platform struct into the custom Rust allocation.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:303-339` (incorrect FFI type) — Non-Linux Unix uses four u32 flags, c_cc[32], and 12 bytes padding, omitting Darwin speed_t fields and 64-bit flag widths.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:346-364` (memory-writing FFI call) — tcgetattr writes the native termios struct into the undersized Rust allocation.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:530-544` (ordinary language entry points) — live blocks and secret input enter this path.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:300-335` (root_control) — A guessed Linux-shaped Termios is also compiled for macOS.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:343-359` (sink) — tcgetattr writes and tcsetattr reads through the incompatible struct pointer.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/FSIoEnvOsTesting.rs:320-346` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Safe input_secret enters the terminal adapter.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:303-334` (root_control) — Main checkout compiles one guessed Termios layout for all Unix targets.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:336-371` (sink) — Main checkout passes the incompatible value to tcgetattr/tcsetattr.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/FSIoEnvOsTesting.rs:320-346` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Safe input_secret reaches the terminal adapter.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:303-334` (root_control) — one hand-written repr(C) Termios is used for every Unix target; the non-Linux form is 60 bytes with u32 flags and no speed_t fields
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:336-359` (sink) — tcgetattr writes the native termios object through a pointer to the mismatched Rust layout
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core/RuntimeControl.rs:530-546` (entrypoint) — ordinary live blocks and secret input call the Unix enter helper without an unsafe source boundary

### Remediation subsumption

- Mapped macOS termios report reaches the AOT RuntimeControl custom allocation and tcgetattr write. Using the target libc layout fixes this instance; the independent JIT IO.rs allocation remains separate. ## d0017-s1-jit-termios-layout — JIT secret-input path uses a non-portable termios FFI layout

### Source

- JIT terminal/secret-input host call
- An ordinary interactive Jet program invokes secret input or a terminal raw-mode operation on 64-bit macOS.

### Closest control

- repr(C) and a 12-byte non-Linux pad are present, but the Darwin flag widths, c_cc length, and speed fields remain wrong.
- The module selects a Linux-specific layout only on Linux and attempts to cover every other Unix with manual padding, but no platform ABI binding or compile-time size/offset assertion exists.

### Sink or broken control

- An undersized and misaligned hand-written Termios is passed to libc tcgetattr, which writes the native Darwin structure.
- On LP64 Darwin the native structure is 72 bytes while this Rust allocation is 60 bytes, so tcgetattr writes 12 bytes beyond it. The hard-coded VMIN/VTIME indices and ICANON value are also Linux values rather than Darwin values.

### Impact

- Stack memory corruption in the JIT host process and possible escape from Jet language memory-safety guarantees.
- Stack memory corruption and process crash, with potential code-execution consequences depending on compiler layout and reachable overwrite targets; terminal state handling is also incorrect.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm independently because this implementation and call stack differ from AOT.
- No macOS binary or sanitizer reproduction was available. Centralized validation should compile on supported macOS targets and measure size/offsets against libc before calibrating exploitability.

### Preconditions

- JIT runtime executes io.secret on an affected non-Linux Unix ABI
- Standard input reaches the terminal-mode path
- 64-bit macOS target
- JIT terminal operation is invoked
- A 64-bit macOS build reaches the Unix terminal helper with file descriptor 0 attached to a terminal.
- The libc ABI matches Apple's published XNU termios definitions.

### Severity-relevant facts

- 12-byte out-of-bounds native write on LP64 Darwin
- Reachable through normal interactive I/O
- No untrusted byte content controls the terminal structure
- Exploitability beyond denial of service is unproven

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:145-154` (safe secret-input entry)
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:157-180` (custom termios layout)
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:182-208` (FFI declarations and write)
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:141-154` (ordinary JIT entry point)
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:157-220` (incorrect FFI type and write) — The same non-Darwin layout is passed to tcgetattr/tcsetattr.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:440-447` (host-call exposure)
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:141-154` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Secret input enters the Unix terminal-mode helper on an interactive terminal.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:157-184` (broken_control) — The hand-written non-Linux repr(C) Termios uses four u32 flags, 32 control bytes, and 12 padding bytes, which does not match Darwin's four unsigned-long flags, 20 control bytes, and two unsigned-long speeds.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:191-210` (sink) — tcgetattr writes the native object through a pointer to the smaller Rust allocation; tcsetattr later reads it using the same false type declaration.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/IO.rs:537-545` (entrypoint/wrapper) — The JIT terminal-enter host function also reaches the helper for raw key input.

## d0017-s3-studio-slowloris — One incomplete Studio HTTP request blocks the single-threaded service indefinitely

### Source

- Client-controlled TCP connection and partial HTTP request.

### Closest control

- 64 KiB size cutoff exists, but no socket timeout, concurrency, or progress deadline exists.
- A 64 KiB buffer threshold limits completed bytes but not time spent waiting; transaction sessions occur after the blocking read.

### Sink or broken control

- read_http_request blocks the only accept/handler loop while client withholds remaining headers/body.
- Serial listener performs deadline-free blocking reads before any route/session logic.

### Impact

- Reliable denial of service of the persistent Studio UI until the connection closes or process restarts.
- One unauthenticated connection prevents every later Studio request from being served.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- OS/network infrastructure may impose an external idle timeout; code sets none.
- Validate with an explicitly exposed address and a partial request; code path is deterministic.

### Preconditions

- Attacker can connect to running Studio listener.
- jetos Studio is running with project context.
- Remote reachability is direct when --serve binds a non-loopback address; browser loopback reachability needs local-network access.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/studio_server.rs:88-93` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Incoming connections are handled synchronously inside the accept loop.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/studio_server.rs:191-203` (root_control) — Blocking reads have no read deadline and wait for request completion.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/studio_server.rs:54-102` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Listener may bind a caller-selected address and processes accepted connections serially.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/studio_server.rs:107-116` (sink) — Single accept loop blocks in request reading before dispatch.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/studio_server.rs:189-203` (root_control) — Socket read has no deadline and waits for request completeness.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0005: Retained separately: Studio has its own single-threaded accept loop and blocking request reader. Fixing the notebook server would leave Studio reachable. Reducer dedup-0006 absorbed only source ledgers identifying this same actionable control and sink; fixing the canonical control fixes every mapped source. Distinct reachable sinks remain separate. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to d0017-s3-studio-slowloris: each identifies the same actionable root control and sink instance, or a broader receipt assigned once to its strongest matching canonical tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes every absorbed instance. Distinct independently reachable implementations remain separate. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## jetos-storage-disk-command-injection — JetOS storage disk value becomes executable second-stage shell syntax

### Source

- A malicious storage disk option or JETOS_STORAGE_DISK value containing shell metacharacters/newlines

### Closest control

- Manual and execute flags gate destructive action, and first-stage assignment is quoted, but no quoting is applied when constructing the executed second-stage script.

### Sink or broken control

- The generated script places the raw disk string into sfdisk and mkfs command lines and executes it with sh.

### Impact

- A crafted storage configuration can execute commands in the privileged installer/activation context and can corrupt arbitrary storage.

### Preconditions

- An operator generates the JetOS system and runs jetos-storage-apply --manual --execute with attacker-influenced configuration/environment.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/module_storage_workload.rs:48-62` (source) — storage.disk.main.device is loaded from module options and can later be overridden by JETOS_STORAGE_DISK.
- `crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/module_storage_workload.rs:112-116` (insufficient_control) — shell_single_quote protects only the first variable assignment, while printf writes the expanded disk value unquoted into a new script.
- `crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/module_storage_workload.rs:112-120` (sink) — With --manual --execute, sh executes apply-plan.sh containing attacker shell metacharacters.

### Remediation subsumption

- Kept separate from ESP-size injection because disk and ESP are independently controlled values and fixing either interpolation alone leaves the other sink reachable. Validate the disk grammar and shell-quote it at second-stage script generation. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

## jetos-storage-esp-command-injection — JetOS ESP size is embedded unescaped in an executed apply script

### Source

- A malicious ESP size containing command substitution or newline/heredoc syntax

### Closest control

- No size grammar or shell escaping is applied; manual/execute flags require operator action but do not neutralize configuration text.

### Sink or broken control

- Command substitution in the generated here-document is evaluated when the second-stage apply script runs.

### Impact

- Attacker-controlled JetOS storage configuration can execute commands in the privileged storage-apply context.

### Preconditions

- An operator runs the generated storage apply command with both --manual and --execute.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/module_storage_workload.rs:61-62` (source) — storage.disk.main.partitions.esp.size is accepted as an unrestricted option string.
- `crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/module_storage_workload.rs:112-116` (sink) — The value is inserted into printf's here-document template and then written into apply-plan.sh, which is executed by sh.

### Remediation subsumption

- Kept separate from disk injection because ESP size has its own source and interpolation; fixing disk handling does not constrain this value. Enforce a size grammar and avoid reparsing it as shell source. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

- `/home/nate/.local/state/codex-desktop/tmp/codex-security-scans-RXsW6B/jet/47fa26f4b77fbaca22268f5fd25d534a800b442a_20260803T121428Z_1xq12eh9/artifacts/deep_discovery/workers/discovery-0013/output/findings/d13-s1-jetos-esp-command-injection/candidate_ledger.jsonl`

## jetpack-dotenv-symlink-read — Project-relative dotenv validation follows symlinks outside the project

### Source

- A project-controlled relative dotenv path and symlink.
- A malicious repository contains a project-relative symlink named by dotenv.

### Closest control

- Lexical component checks do not canonicalize and re-check containment or prohibit symlinks.
- Lexical path validation does not resolve the final path beneath the project.

### Sink or broken control

- The dotenv reader follows the link and imports target assignments.
- read_dotenv follows the link and consumes a host file outside the project.

### Impact

- Reading and propagating environment-formatted data from outside the project into hooks, services, or shells.
- Host file values that parse as KEY=value are disclosed into the project environment and its child processes.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Low on containment failure; useful disclosure depends on target format.

### Preconditions

- A project symlink targets a readable KEY=value file.
- The checkout preserves symlinks and the external target is readable/dotenv-compatible.

### Severity-relevant facts

- The checkout preserves symlinks and the external target is readable/dotenv-compatible.
- Host file values that parse as KEY=value are disclosed into the project environment and its child processes.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs:276-291` (root_control) — Rejects absolute and .. components only.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs:326-354` (sink) — read_to_string follows the resulting path.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs:292-299` (concrete_implementation) — Parsed values enter the child environment.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Environment.rs:1212-1223` (lexical control) — Only absolute and parent components are rejected.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs:276-299` (read and injection sink) — current_dir.join(relative) is read without canonical containment and parsed into environment variables.

### Remediation subsumption

- Single dotenv read boundary. Canonical containment or no-follow traversal before read_to_string fixes the mapped source. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to jetpack-dotenv-symlink-read: each identifies the same actionable root control and sink instance, or a broader receipt assigned once to its strongest matching canonical tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes every absorbed instance. Distinct independently reachable implementations remain separate. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

## jetpack-typed-environment-trust-bypass — Typed Jetpack environments bypass trust for lifecycle hooks and services when packages and secrets are empty

### Source

- Dev-service commands from an untrusted project environment.
- Attacker-controlled lifecycle on_enter command in an env.jet file.

### Closest control

- The typed flag is ignored by the precondition that returns Ok for empty refs/secrets.
- Trust::gate_with_environment prompts only when is_trust_sensitive_ext reports package refs or declared secrets.

### Sink or broken control

- Service startup executes project-defined service processes.
- A plain-string hook becomes trusted and is executed by Platform::shell_command even when the environment never triggered a trust prompt.

### Impact

- Project process execution without the intended trust decision.
- Arbitrary command execution with developer privileges when entering or activating an attacker-supplied repository.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm exact ordering for every shell hook variant and whether another outer trust layer exists in released CLI wiring.
- Low; direct call path and early return are explicit.
- Low.
- Medium; concrete downstream impact depends on variable names and invoked tooling.

### Preconditions

- Project declares a trusted lifecycle hook but no package refs or secrets; user enters/runs the environment.
- The environment has services but no packages or declared secrets and the user starts/enters it.
- Developer installed the Jet environment hook or explicitly activates the environment
- Attacker-controlled project defines lifecycle hooks but no package refs or declared secrets
- Victim enters/runs the attacker project with a lifecycle hook and no refs/secrets.
- Victim runs the environment test/check workflow.
- Victim runs jet services up/restart/watch or jet dev.
- Victim starts or waits for the malicious service.
- Victim enters/runs the project environment.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Victim enters/runs the attacker project with a lifecycle hook and no refs/secrets.
- Developer-privilege command execution without the trust prompt the typed trust model promises.
- Victim runs the environment test/check workflow.
- Developer-privilege command execution without environment approval.
- Victim runs jet services up/restart/watch or jet dev.
- Unapproved developer-privilege process execution.
- Victim starts or waits for the malicious service.
- Unapproved command execution, potentially repeated during readiness polling.
- Victim enters/runs the project environment.
- Unapproved environment manipulation, including PATH/tool/config variable influence and unintended secret propagation.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:884-895` (root_control) — Early return ignores typed environment sensitivity.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:475-488` (evidence) — Lifecycle hooks are classified as typed trust-sensitive facts.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:672-699` (entrypoint/wrapper)
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:146-213` (sink) — A trusted:true project hook is passed to a shell.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:884-895` (root_control)

- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:349-360` (entrypoint/wrapper)
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:238-258` (sink) — Service startup reaches Services::up_one.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Environment.rs:1222-1239` (source) — Plain-string lifecycle commands from env.jet are accepted and marked trusted.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:343-345` (broken_control) — Trust sensitivity considers package refs and declared secrets only; lifecycle commands are ignored.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:1096-1150` (entrypoint) — Automatic environment activation gates only trust-sensitive environments, then runs lifecycle hooks.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:146-213` (sink) — Trusted lifecycle hook strings execute through the platform shell.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:257-365` (typed trust identity) — Lifecycle, files, and services are explicitly hashed as executable policy.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:884-903` (broken gate) — gate_with_hash returns success solely when refs and secrets are empty, before evaluating typed trust.

- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:146-213` (command sink) — The clean-mode shell command still executes project text.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/DevService.rs:30-66` (source parser) — Project service run arrays become DevServicePlan.run.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:336-364` (caller) — Service actions invoke the typed gate.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Services.rs:1173-1235` (process sink) — Command::new executes run[0] and arguments.
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/DevService.rs:41-49,63-75` (source parser) — Project ready probes and legacy readiness commands enter the service plan.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:1425-1464` (caller) — jet dev skips approval then waits for services.

- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Environment.rs:1158-1235` (source parser) — Project controls dotenv path and an empty allowlist imports every variable.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/trust_env_build.rs:276-299` (environment sink) — All parsed assignments are inserted into the command/shell environment.

### Remediation subsumption

## provider-registry-private-network-ssrf — Project provider policy can authorize private-network HTTPS fetches

### Source

- Project-controlled policy.providers.<kind>.registry/allow and provider package metadata URLs
- Project-controlled provider registry/allow policy and provider metadata URLs.
- Attacker-controlled provider registry hostname in project configuration, including a domain whose DNS answers the attacker can change.
- A malicious project manifest supplies policy.providers registry data and package metadata that causes a fetch.

### Closest control

- Authority::check_url enforces HTTPS, port 443, deny/allow hostname membership, redirect count, size, and time limits, but the project defines the registry/allow set and the control does not reject private/reserved IPs or validate resolved addresses.
- HTTPS, port, redirect, size, time, and hostname-membership checks exist, but the project supplies allowed authorities and resolved private/reserved addresses or DNS rebinding are not rejected.
- Scheme, port, credentials, redirects, and authority allow/deny checks are hardened, but the primary authority is self-authorized from the untrusted manifest and private/loopback address classes are not rejected.
- check_url enforces HTTPS, port 443, and an authority allowlist on every redirect, but never resolves the host or rejects loopback, private, link-local, or otherwise internal destination addresses.
- HTTPS/443, disabled proxies, and an authority allowlist are enforced, but the project-selected registry is auto-allowed and resolved private or loopback IPs are not rejected.

### Sink or broken control

- hardened curl execution from Authority::to_path during ScriptRegistryProvider::realize
- Provider realization invokes hardened curl against the accepted authority and manually follows accepted redirects.
- curl connects from the developer/build host to the attacker-selected HTTPS authority and path.
- hardened curl performs the network request after hostname-only checks, leaving DNS resolution outside the enforced boundary.
- hardened_curl performs an outbound request to the attacker-selected hostname.

### Impact

- Network reachability from the developer host to loopback, link-local, or private HTTPS services; response bytes may also influence provider resolution before integrity validation of source archives.
- Developer-host network reachability to loopback, link-local, or private HTTPS services; returned bytes can influence provider resolution.
- Server-side request forgery against internal HTTPS services, including disclosure through fetched metadata/artifacts or state-changing GET behavior.
- Potential requests to internal HTTPS services under attacker-controlled DNS, with response bytes accepted as provider artifacts.
- A hostile project can make a developer or CI host send HTTPS requests to internal services, including through DNS rebinding.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Static trace establishes request reachability, but no live internal service was contacted. Central validation should determine whether the project trust model intentionally grants arbitrary network authority and whether provider realization can occur before an equivalent arbitrary-code boundary.
- An explicit project trust prompt or provider-policy approval in an outer caller may be an adequate control; validation should trace that boundary before reportability.
- TLS hostname verification substantially constrains exploitation; validation should determine realistic internal targets and whether curl pinning or resolver behavior provides unstated protection.
- TLS and fixed-port restrictions narrow targets; validate with controlled DNS and a private HTTPS service.

### Preconditions

- A provider operation runs in the project and an internal HTTPS destination is reachable.
- Victim invokes an online registry-provider realization for an attacker-influenced project
- Target service accepts HTTPS on port 443
- Project trust/realization gates permit reaching the provider fetch
- The user runs provider resolution for the untrusted project
- Network/provider effects are enabled
- The internal target serves HTTPS on port 443 with a trusted certificate or attacker-controlled local trust conditions
- Victim processes an attacker-controlled provider configuration; attacker controls DNS for an allowlisted hostname; target HTTPS service presents a certificate valid for that hostname or the environment trust store otherwise accepts it.
- The victim resolves the malicious project. A private HTTPS service must accept port 443 with a valid certificate for the chosen hostname, or DNS rebinding must satisfy that condition.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:52-80` (project registry admission)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:130-200` (network sink)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:440-475` (host validation)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:52-84` (project-controlled registry and allow source) — Loads provider policy from the project manifest and automatically inserts the configured registry authority into the allow set.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:128-200` (redirect-aware request sink) — Checks only URL authority membership, then invokes curl for each URL/redirect.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:204-228, 443-475` (DNS-blind hostname validation) — Hardens curl protocol/options but accepts numeric host labels and applies no resolved-address private-range policy.

## buildrecipe-exec-unsandboxed — BuildRecipe run executes tools with ambient host authority

### Source

- An approved recipe selects a realized tool and arguments.

### Closest control

- Validation checks membership but never enters the OS sandbox or removes ambient authority.

### Sink or broken control

- Command executes directly in the source directory with inherited host privileges.

### Impact

- A malicious build tool can read secrets, modify user files, or use undeclared network.

## compiler-extension-json-depth-dos — Shared package-model JSON parser permits stack-exhausting nesting

### Source

- Untrusted compiler-extension response
- An unauthenticated Studio POST body containing many nested arrays or objects.

### Closest control

- Wasm fuel/memory/time limits constrain the guest, not the host JSON decoder; a raw byte limit exists but is enforced too late and has no depth component.
- The server's 64 KiB request cap limits bytes but not structural nesting depth.
- Download size is capped at 64 MiB, but no JSON nesting depth is capped; a much smaller payload can exhaust stack.

### Sink or broken control

- Array/object parsing recursively calls value with no nesting limit, and max_response_bytes is checked only after decode returns.
- Recursive JSON descent allocates one native stack frame per nesting level with no depth check.
- Recursive Parser::value/object/array call chain.

### Impact

- A deeply nested response can overflow the compiler host thread stack and crash the build despite extension sandboxing.
- Denial of service of the Studio process, potentially terminating the CLI/server.
- A registry response can crash Jetpack package search/realization processes and automated dependency workflows.

### Impact path

- POST /studio/transaction or /studio/run -> <=64KiB nested JSON -> JSON::parse -> value/array recursion -> stack exhaustion

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Generate nested arrays within the configured response limit and measure host stack exhaustion threshold.
- Exact crash depth varies by build, thread stack, and platform and was not measured.
- Need measure stack exhaustion threshold and whether Rust panic mode aborts this binary.

### Preconditions

- A project loads an attacker-controlled compiler extension
- Attacker can reach the Studio listener.
- A sufficiently nested payload fits within the request cap.
- Platform stack size and Rust overflow handling permit process termination.
- Victim contacts an allowed malicious/compromised provider authority.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/JSON.rs:50-151` (unbounded recursive parser)
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/CompilerExtension.rs:464-478` (untrusted response decode)
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/CompilerExtension.rs:488-505` (late byte-size validation)
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/studio_server.rs:189-220` (network body bound) — Studio stops reading only after roughly 64 KiB and forwards complete request bodies.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/studio_transactions.rs:1353-1365` (network parser call) — Studio parses attacker-controlled JSON using jet_pkg_model::JSON::parse.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/JSON.rs:50-62,86-151` (unbounded recursion) — value recursively calls object/array and back to value without a depth or node budget.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/JSON.rs:50-61` (root_control) — Shared JSON parser initializes no nesting budget.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/JSON.rs:86-150` (sink) — Object and array parsing recursively invokes value without a depth check.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/script_registry.rs:850-861` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Fetched RubyGems/CPAN/Packagist JSON metadata is passed to crate::JSON::parse.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/fetch.rs:121-125` (source) — Provider response bytes are read and decoded as metadata text.

### Remediation subsumption

- Distinct host parser and compiler-extension response boundary. Enforce byte and depth limits before or during this decode. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 mapped 2 supplied source ledger(s) to compiler-extension-json-depth-dos: each identifies the same actionable root control and sink instance, or a broader receipt assigned once to its strongest matching canonical tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes every absorbed instance. ## nix-json-depth-dos — Nix evaluator JSON parser has no nesting limit

### Source

- Repository-controlled builtins.fromJSON string

### Closest control

- Syntax and trailing-data checks exist, but neither input length nor structural depth is bounded at this parser boundary.
- json_to_value enforces MAX_EVAL_DEPTH only after the entire recursive JSON tree has already been constructed.

### Sink or broken control

- Parser::value recursively enters object/array without a depth counter or iterative stack.
- Unbounded Rust call-stack recursion in Parser::value/object/array.

### Impact

- A deeply nested string can overflow the evaluator process stack and deny service during evaluation.
- Malformed project/flake input can stack-overflow and abort Jetpack evaluation instead of returning the advertised resource-limit error.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Use a generated nested-array expression to determine whether panic aborts or unwinds in shipped binaries.
- Exact abort depth is platform and build-profile dependent.

### Preconditions

- Victim evaluates attacker-controlled project Nix
- Victim evaluates a foreign flake containing builtins.fromJSON on attacker-controlled deeply nested JSON.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/JSON.rs:40-141` (recursive parser)
- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/Evaluator.rs:2300-2305` (project-language entry point)
- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/JSON.rs:40-46` (root_control) — Parser is created without a nesting counter.
- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/JSON.rs:78-141` (sink) — value recursively enters object/array and back into value for every nesting level.
- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/Evaluator.rs:2300-2306` (concrete_implementation) — builtins.fromJSON parses foreign-flake-controlled text before json_to_value applies MAX_EVAL_DEPTH.

### Remediation subsumption

- Distinct evaluator parser and project-language entry point. Add a structural-depth limit to this parser. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. ## transitive-path-dependency-escape — Transitive path dependencies can escape their fetched dependency root

### Source

- A fetched dependency controls its own transitive path dependency string.

### Closest control

- Lexical normalization removes dot components but no containment check keeps the resolved path below the fetched dependency root; absolute paths are accepted.

### Sink or broken control

- Manifest loading, hashing, package-store ingestion, and build linking consume the escaped host path.

### Impact

- A malicious dependency can ingest and compile a guessed local package outside its checkout, exposing or promoting local source into trusted package flow.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Evidence references a historical mirror path. Current-tree equivalence and root-versus-transitive policy intent require centralized validation.

### Preconditions

- A fetched dependency declares an absolute or ../-prefixed path dependency.
- A useful package manifest exists at the targeted host path.

### Affected locations

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/Fetch.rs:254-263` (root_control) — Absolute paths are accepted and relative paths are normalized without a parent-root containment check.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/Fetch.rs:288-318` (sink) — The escaped directory is hashed, copied into the store, verified against its self-derived hash, and linked into the build.

### Remediation subsumption

- Kept separate from dependency-name traversal because this source is a transitive path value and its containment control is independent. Reject absolute paths and enforce containment beneath the declaring dependency root. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. ## jit-http-worker-runtime-uaf — Resident JIT teardown can leave HTTP workers with stale runtime and code pointers

### Source

- An HTTP request races with resident teardown/recompile while a Jet HTTP server worker or accept loop remains alive.

### Closest control

- Runtime accesses normally acquire RuntimeAccessGuard, and the shared pointer is eventually cleared.

### Sink or broken control

- Destruction does not acquire the runtime-access guard or synchronously stop/join server workers; module/runtime storage is dropped before the atomic shared pointer is cleared.

### Impact

- Use-after-free of JitRuntime or execution through a freed JIT code pointer, causing memory corruption or process compromise.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validation must confirm Arc/server-thread ownership and the exact shutdown behavior of included HTTPServer code at runtime.

### Preconditions

- A resident JIT program starts an HTTP server
- Teardown or recompilation occurs while a worker can dispatch a request

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-jit/src/Concurrency.rs:146-180` (affected_location) — A raw JitRuntime pointer is published process-wide and loaded by HTTP worker threads.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:35-47` (affected_location) — Teardown clears only the handle vector; server/handler Arcs may remain owned by server threads.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/net_http_hosts.rs:245-281` (affected_location) — Handler closures retain a transmuted JIT function pointer and dereference the shared runtime during requests.

## process-pipeline-limits-ignored — JIT process pipelines ignore configured timeout and output limits

### Source

- A pipeline child hangs or emits unbounded output after the caller configures safety limits on its ProcessSpec.

### Closest control

- Each ProcessSpec can carry timeout_ms and output_limit.

### Sink or broken control

- run_pipeline neither polls timeouts nor checks output limits and uses the same unbounded drain_reader.

### Impact

- Indefinite hang or memory exhaustion of the JIT host despite configured process limits.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- The API contract should be confirmed to require per-spec limits in pipelines, but passing full ProcessSpec values strongly implies it.

### Preconditions

- A Jet program invokes process.pipeline
- A child is slow, nonterminating, or emits excessive output

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-jit/src/Process.rs:339-386` (affected_location) — Pipeline execution waits synchronously and drains unbounded output without reading any spec timeout/output_limit.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/Process.rs:400-419` (affected_location) — The public pipeline host passes configured ProcessSpecs into that implementation.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/Process.rs:440-456` (affected_location) — ProcessSpec exposes timeout and output limit controls that pipeline does not honor.

### Remediation subsumption

- Kept separate from late single-process output-limit enforcement because pipeline execution also ignores timeouts and uses a distinct run_pipeline path. Honor each ProcessSpec limit during pipeline execution. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.
