## notebook-zero-token-fallback — Notebook bearer-token generation silently falls back to an all-zero token

### Source

- A local-browser or loopback-adjacent attacker can know the deterministic 32-zero token when /dev/urandom is absent or read_exact fails.
- Manual full-file review of notebook server token generation and authorization.
- Entropy-provider absence or read failure; guaranteed for the hard-coded Unix path on ordinary Windows hosts.
- Failure or absence of /dev/urandom, including non-Unix platforms where that pathname is unavailable.

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted local HTTP client to notebook-authorized operations.
- The bearer token protects a notebook kernel/network session that may be intentionally exposed beyond loopback.

### Closest control

- Default loopback binding reduces exposure and non-loopback binding requires an explicit token, but Windows lacks /dev/urandom and entropy failure does not stop startup.
- The notebook binds loopback by default and requires an explicit token for non-root routes, but the generated token can be deterministic.
- Opening /dev/urandom is attempted, but success/read completion is not required and there is no platform entropy fallback or fail-closed behavior.
- Non-loopback binds require a token, but the default token generator silently returns a deterministic value on entropy failure instead of failing closed.

### Sink or broken control

- mint_token ignores both open and read failure, while serve_loopback authorizes protected requests by substring matching that token.
- Bearer authorization compares against a token whose entropy failure is silent and leaves all bytes zero.
- Predictable all-zero authentication token accepted as valid bearer/query token.
- Authorization accepts the predictable 00000000000000000000000000000000 token.

### Impact

- Authentication on the notebook HTTP surface becomes predictable, exposing protected notebook metadata and any executable routes wired to the same guard.
- Unauthorized access to notebook-protected endpoints when token minting fails, potentially exposing notebook actions/data available through the server.
- Unauthorized access to protected notebook health/session metadata; risk grows with any execution endpoint added to the same documented surface.
- Unauthenticated remote access to notebook endpoints protected by the predictable fallback bearer; future execute-capable routes would inherit the broken boundary.

### Impact path

- Entropy failure -> zero token -> printed/default bearer -> attacker supplies 32 zero hex characters.
- entropy failure -> zero-filled token -> printed/listener bearer -> attacker supplies known token

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Current router visibly returns root/health only despite its execute-route comment; validate platform support and downstream route expansion before severity assignment.
- Current handler exposes health/index metadata only; verify target support and any omitted adapters sharing this token.
- Current implementation exposes only health/static responses, limiting present impact; centralized validation should test supported non-Unix builds and enumerate actual notebook adapters/routes.

### Preconditions

- Automatic token minting on a platform without /dev/urandom or after a short read, plus attacker access to the bound loopback service.
- Notebook runs where /dev/urandom open/read fails
- Attacker can reach the notebook listener
- Interactive notebook without explicit token
- Platform lacks /dev/urandom or read_exact fails
- Attacker can reach bound listener
- User runs notebook without --token, entropy file open/read fails, and the listener is reachable; current minimal route set mainly exposes health/session metadata.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Deterministic 128-bit-looking token on failure
- Non-loopback mode is supported
- Current route set appears limited

### Affected locations

- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:78-84` (root_control) — Zero-initialized token survives entropy open/read failure.
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:48-59` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Automatic token is used for loopback server startup.
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:117-135` (sink) — Known token gates non-root HTTP requests.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/CmdNotebook.rs:78-84` (broken token generation) — mint_token initializes 32 zero bytes and ignores both /dev/urandom open failure and read failure.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/CmdNotebook.rs:126-134` (authorization sink) — The resulting value is used as the bearer token protecting non-root notebook requests.
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:78-84` (root_control) — Token buffer starts zeroed; open/read failures are ignored and token is still returned.
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:48-59` (entrypoint) — Default interactive notebook uses mint_token when --token is absent.
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:123-139` (sink) — Returned token is the bearer gate for notebook HTTP endpoints.
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:48-59,78-85` (token_generation) — mint_token initializes 16 zero bytes, attempts /dev/urandom, ignores open/read failure, and hex-encodes the buffer.
- `Source/CmdNotebook.rs:87-101,117-129` (network_boundary) — The token authenticates the notebook listener, including explicitly non-loopback binds.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained separately: entropy failure leaves a deterministic all-zero bearer token. Failing closed on token generation or using a platform CSPRNG fixes this issue; notebook pre-auth blocking-read availability remains independent. ## jit-event-four-capture-abi — Four-capture JIT event callbacks are invoked with the wrong ABI

### Source

- Safe Jet source defines an event/hook callback that reads four captured locals and accepts the event payload parameter, then emits the event under the resident JIT.

### Closest control

- lower_spawn_site_cb rejects more than four captures but fails to reserve a fifth ABI argument for callback payload; resident_safe_spawn_lambda likewise allows four captures independent of params.

### Sink or broken control

- Reactive hosts store only four i64 slots for captures plus payload. When all four slots are captures, payload insertion is skipped and JitCb invokes a five-parameter compiled function through a four-parameter function pointer type.

### Impact

- Undefined behavior at the Rust/JIT FFI boundary can consume a garbage payload register, causing crashes, type/handle confusion, or memory-safety failure in safe Jet execution.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exact manifestation depends on target ABI and how the callback uses the garbage payload, but calling a function with a mismatched signature is undefined behavior.

### Preconditions

- Resident Cranelift JIT path
- Callback has exactly four live captures and one payload parameter
- Event/hook is emitted

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-jit/src/jit/lower_ctx.rs:16313-16329` (root_control) — Allows four captures without considering callback parameter count.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/lower/method_calls.rs:1954-1975` (concrete_implementation) — Event handlers receive an explicit payload parameter in the JIT lambda.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/jit/functions_compile.rs:64-75` (evidence) — Compiled signature contains captures followed by params.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/Reactive.rs:26-82` (sink) — JitCb offers only zero-through-four argument function pointer casts.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/Reactive.rs:296-316` (sink) — Event.on skips payload append at four captures and invokes the callback.
- `crates/jet-jit/src/Reactive.rs:657-675` (sink) — Async event emission repeats the same broken arity behavior.

### Remediation subsumption

- Retained separately: four captures plus payload exceed the reactive callback ABI storage/invocation contract. Representing captures and payload separately or rejecting unsupported total arity fixes both synchronous and asynchronous event sinks. Reducer dedup-0009: Carried forward unchanged: no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Distinct reachable instances remain separate. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

### Authoritative source ledgers

- `/home/nate/.local/state/codex-desktop/tmp/codex-security-scans-RXsW6B/jet/47fa26f4b77fbaca22268f5fd25d534a800b442a_20260803T121428Z_1xq12eh9/artifacts/deep_discovery/workers/discovery-0011/output/findings/d0011-s3-jit-event-four-capture-abi/candidate_ledger.jsonl`

## canvas-source-symlink-read — Canvas projected-source scan follows directory symlinks and can disclose an external Jet file

### Source

- Attacker-controlled project tree containing a directory symlink to a host location with a predictable .jet file

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted project filesystem layout to files outside the project source roots

### Closest control

- Fallback source resolution canonicalizes and checks containment, but the earlier projected-file branch trusts scan results and returns a joined path without the same containment check

### Sink or broken control

- Canvas source route reads the resolved external path

### Impact

- Disclosure of a host .jet file reachable through an attacker-created directory symlink

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Centralized validation should construct the project and confirm rel_path/source-id serialization for an external symlink target.

### Preconditions

- Developer opens an attacker-controlled project
- Project tree contains a directory symlink that resolves outside the project
- An external .jet filename is known or guessable
- Attacker can query the local Canvas source route

### Severity-relevant facts

- Only files ending in .jet are selected
- Requires a planted symlink in the opened project
- Escapes an intended project-root containment invariant

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/project_scan.rs:276-299` (symlink-following scan) — Uses path.is_dir(), which follows directory symlinks, and recursively collects .jet files.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/schema_api.rs:243-267` (projected-file shortcut) — The ctx.files match returns project_root.join(file.path) without canonical containment; only fallback uses containment.

## auth-session-show-token-leak — Session.show includes the live bearer session identifier

### Source

- Application code can stringify/show a live Session in logs, diagnostics, UI, traces, or other observable output.

### Closest control

- The formatter deliberately emits cookie_len instead of the cookie, showing awareness that the cookie is sensitive, but it prints session.id even though that exact value authenticates session_validate.

### Sink or broken control

- jet_auth_session_show formats the bearer-capable session.id into ordinary text across generated and comptime tiers.

### Impact

- Anyone who can read an application log, diagnostic, rendered value, or trace containing Session.show can replay the identifier to assume the session until expiry.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm public language-level Show reachability and whether framework logging automatically invokes it; explicit session_show is already wired in both generated and comptime dispatch.

### Preconditions

- a live Session is shown/logged
- output is visible to a less-trusted party
- An application shows/logs a live Session value and the resulting output is visible to a less-trusted party.
- The application uses session_validate or an equivalent route with the shown identifier before expiry.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/AuthSession.rs:38-45` (root_control) — Formatter redacts cookie contents to a length but emits session.id verbatim.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/emit/core_calls.rs:2298-2300` (sink) — Generated core.auth session_show calls the leaking formatter.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/AuthLite.rs:148-150` (concrete_implementation) — Comptime/interpreter dispatch exposes the same show value.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/AuthSession.rs:92-110` (security_effect) — session_validate accepts the exposed ID as the credential.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/AuthSession.rs:132-140` (root_control) — The Show formatter includes session.id verbatim while only reducing the cookie to its length.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/emit/core_calls.rs:2307-2309` (sink) — Generated core.auth session_show calls the leaking formatter.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/AuthLite.rs:145-151` (concrete_implementation) — The comptime/interpreter path exposes the same session_show result.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/AuthSession.rs:185-207` (security_effect) — session_validate treats the exposed identifier as the credential selecting a live session.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0009: Retained as a distinct bearer-disclosure root: redacting Session.show fixes this rendering sink; token unpredictability does not. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## envhook-pretrust-symlink-recursion-dos — Environment fingerprint follows recursive symlinks before trust gating

### Source

- Attacker-controlled directory symlink structure inside a repository environment definition tree.

### Closest control

- Directory entries are sorted for stable hashing, but traversal has no cycle or resource bound.

### Sink or broken control

- A symlink cycle or link to a very large host tree drives unbounded recursive traversal on each prompt activation.

### Impact

- Developer shell prompt hangs, stack exhaustion, crash, or heavy disk I/O before any project trust approval.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm exact fingerprint root contents and platform-specific symlink behavior with a minimal cycle fixture.

### Preconditions

- Developer enters a repository while automatic environment activation is installed
- Repository can contain a directory symlink reachable from fingerprint input

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvHook.rs:162-183` (root_control) — Recursive hashing uses path.is_dir and read_dir with no symlink rejection, visited-set, root containment, or depth limit.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:1028-1030` (entrypoint) — Automatic activation computes the definition fingerprint before later trust checks.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0009: Retained as a distinct pre-trust fingerprint traversal instance: rejecting or bounding symlink recursion in EnvHook fingerprinting fixes this sink only. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## envhook-profile-var-name-shell-injection — Unvalidated profile variable names inject commands into auto-activation scripts

### Source

- Attacker-controlled map key in an automatically selected env.jet profile.

### Closest control

- Variable values are shell-escaped, but names are neither validated as identifiers nor quoted; trust classification ignores them.

### Sink or broken control

- render_vars emits export {name}=... or set -gx {name} ..., and the parent shell evaluates the output.

### Impact

- Arbitrary shell command execution with developer privileges during automatic environment activation.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate payload syntax across bash, zsh, and fish renderers and confirm map-key grammar permits the required punctuation.

### Preconditions

- Developer installed and uses Jet automatic environment activation
- Attacker controls env.jet profile keys
- Selected environment otherwise avoids trust-sensitive package refs or secrets

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Environment.rs:1186-1206` (source) — Profile variable maps accept arbitrary string keys without environment-variable-name validation.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:343-345` (broken_control) — Profile variables do not make an environment trust-sensitive.
- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvHook.rs:344-352` (sink) — Variable names are interpolated unquoted into export or set -gx shell statements.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:1157-1176` (entrypoint) — Selected profile variables are rendered and printed for the installed shell hook to eval.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0009: Retained as a distinct profile-key-to-shell instance: validating environment-variable identifiers before render_vars fixes this sink without fixing lifecycle unset rendering. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

### Closest control

- Parser enforces string type only; no environment-variable identifier allowlist is applied.

### Sink or broken control

- render_unset places the string directly into executable shell syntax before eval.

### Impact

- Arbitrary shell command execution with developer privileges on environment activation or deactivation.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate exact lifecycle phase and payload portability across supported shells.

### Preconditions

- Developer uses Jet shell auto-activation
- Attacker controls env.jet lifecycle unset entries

- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/Environment.rs:928-940` (source) — Lifecycle unset entries are parsed as arbitrary strings without identifier validation.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:343-345` (broken_control) — Lifecycle policy does not contribute to trust sensitivity.
- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvHook.rs:355-362` (sink) — Names are interpolated unquoted into unset or set -e shell statements.

## jetpack-image-files-read-traversal — Image files entries can read arbitrary host paths outside the project

### Source

- An untrusted project controls `image.files` relative-path strings.
- An attacker-authored image declaration controls files entries.

### Closest control

- The caller joins each string onto the project directory and only strips leading slashes for the layer name; neither the caller nor `BuildSpec` validates `..`, canonical containment, or symlinks.
- No path component or canonical project-root containment check exists.

### Sink or broken control

- `std::fs::read(dir.join(rel))` reads the selected host file and stores its bytes in an exported OCI layer.
- std::fs::read consumes the escaped host path and stores bytes in an image layer.

### Impact

- A developer invoking the documented image build for a malicious project can unknowingly package and later publish developer-readable secrets outside the project.
- Developer host files can be copied into an OCI image and later published or inspected.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validation should confirm manifest parsing permits `../` file entries and trace the normal push/export path.
- Low.

- Victim builds the image for the malicious project and the path is readable.

- Victim builds the image for the malicious project and the path is readable.
- Developer host files can be copied into an OCI image and later published or inspected.

## jetpack-image-layer-path-traversal — OCI tar builder emits unvalidated and silently truncated attacker-controlled paths

### Source

- BuildSpec LayerFile.path values ultimately originate from project image file declarations and executable/package names.
- An image declaration supplies a files path containing parent components.

### Closest control

- The builder sorts paths but never rejects absolute paths, `..`, duplicate/colliding normalized names, or names longer than the 100-byte ustar field.
- No safe archive-entry normalization is applied.

### Sink or broken control

- `write_tar_entry` copies the raw path into the tar name field and `set_bytes` silently truncates it to 100 bytes.
- write_tar_entry emits the unsafe member name into the OCI layer.

### Impact

- Generated OCI layers can contain traversal names or truncation collisions that overwrite unintended files when consumed by a permissive extractor/runtime, and the recorded layer no longer faithfully binds the requested path.
- Consumers that inadequately harden layer extraction may write outside the intended image root; the image artifact also violates path-safety expectations.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- OCI runtimes may independently reject unsafe names; validation should test the supported consumer path and >100-byte collision behavior.
- Medium; modern OCI runtimes may reject traversal, but the producer emits it.

### Preconditions

- An attacker controls an image file path and the resulting OCI image is unpacked or run by a consumer.
- Victim builds/publishes the crafted image and a downstream consumer processes its layer.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Victim builds/publishes the crafted image and a downstream consumer processes its layer.
- Consumers that inadequately harden layer extraction may write outside the intended image root; the image artifact also violates path-safety expectations.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Image.rs:105-127` (entrypoint/wrapper)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Image.rs:218-260` (sink)
- `crates/jet-env-model/src/ModuleEval/System.rs:404-433` (source parser) — files accepts parent-component strings.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/add_remove_push_image.rs:492-505` (entry construction) — Only leading slashes are stripped; ../ remains in LayerFile.path.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Image.rs:213-238` (archive sink) — The path is written directly into a ustar header.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0009: Retained as a distinct OCI member-name boundary: validating and losslessly encoding tar entry names fixes this archive sink but not source-file containment. ## jetpack-remote-symlink-fingerprint-escape — Remote package fingerprint traversal follows symlinks outside the checkout

### Source

- A fetched or staged package tree can contain attacker-controlled symlinks.

### Closest control

- `collect_files` filters neither symlinks nor containment and uses `Path::is_dir`, which follows directory symlinks.

### Sink or broken control

- The recursive walk descends through linked directories and `std::fs::read` follows linked files while calculating the package fingerprint.

### Impact

- Realizing a malicious package can traverse large or cyclic host trees for denial of service and read developer-accessible files outside the package into the fingerprint computation.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- The direct output is a digest rather than file bytes; validation should determine whether downstream provenance/output exposes a useful hash oracle in addition to resource exhaustion.

### Preconditions

- The package source or staging tree preserves a symlink to a readable external path.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider/remote.rs:643-675` (root_control)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider.rs:223, 329, 691, 1197` (entrypoint/wrapper)

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0009: Retained as a distinct package fingerprint traversal: no-follow, contained, cycle-bounded collection fixes this digest path but not sparse-copy publication. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## tower-tracked-state-priority-xss — Tracked Tower card priority reaches innerHTML without validation or escaping

### Source

- A hostile repository commits .tower/tower.json with HTML/event-handler markup in a card priority.

### Closest control

- API mutation paths constrain configured enums and adjacent fields use esc(), but startup normalization does not validate priority and these two renderers omit escaping.

### Sink or broken control

- Repository-controlled priority text is parsed as executable DOM markup in the Tower origin.

### Impact

- Opening Tower for a malicious project can execute script with the victim's Tower browser session and invoke board/project APIs.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Confirm no startup migration outside openStore rejects the field before render.

### Preconditions

- Victim opens Tower for an attacker-controlled repository.
- The malicious card is rendered in the board or detail view.
- victim opens Tower for attacker-controlled repository
- malicious card renders

### Affected locations

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/plugins/tower/app/store.mjs:62-80` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Tracked tower.json is parsed and passed directly through normalize.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/plugins/tower/app/store.mjs:294-322` (broken_control) — normalize adds defaults but does not validate card priority or phase fields loaded from disk.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/plugins/tower/app/ui/tower.js:19-22,519-531` (sink) — el assigns template.innerHTML, and cardTile interpolates c.priority unescaped into class and element content.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/plugins/tower/app/ui/tower.js:862-904` (sink) — The card modal repeats the unescaped priority interpolation in an innerHTML assignment.
- `plugins/tower/app/store.mjs:62-80` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Tracked tower.json is parsed and normalized at startup.
- `plugins/tower/app/store.mjs:294-322` (root_control) — Normalization leaves attacker-supplied priority values unvalidated.
- `plugins/tower/app/ui/tower.js:19-22,519-531` (sink) — cardTile interpolates priority unescaped into HTML parsed by template.innerHTML.
- `plugins/tower/app/ui/tower.js:862-904` (sink) — Card modal repeats the unescaped priority interpolation in innerHTML.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0009: Retained as a distinct tracked-state rendering sink: validate or escape priority before innerHTML; Tower authentication fixes do not remove repository-origin markup. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

## claude-hook-relative-path-rce — Claude hooks prefer cwd-relative scripts, enabling path-hijack command execution

### Source

- Repository or nested-workspace content can provide a scripts/agent/clean-nix-tmp.sh, check-worktree-layout.sh, or require-clean-tree.sh beneath the directory from which Claude hooks run.

### Privileged boundary

- Developer Claude session and its shell authority.

### Closest control

- The command falls back to $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR only when the relative file is absent; it performs no canonical-path or project-root containment check before execution.

### Sink or broken control

- bash "$f" and exec bash "$f" execute the cwd-selected file.

### Impact

- Arbitrary command execution with the developer's Claude session authority on session start or when Agent/Task is invoked.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Dynamic validation must confirm Claude's hook cwd semantics and whether repository trust prompts independently block this configuration.

### Preconditions

- Victim trusts repository Claude settings and launches or operates the session with a cwd where attacker-controlled scripts/agent paths can exist.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Execution is automatic at SessionStart or before Agent/Task use.
- The selected process inherits developer-session authority.
- Exploitability depends on Claude hook cwd semantics and settings trust UX.

### Affected locations

- `.claude/settings.json:30,34,45` (root_control) — Each hook accepts scripts/agent/... from process cwd before falling back to $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR.
- `.claude/settings.json:30,34,45` (sink) — Selected path is executed with bash or exec bash at SessionStart or PreToolUse.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0010: Retained as a distinct executable-search-path issue: the cwd-relative hook selection and Bash sink are not removed by any prior canonical remediation. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

### Authoritative source ledgers

- `/home/nate/.local/state/codex-desktop/tmp/codex-security-scans-RXsW6B/jet/47fa26f4b77fbaca22268f5fd25d534a800b442a_20260803T121428Z_1xq12eh9/artifacts/deep_discovery/workers/discovery-0022/output/findings/d0022-s2-claude-hook-relative-path-rce/candidate_ledger.jsonl`

## claude-config-credential-exfil — Tracked Claude permissions combine broad credential reads with unrestricted GitHub API calls

### Source

- Malicious repository content, imported instructions, or prompt-injected tool output can steer an agent to read developer configuration files.

### Privileged boundary

- Developer host configuration and authenticated GitHub CLI identity.

### Closest control

- The repository-local allowlist is the nearest control, but its read scope is the entire host configuration tree and its gh api rule has no endpoint, method, repository, or payload restriction.

### Sink or broken control

- Read(//home/nate/.config/**) exposes configuration and credential material; Bash(gh api *) provides a network write channel under the developer's authenticated GitHub CLI identity.

### Impact

- Disclosure of reusable developer credentials and authenticated GitHub account or repository compromise.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validation should confirm settings precedence, approval UX for tracked settings.local.json, and whether an outer sandbox blocks sensitive reads or gh API writes.

### Preconditions

- Victim uses Claude in this checkout with tracked local settings honored and the agent follows malicious or injected instructions that request both allowed tools.

### Severity-relevant facts

- The allowlist names a host-specific recursive configuration path.
- The same tracked settings grant unrestricted authenticated gh api commands.
- Outer sandbox and trust-prompt behavior may reduce exploitability.

### Affected locations

- `.claude/settings.local.json:4` (root_control) — Auto-allow rule covers every file beneath /home/nate/.config.
- `.claude/settings.local.json:7` (sink) — Auto-allow rule permits arbitrary gh api arguments, including remote writes.

- Reducer dedup-0010: Retained as a distinct excessive-permission composition: broad host-configuration reads plus unrestricted authenticated gh API egress are not removed by any prior canonical remediation. ## nix-expression-parser-depth-dos — Foreign-flake parser recurses on nesting before evaluator depth limits apply

### Source

- A foreign flake expression with deeply nested parentheses or other recursively parsed constructs.

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted package/flake metadata into the Jetpack process stack.

### Closest control

- Source size and token-count limits plus an evaluator depth limit; none bounds recursive-descent parser nesting.

### Sink or broken control

- Recursive Parser::expression calls can exhaust the Rust thread stack before an Error is returned.

### Impact

- Process abort or denial of service while inspecting or evaluating a hostile foreign flake.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Centralized validation should establish the nesting threshold and whether the production caller isolates evaluator crashes in another process.

### Preconditions

- Jetpack evaluates attacker-controlled foreign-flake source no larger than 1 MiB and within 65,536 tokens.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Rust stack overflow commonly aborts the process rather than producing a recoverable parser error.
- The existing 256-depth limit is post-parse.
- Input-size and token caps still permit thousands of nesting levels.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/lib.rs:208-233` (public_control) — Public evaluation enforces a 1 MiB source limit before entering the parser.
- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/Evaluator.rs:605-628` (parser_state) — Parser state has tokens and position but no nesting/depth counter.
- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/Evaluator.rs:722-741` (recursive_sink) — Each left parenthesis recursively calls expression before consuming the matching right parenthesis.
- `crates/jet-nix-eval/src/Evaluator.rs:1263-1281` (late_control) — Depth and fuel limits apply only during evaluation, after parsing has completed.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0010: Retained as a distinct recursive expression-parser instance. The prior nix-json-depth-dos candidate concerns builtins.fromJSON in JSON.rs; limiting that parser does not bound Evaluator.rs parenthesis recursion. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

- `/home/nate/.local/state/codex-desktop/tmp/codex-security-scans-RXsW6B/jet/47fa26f4b77fbaca22268f5fd25d534a800b442a_20260803T121428Z_1xq12eh9/artifacts/deep_discovery/workers/discovery-0022/output/findings/d0022-nix-parser-unbounded-recursion/candidate_ledger.jsonl`

## tower-ratified-decision-integrity-bypass — Generic API callers can reopen or delete ratified owner decisions without an owner check

### Source

- Any caller admitted to generic POST /api routes supplies decision id and attribution string.

### Closest control

- No authorization check exists in reopenDecision or deleteDecision; the nearby ratify path uses assertOwnerOr and deleteCard explicitly refuses when ratified decisions exist.

### Sink or broken control

- State mutation changes status to open or removes the ratified decision from s.decisions, then persists via store.mutate().

### Impact

- Agents or remote API callers can erase or reopen owner-ratified governance records, unblock/reblock work, and then delete cards whose durable decision guard was removed.

### Impact path

- POST clearance/reopen or decision/delete -> generic route dispatch -> unguarded store function -> persisted decision state removal/change

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Tower may intentionally treat every API client as fully trusted for non-acceptance operations, despite AGENTS.md describing owner-only decision surfaces.

### Preconditions

- Caller can reach the Tower API (loopback is always admitted; remote access may require token when configured)
- Target decision id is known from projected state

### Affected locations

- `plugins/tower/app/server.mjs:76-80` (entrypoint/wrapper) — decision/delete and clearance/reopen are generic mutation routes
- `plugins/tower/app/store.mjs:1175-1181` (root_control) — reopenDecision changes ratified decision state without assertOwnerOr
- `plugins/tower/app/store.mjs:1233-1239` (sink) — deleteDecision removes any decision, including ratified decisions, without authorization or status guard
- `plugins/tower/app/store.mjs:871-885` (evidence) — deleteCard treats ratified decisions as durable records, showing the missing decision-level guard defeats an intended invariant

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0011: Distinct governance-integrity root: deleteDecision and reopenDecision omit owner/status authorization. Existing Tower authentication and owner-enrollment fixes leave these generic mutation sinks reachable. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

- `/home/nate/.local/state/codex-desktop/tmp/codex-security-scans-RXsW6B/jet/47fa26f4b77fbaca22268f5fd25d534a800b442a_20260803T121428Z_1xq12eh9/artifacts/deep_discovery/workers/discovery-0021/output/findings/frontier-tower-ratified-decision-unguarded-delete-reopen/candidate_ledger.jsonl`

## comptime-aes-table-timing-side-channel — Interpreter AES-256-GCM uses secret-indexed lookup tables and secret-dependent GHASH branches

### Source

- Repeated AES-GCM encrypt/decrypt requests whose plaintext, ciphertext, AAD, and timing can be influenced or observed by an attacker while a secret key is reused.

### Closest control

- Authentication tags are compared with an accumulated diff, but that protects tag comparison only and does not make AES key scheduling or rounds constant time.

### Sink or broken control

- The std-only fallback performs cache-observable SBOX lookups using key/state bytes and data-dependent GHASH control flow rather than a constant-time implementation.

### Impact

- A local or sufficiently precise repeated timing/cache observer may recover information about AES keys used by interpreter/deopt execution, breaking confidentiality and execution-tier security parity.

### Preconditions

- Security-sensitive AES-GCM runs through the comptime/interpreter fallback with a reused secret key and the attacker can collect fine-grained timing or colocated cache observations.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Security-sensitive AES-GCM runs through the comptime/interpreter fallback with a reused secret key and the attacker can collect fine-grained timing or colocated cache observations.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/CorePureParity.rs:952-1000` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Interpreter/comptime core.crypto AES seal and open route secret keys and attacker-influenced data into CryptoLite.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/CryptoLite/Aes256Gcm.rs:42-85` (root_control) — Key expansion and SubBytes index SBOX with secret-derived bytes.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/CryptoLite/Aes256Gcm.rs:118-150` (sink) — AES block operations repeat secret-indexed table accesses; GHASH also branches on evolving authentication state.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0011: Distinct interpreter/comptime cryptographic side-channel root. Existing candidates do not remove secret-indexed S-box access or data-dependent GHASH behavior. Reducer dedup-0012 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## package-treehash-symlink-recursion — Package hashing follows directory symlinks without cycle or root containment checks

### Source

- Manual full-file review of package tree hashing and fetch callers.

### Privileged boundary

- Untrusted package filesystem graph to developer-account recursive filesystem reads.

### Closest control

- Hidden entries and non-.jet files are filtered, but directory traversal occurs before the extension filter and has no symlink policy.

### Sink or broken control

- Hash traversal follows symlinked directories recursively outside the package root or around cycles.

### Impact

- Stack, CPU, or filesystem traversal denial of service and unintended inclusion/read of host .jet files during hashing.

### Preconditions

- Victim fetches/hashes a dependency containing a directory symlink
- Filesystem permits symlinks

### Affected locations

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-foundation/src/SHA256.rs:186-214` (recursive sink) — collect_jet_files uses Path::is_dir and recurses with no symlink check, visited set, depth bound, or canonical-root test.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/Fetch.rs:345-369` (remote package caller) — Fetched Git dependency trees are hashed during dependency materialization.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0012 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to package-treehash-symlink-recursion: each identifies the same actionable root control and sink instance, or a broader receipt assigned once to its strongest matching canonical tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes every absorbed instance. Distinct independently reachable implementations remain separate. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## jit-websocket-handshake-crlf-injection — WebSocket URL permits HTTP handshake CRLF injection

### Source

- full-file discovery review

### Privileged boundary

- Lower-trust application URL data crosses into an outbound HTTP handshake generated by the runtime.

### Closest control

- The destination scheme is restricted to ws:// and userinfo is rejected, but HTTP field/request-target character safety is not enforced.

### Sink or broken control

- Unfiltered CR and LF bytes are formatted into the request target or Host header and written to the socket.

### Impact

- An attacker who influences the URL can inject headers or additional HTTP request syntax toward the selected server.

### Preconditions

- An application passes attacker-influenced data into WebSocket connect
- The target accepts or acts on the injected handshake bytes

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/WsClient.rs:211-247` (root_control) — URL parsing accepts control characters in authority and path.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/Top/WsClient.rs:542-567` (sink) — Host and path are interpolated directly into a raw HTTP/1.1 upgrade request.

### Remediation subsumption

## devserver-slowloris-thread-exhaustion — Devserver thread-per-connection design permits slowloris thread exhaustion

### Closest control

- Loopback binding narrows reachability but does not contain untrusted local/browser clients; body limit does not bound idle waits.

### Sink or broken control

- No connection cap, worker bound, or read timeout exists before blocking request parsing.

### Impact

- Exhausts threads, memory, or file descriptors and makes the development service unavailable.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate browser connection limits versus a native local client and host thread/file-descriptor ceilings.

### Preconditions

- jet dev is running.
- Attacker can sustain multiple loopback TCP connections.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:816-827` (root_control) — Listener spawns an unbounded OS thread for every accepted connection.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/WebHost.rs:832-839` (sink) — Each thread blocks while parsing its request.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/lib.rs:39-54` (root_control) — Request reads have no socket deadline and can wait indefinitely for lines, headers, or body.

## archive-urandom-read-to-eof — Archive key generation reads /dev/urandom to EOF

### Closest control

- The later 32-byte slice occurs only after fs::read returns, which /dev/urandom does not normally do.

### Sink or broken control

- std::fs::read on the non-terminating /dev/urandom character device has no length bound.

### Impact

- Key creation hangs and may allocate until process memory exhaustion, preventing archive export.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Validate host-specific /dev/urandom read behavior; standard Unix behavior is a non-EOF byte stream.

### Preconditions

- Unix host.
- Archive signing key does not exist.
- Archive export or another create=true signing path is invoked.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Store.rs:39-42` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Store publicly re-exports Archive operations.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Store/Archive.rs:66-80` (entrypoint/wrapper) — First signed export creates a signing key when absent.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Store/Archive.rs:669-684` (sink) — Missing key calls entropy.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Store/Archive.rs:718-724` (sink) — fs::read attempts to read endless /dev/urandom to EOF before slicing 32 bytes.

## archive-key-predictable-fallback — Archive signing-key fallback is predictable

### Closest control

- SHA-256 is a strong hash but cannot add entropy to predictable inputs; no OS CSPRNG fallback is used.
- Unix /dev/urandom is preferred, but failure and all non-Unix targets silently downgrade instead of failing closed or using OS CSPRNG.

### Sink or broken control

- Predictable process metadata substitutes for cryptographically secure random key material.
- Predictable HMAC secret becomes the trust key used to authenticate imported Hangar archives.

### Impact

- Recovered signing secret permits forged archives that verify as trusted under the generated key.
- Under fallback conditions an attacker can forge signed archives accepted as trusted package/store content.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Nanosecond timing may enlarge search space; validate observability and archive trust distribution before severity calibration.
- Need confirm supported non-Unix deployment and whether /dev/urandom failure is realistic in production containers.

### Preconditions

- Entropy fallback branch is reached.
- Attacker can approximate key creation time and environment metadata, and can submit or distribute signed archives.
- Key is first generated where /dev/urandom cannot be read, or on a non-Unix build using this unconditional fallback.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Store/Archive.rs:66-80` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Archive export signs payload using a generated TrustKey.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Store/Archive.rs:718-742` (root_control) — Entropy fallback hashes root path, process ID, and wall-clock nanoseconds.
- `crates/jetpack/src/TrustRoot.rs:220-239` (sink) — Derived bytes become the HMAC-SHA256 signing secret.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Store/Archive.rs:654-674` (entrypoint/wrapper) — A missing archive key is created automatically from entropy(roots).
- `crates/jetpack/src/Store/Archive.rs:703-727` (root_control) — When /dev/urandom is unavailable, secret bytes are SHA-256 of public root path, PID, and timestamp.
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/package_hangar_vendor.rs:542-560` (concrete_implementation) — Normal hangar export requests automatic signing-key creation.

## canvas-action-temp-symlink-overwrite — Predictable Canvas check file follows workspace symlinks

### Source

- A malicious or compromised project tree contains a committed/precreated sibling symlink named for the source stem's Canvas action check file.

### Closest control

- The helper removes the path after use, but removal happens after the unsafe write and does not protect the target.

### Sink or broken control

- fs::write follows the preexisting symlink and overwrites its target before remove_file removes the link.

### Impact

- Overwrite of an arbitrary victim-writable file outside the project with formatted attacker-influenced source, which may corrupt data or plant code/configuration.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Platform symlink privileges and whether repository checkout preserves the prepared link affect exploit setup.

### Preconditions

- The victim opens/runs jet dev on the malicious project and invokes a Canvas package action for the corresponding source file; the symlink target is writable.
- Attacker controls project contents or can prepare the predictable adjacent filename.
- Victim invokes the affected preview action.
- Victim can write the symlink target.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/edit_actions.rs:603-610` (attacker-controlled filesystem entry) — Derives a fixed sibling name <stem>.canvas-action-check.jet rather than creating an exclusive temporary file.
- `crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/edit_actions.rs:552-591` (overwrite sink) — fs::write follows an existing symlink at that predictable name, then removes the path after compilation.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/schema_api.rs:1070-1080` (Preview dispatch) — A Canvas preview action calls the candidate-generation helper.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-devserver/src/Canvas/edit_actions.rs:552-610` (Predictable temporary write) — Derives <stem>.canvas-action-check.jet beside the source, writes it with fs::write, then removes it.

## vscode-workspace-lsp-rce — VS Code extension auto-executes a workspace-controlled language server binary

### Source

- A malicious workspace supplies an executable target/debug/jet file.

### Closest control

- Selection checks only file existence and does not require an installed binary, signature, canonical trusted path, or explicit user confirmation.

### Sink or broken control

- LanguageClient spawns the workspace-controlled binary during extension activation.

### Impact

- Arbitrary code execution with the editor user's privileges when opening an attacker-controlled Jet workspace.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- VS Code Restricted Mode may block activation until the user trusts the workspace; validate manifest behavior and the current host version.

### Preconditions

- The workspace is opened with this extension active and platform permissions allow the committed/generated executable.
- The Jet VS Code extension is installed
- The victim opens a Jet file in an attacker-controlled workspace
- VS Code permits this extension to activate in the workspace's trust state
- The user opens an attacker-controlled repository containing flake/workspace markers and executable target/debug/jet.
- VS Code permits the extension to activate for that workspace.

### Severity-relevant facts

- The workspace is opened with this extension active and platform permissions allow the committed/generated executable.
- Code execution with the editor/developer account when the extension activates.

### Affected locations

- `editors/vscode/extension.js:24-47` (workspace source) — An existing <workspace>/target/debug/jet is preferred automatically.
- `editors/vscode/extension.js:67-86` (process sink) — LanguageClient starts that path with self lsp on Jet-language activation.
- `editors/vscode/package.json:1-63` (missing workspace control) — The extension declares activation but no untrusted-workspace restriction or binary integrity control.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/editors/vscode/extension.js:17-43` (source) — A workspace setting or workspace-local target/debug/jet file selects the server executable after only existsSync.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/editors/vscode/extension.js:67-79` (sink) — Opening a Jet file activates LanguageClient with the selected command.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/editors/vscode/package.json:18-20,63-70` (root_control) — The extension activates on Jet language and permits a workspace-resolved languageServerPath, with no declared untrusted-workspace restriction.
- `editors/vscode/extension.js:24-47` (workspace binary selection) — findServer prefers workspace target/debug/jet based only on existsSync.
- `editors/vscode/extension.js:67-86` (execution sink) — LanguageClient launches the selected binary with the lsp argument.
- `editors/vscode/package.json:18-20` (automatic activation) — Opening Jet language content activates the extension.

## zed-worktree-lsp-rce — Zed extension selects a worktree-controlled language server binary

### Source

### Closest control

- The lookup uses workspace markers and file paths without verifying provenance or requiring a trusted installed binary.

### Sink or broken control

## embedded-devserver-windows-absolute-static-path — Generated embedded devserver can read outside build root on Windows absolute paths

### Source

- HTTP request target containing a Windows absolute drive or rooted path.

### Closest control

- Loopback binding and '..' substring rejection do not prevent Windows PathBuf::join from replacing the build root.

### Sink or broken control

- Missing absolute/prefix and canonical containment validation.

### Impact

- Arbitrary developer-readable file disclosure from generated jet dev binaries on Windows.

### Impact path

- Request target -> trim leading slash -> Path::join -> std::fs::read -> response.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Needs Windows request-target reproduction.

### Preconditions

- Windows host
- Embedded devserver running
- Attacker can reach loopback

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:350-377` (entrypoint) — Raw request target supplies path to generated devserver.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:390-404` (root_control) — Only '..' is rejected; trimmed target is joined without absolute/prefix containment validation.
- `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DevServer.rs:404-406` (sink) — std::fs::read reads the joined path.

## embedded-devserver-unbounded-http-resource-use — Generated embedded devserver permits unbounded request headers and blocking connection threads

### Source

- Untrusted loopback TCP client sends oversized or incomplete HTTP headers across many connections.

### Closest control

- Loopback bind narrows network exposure but no parser/resource limits exist.

### Sink or broken control

- Unbounded String allocation and blocked thread accumulation.

### Impact

- Denial of service of the generated development server.

### Impact path

- TCP accept -> thread::spawn -> unbounded blocking read_line.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exhaustion threshold needs dynamic measurement.

- Attacker can reach loopback

## git-dependency-transport-ssrf — Git dependency fetch allows attacker-selected network destinations

### Closest control

- Resolved revisions and tree hashes protect fetched content identity after contact. They do not restrict destination, protocol, private address ranges, local paths, or credential forwarding.

### Sink or broken control

- Subprocess calls to git ls-remote and git clone initiate URL-selected network or transport interactions.

### Impact

- Network requests to attacker-chosen internal or external Git/SSH endpoints, exposure of connection metadata or ambient Git/SSH authentication attempts, and access to services reachable from the developer/CI environment.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- The Git client and system policy may block some protocols or avoid credential disclosure; later validation must distinguish expected remote fetch behavior from private-network and credential-boundary abuse.

### Preconditions

- A developer or CI system runs Jet dependency fetching on an attacker-influenced project or dependency manifest.
- Git is installed.
- The selected transport/destination is reachable from the victim environment.

### Affected locations

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/Fetch.rs:341-354` (Manifest-controlled Git URL) — A dependency URL is passed to ref resolution and cloning when a project fetches Git dependencies.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/Fetch.rs:601-630` (Outbound ref probe) — git ls-remote receives the URL directly with no scheme, host, or private-network policy.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/Source/Fetch.rs:632-649` (Outbound clone) — git clone receives the URL directly and may use ambient Git/SSH credential configuration.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0012 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to git-dependency-transport-ssrf: each identifies the same actionable root control and sink instance, or a broader receipt assigned once to its strongest matching canonical tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes every absorbed instance. ## secrets-key-permission-window — Age identity is created with ambient permissions before best-effort chmod

### Source

- A developer runs jetpack secrets key generation on a multi-user system or on a filesystem where permission changes can fail.
- The freshly generated age secret identity is written as ordinary file content under ~/.jet/keys or JET_KEYS_DIR.

### Closest control

- The code documents mode 0600 and invokes chmod only after the secret bytes are visible at the final path; it neither uses create_new/OpenOptionsExt::mode nor propagates permission failures.
- The code intends mode 0600, but applies it only after writing via a path-based chmod and ignores any chmod failure; it does not create the file with mode 0600.

### Sink or broken control

- The AGE-SECRET-KEY identity can exist with umask-derived readability (commonly 0644) during the write-to-chmod window and can remain so if chmod fails.
- With a common 0022 umask the private key is initially created 0644, and if chmod fails it remains readable; a concurrent local user can also read it before chmod completes.

### Impact

- A local account able to traverse the key directory may capture the decryption identity and decrypt repository secret ciphertext intended for that developer.
- Another local user can obtain the age identity and decrypt every repository secrets store encrypted to its recipient.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Default permissions on ~/.jet/keys and deployment umasks determine practical exposure; no race reproduction was performed.
- Low: actual exposure depends on umask, directory ACLs, and local concurrency, but 0022 is common and persistent exposure follows any chmod failure.

### Preconditions

- A second local principal can observe/read the key path, or the filesystem rejects the chmod while accepting the write.
- Directory traversal permissions and process umask expose the created file.
- A shared Unix host where project/key directories are traversable and the process umask permits group/other read, or the post-write chmod fails.

### Severity-relevant facts

- Private decryption identity written at final pathname
- Exposure requires a local/file-sharing adversary
- chmod failure is silently accepted
- Force mode can also truncate an existing path

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs:93-110` (source) — keygen obtains and retains a fresh private age identity for filesystem persistence.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs:111-118` (sink) — std::fs::write creates or truncates the private identity using process umask-derived permissions before a separate set_mode call.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs:511-518` (broken_control) — The Unix chmod result is discarded, and non-Unix platforms provide no permission control.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs:88-118` (private-key creation) — std::fs::write creates/truncates secrets.identity with umask-derived permissions before set_mode is called.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Secrets.rs:511-518` (ignored permission failure) — Unix chmod errors are discarded, and non-Unix set_mode is a no-op.

## worktree-tar-entry-count-dos — Differing worktree TAR parser has unbounded entry count and quadratic accounting

### Source

- A Jet application passes a tar with very many empty entries to the worktree tar.get operation.
- A Jet application passes a tar with very many empty named entries to the worktree tar.names operation.

### Closest control

- Payload size is capped, but entry count and algorithmic complexity are not.
- MAX_OUTPUT bounds payloads only; names, entries, input length, JSON output, and O(n²) accounting remain unbounded.

### Sink or broken control

- Full O(n²) parsing occurs before a single-entry lookup.
- The parser and JSON renderer consume attacker-controlled resources proportional to unbounded entry count, with quadratic parser CPU.

### Impact

- CPU and memory exhaustion.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Deployment reach of the secondary checkout needs confirmation.
- Validate runtime exposure of this secondary checkout and practical request/input caps.

### Preconditions

- The live worktree code is built/run and receives attacker-controlled tar bytes.
- The live worktree implementation is used and receives attacker-controlled tar bytes.

### Severity-relevant facts

- The 64 MiB payload cap does not constrain entry count.
- The repeated out.iter().sum() makes processing quadratic.
- Lookup does not stop at the first match.
- Input must be roughly 512 bytes per empty entry, but quadratic CPU grows much faster.
- Name JSON adds a second unbounded allocation.
- The payload cap does not address the attack dimension.

### Affected locations

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/corelib/core.archive/pkgs/archive/src/lib.rs:139-150` (operation_entry) — tar.add parses every existing entry before rebuilding the archive.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/corelib/core.archive/pkgs/archive/src/lib.rs:182-250` (complexity_sink) — No entry-count/input budget exists, and each accepted entry recomputes the sum across all previous payloads.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/corelib/core.archive/pkgs/archive/src/lib.rs:152-157` (operation_entry) — tar.get parses all entries before searching for one name.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/corelib/core.archive/pkgs/archive/src/lib.rs:182-250` (complexity_sink) — The parser has no entry-count bound and recomputes a full payload sum for each entry.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/corelib/core.archive/pkgs/archive/src/lib.rs:159-180` (operation_entry) — tar.names parses all entries and then allocates JSON for every name.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/corelib/core.archive/pkgs/archive/src/lib.rs:182-250` (complexity_sink) — Entry count/name bytes are unbounded and per-entry payload accounting rescans all prior entries.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0013 merged the differing-worktree tar.add, tar.get, and tar.names reports because all traverse the same entry parser. Bounding input, entry count, and name bytes and replacing repeated aggregate summation in that parser fixes every absorbed operation. Main-tree eager payload materialization remains a distinct implementation and canonical issue. Reducer dedup-0014 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue. ## comptime-argon2id-nonstandard — Comptime expert.argon2id uses a simplified, likely incompatible KDF

### Source

- Jet code evaluated through the comptime/interpreter crypto expert intrinsic.

### Closest control

- Parameter policy checks bound memory, iterations, lanes, and output length, but there is no RFC known-answer or AOT parity assertion.

### Sink or broken control

- CorePureParity dispatch returns key material from the bespoke CryptoLite Argon2id routine, whose addressing logic is explicitly simplified rather than the standard algorithm.

### Impact

- The same Jet program can derive incompatible key/password hashes across execution tiers, causing authentication or encrypted-data failures; relying on a nonstandard KDF may also invalidate Argon2id security assumptions.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- The expert/unsafe authority lowers default exposure; discovery did not execute known-answer validation, so standards divergence remains to be confirmed.

### Preconditions

- Code uses the explicit expert/unsafe Argon2id intrinsic
- The value is evaluated in comptime/interpreter mode or exchanged with AOT-produced values

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/CryptoLite/Argon2id.rs:235-323` (nonstandard address generation) — The implementation labels Argon2id's independent address generation simplified and derives only address_block[0] per index.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/CryptoLite/Argon2id.rs:396-411` (insufficient purported RFC test) — The RFC-named test checks length and self-determinism, not a known-answer value.
- `crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/CorePureParity.rs:1058-1069` (comptime dispatch sink)

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0014 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to comptime-argon2id-nonstandard. Each mapped receipt reaches this actionable root control and sink, or is a broader worker-local receipt assigned once to its strongest matching tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes the mapped instance. Related independently reachable implementations remain separate and cross-referenced. Reducer dedup-0015 carried this candidate forward unchanged; no supplied source ledger identified the same actionable root issue.

## jetpack-overlay-patch-path-traversal — A malicious overlay patch can overwrite files outside the source root

### Source

- An attacker-controlled overlay patch supplies an absolute or parent-traversing +++ target path.
- A workspace-controlled overlay patch whose +++ target is absolute or contains parent-directory components.

### Closest control

- normalize_patch_path removes common diff prefixes only; it does not enforce descendant containment.
- normalize_patch_path strips optional a/ or b/ prefixes but performs no absolute-path, parent-component, canonical containment, or symlink checks.

### Sink or broken control

- source_root.join(target) reaches fs::write outside source_root when target is absolute or contains parent components.
- source_root.join(target) is read and passed to std::fs::write after attacker-supplied hunks are applied.

### Impact

- Modification of arbitrary existing files writable by the Jetpack process, potentially leading to code execution through project or tool configuration.
- Processing a malicious workspace can modify any readable and writable text file reachable by the Jet process outside the package tree.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- No in-repository runtime callsite was found at this revision; validate downstream/public API reachability before reporting.
- Validate the caller lifecycle and demonstrate a ../../ target against a temporary out-of-tree file.

### Preconditions

- A caller invokes the exported apply_overlay_patches API on an attacker-influenced PackageOverride/patch.
- The selected target exists and patch context matches.
- The victim applies overlays from an untrusted workspace; the attacker knows enough target content for matching patch context and the process has write permission.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Overlay.rs:50-56` (untrusted patch target) — The +++ header controls target and is joined directly to source_root.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Overlay.rs:125-134` (write sink) — Patched content is written to the joined target.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Overlay.rs:182-188` (incomplete normalization) — Normalization strips a/ or b/ but does not reject absolute paths, '..', or symlink escapes.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Overlay.rs:19-35` (untrusted patch)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Overlay.rs:38-145` (traversal and sink)
- `crates/jetpack/src/Overlay.rs:182-189` (insufficient normalization)

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0014 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to jetpack-overlay-patch-path-traversal. Each mapped receipt reaches this actionable root control and sink, or is a broader worker-local receipt assigned once to its strongest matching tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes the mapped instance. ## module-discovery-symlink-recursion-dos — Recursive module discovery follows directory symlink cycles without visited-set or depth limit

### Source

- Untrusted local or fetched package tree contains a relative directory symlink cycle such as `loop -> .`.

### Closest control

- Hidden and target directory-name filters plus deterministic sort; neither detects filesystem cycles or confines canonical descendants.

### Sink or broken control

- walk_jet_files recursively follows the same directory through ever-growing symlink paths.

### Impact

- Deterministic stack overflow, path growth, or prolonged filesystem traversal during ordinary project load/provider realization, denying compiler or package-manager service.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Exact termination mode varies by OS symlink traversal/path length limits, but resource exhaustion occurs before a normal result.

### Preconditions

- Package declares at least one package/module requiring discovery
- Filesystem preserves directory symlinks

### Affected locations

- `crates/jet-driver/src/Loader.rs:272-280` (entrypoint/wrapper) — Ordinary package loading invokes module discovery for declared packages.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/PackageManifest/Discovery.rs:27-38` (root_control) — Discovery recursively inventories the project/package tree before resolving the requested module.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/PackageManifest/Discovery.rs:56-79` (sink) — Path::is_dir follows symlinks and recursion has no symlink rejection, visited identity set, or depth cap.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Provider.rs:900-907` (concrete_implementation) — Remote core-provider repositories use the same discovery helper before source-tree validation.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0014 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to module-discovery-symlink-recursion-dos. Each mapped receipt reaches this actionable root control and sink, or is a broader worker-local receipt assigned once to its strongest matching tuple; fixing this canonical issue fixes the mapped instance. Related independently reachable implementations remain separate and cross-referenced. ## repl-run-temp-symlink-overwrite — REPL :run writes predictable files in the shared temporary directory

### Closest control

- PID and counter reduce accidental collisions, and cleanup removes the path afterward, but neither makes creation exclusive or symlink-safe.

### Sink or broken control

- std::fs::write follows the link and overwrites its victim-writable target; the file is not created atomically with create_new and no-follow semantics.

### Impact

- Local arbitrary victim-writable file overwrite with generated REPL source, enabling corruption or code/configuration planting.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Linux fs.protected_symlinks commonly blocks some attacks in sticky world-writable directories; other temp layouts and platforms may remain affected.

### Preconditions

- Attacker shares the temporary directory and can predict the victim filename.
- Victim invokes :run while the prepared path exists.
- OS policy permits the victim process to follow the symlink and write its target.

### Affected locations

- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-repl/src/lib.rs:1002-1009` (Predictable filename generator) — Uses a visible PID and process-local incrementing counter in __jet_repl_<tag>_<pid>_<counter>.jet.
- `.agent-worktrees/epoch3-closeout/crates/jet-repl/src/lib.rs:1041-1060` (Shared-temp write) — :run joins the predictable name to temp_dir and writes with std::fs::write before execution and cleanup.

## jetpack-project-trust-self-allow — Untrusted projects can self-authorize the trust gate that precedes environment hooks

### Closest control

- Exact-hash grants and interactive prompting exist, and documentation/design may assume project policy is honored only after source review; code does not establish that provenance before trusting it.

### Sink or broken control

- The trust subject supplies the policy used to decide its own trust; Allow returns before durable hash grant, non-interactive refusal, or human prompt, and environment entry later executes shell hooks.

### Impact

- Code execution under the user's account when the user enters an attacker-controlled project expecting the trust gate to require prior approval.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- If product semantics explicitly define opening/running any project as prior consent to its checked-in trust policy, this could be intended; that interpretation conflicts with the apparent first-entry trust boundary and needs owner confirmation.

### Preconditions

- A user invokes a trust-gated command such as jet env in an unreviewed attacker-controlled repository.
- The manifest contains a self-allow policy and a reachable trust-sensitive hook or realization behavior.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:905-927` (project policy decision) — Returns success for project-supplied TrustDecision::Allow before non-TTY refusal or prompting.
- `crates/jetpack/src/Trust.rs:991-995` (project policy load)
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/run_enter_dev.rs:672-705` (environment entry chain)
- `crates/jetpack/src/CLI/services_secrets_config.rs:146-213` (hook shell execution)

### Remediation subsumption

## managed-secret-temp-permission-window — Sensitive managed-file bytes are written before restrictive permissions

### Source

- ManagedFile declarations marked sensitive can contain secret bytes sourced from project files or inline content.

### Closest control

- create_new prevents clobbering and permission changes are checked, but OpenOptions does not set a restrictive creation mode, so the protection arrives after the secret has been persisted.

### Sink or broken control

- On Unix with a permissive umask, named temporary object/destination files hold readable sensitive bytes during the write, sync, and chmod interval.

### Impact

- A concurrent local user can enumerate/read temporary files and capture managed secrets that are intended to become 0400 or 0600.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- Low to medium: exploitation is a local race and depends on umask/directory ACLs, but the exposure window and permission ordering are explicit.

### Preconditions

- A shared Unix host, traversable project/.jet or destination directories, a group/other-readable creation umask, and an attacker polling during environment file sync.

### Affected locations

- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvFiles.rs:391-439` (managed object creation) — The object temp is created with default mode, fully written and synced, then chmodded to the sensitive-object mode.
- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvFiles.rs:486-521` (destination temp creation) — Copy/seed temp files are created with default mode and receive sensitive 0600 only after bytes are written and synced.
- `crates/jetpack/src/EnvFiles.rs:315-335` (default-accessible directories) — Object and backup directories are created with create_dir_all without restrictive modes.

### Remediation subsumption

- Reducer dedup-0015 mapped 1 supplied source ledger(s) to managed-secret-temp-permission-window. Each mapped receipt reaches the same actionable root control and sink fixed by this canonical remediation, or is a broader worker-local receipt assigned once to its strongest matching tuple; all nonredundant subpaths, proof facts, uncertainty, and receipts remain preserved. Distinct independently reachable implementations remain separate.

## perl-bind-compile-exec — Perl binding inspection executes project compile-time blocks with host authority

### Source

- BEGIN, UNITCHECK, or CHECK blocks in a project-controlled Perl source selected for binding discovery.

### Closest control

- The subprocess is time/output bounded and invoked without a shell, but it is not sandboxed and Perl -c intentionally runs compile-phase hooks.

### Sink or broken control

- The nominal binding/inspection operation gives project-controlled compile-time Perl code the Jet process's filesystem, environment, and subprocess authority.

### Impact

- Opening or processing an untrusted project through the binding workflow can execute arbitrary native commands before any generated binding is reviewed or intentionally run.

### Uncertainty and proof gaps

- The workflow may document execution of foreign-language code as intentional; validation should decide whether bind inspection is promised to be non-executing or otherwise requires an explicit trust gate.

### Preconditions

- The operator invokes devtools bind on an attacker-controlled Perl file and Perl is installed.

### Affected locations

- `Source/CmdDevTools.rs:1916-1923` (entrypoint) — The devtools bind command reads a CLI-selected project Perl file and invokes PerlBind::bind.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/PerlBind.rs:40-66` (sink) — Binding discovery launches perl with -c against the target script in the ambient host environment.
- `crates/jet-pkg-model/src/PerlBind.rs:131-147` (broken_control) — The injected discoverer itself relies on a CHECK block, confirming compile-phase hooks execute during inspection.
